title: What Can Energy Become? Energy-to-Data and Energy-to-Material Pathways for Resource-rich Economies
affiliations: , University of Science and Technology of Oran Mohamed Boudiaf (USTO-MB), University of Science and Technology of Oran Mohamed Boudiaf (USTO-MB) and University of Sciences and Technology Houari Boumediene

detail.title: What Can Energy Become? Energy-to-Data and Energy-to-Material Pathways for Resource-rich Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants, animals, clinical materials or confidential personal data were involved in this scoping review and framework synthesis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Resource-rich economies are commonly assessed through what they possess: fuels, renewable resources, mineral deposits, land, ports or export corridors. This article starts from a prior policy and business question: what can energy become? It defines Energy-to-Value as the conversion of energy resources, electricity, heat, fuels and energy-related infrastructure into identifiable forms of economic, social, environmental, strategic and institutional value. The review distinguishes two primary frontiers. Energy-to-Data converts electricity and supporting infrastructure into non-material value, including computation, artificial-intelligence inference, data storage, cloud services and digital capability. Energy-to-Material converts energy, water, air, carbon, minerals and feedstocks into material value, including ammonia, fertilisers, desalinated and reused water, methanol, synthetic fuels, critical minerals, metals and industrial products. Using a transparent scoping-review protocol and framework synthesis, the article draws on international institutional sources, official policy materials, major project-facing reports and targeted academic literature while avoiding claims of exhaustive PRISMA coverage. It argues that fossil-based, renewable-based and hybrid routes are energy-source pathways rather than competing definitions of value. For resource-rich economies, Energy-to-Value may support value retention, lower avoidable system losses, diversification and more credible transition strategies, but only under conditions of infrastructure readiness, firm or firmed electricity, water planning and allocation, offtake, institutional coordination, skills, environmental safeguards and bankability. The article gives particular attention to failure modes, including electricity-intensive enclaves, water-burden transfer, fossil lock-in, limited domestic capability formation and quality-blind FDI. Algeria-related examples are used only as bounded, nonranking illustrations, not as country reviews or readiness judgements. The article contributes a decision category through which policymakers, public-finance institutions, infrastructure investors and business leaders can identify what counts as Energy-to-Value before deciding which pathways are feasible, credible or investable.

title: The Role of the SCM Marketplace Application in Supporting Material Procurement and Management in the Trade and Customer Management Sector of PT PLN (Persero) UID West Java
affiliations: Telkom University and

detail.title: The Role of the SCM Marketplace Application in Supporting Material Procurement and Management in the Trade and Customer Management Sector of PT PLN (Persero) UID West Java
detail.abstract: Advances in information technology have encouraged companies to implement digital systems to support the effectiveness of business processes, including procurement and material management. PT PLN (Persero) West Java Distribution Unit utilizes this application.Supply Chain Management (SCM) Marketplace is a system used to manage the material procurement process in an integrated manner. This application supports various activities, such as procurement monitoring, material requirements monitoring, contract management, and data integration with SAP systems. This article aims to explain the role of the SCM Marketplace application in supporting material procurement and management in the Commerce and Customer Management Division of PT PLN (Persero) West Java Distribution Unit. The preparation of the article was carried out through observation, documentation, and literature studies related to the business processes and information systems used. Based on the results of observations, the use of SCM Marketplace helps the material procurement process become more structured, facilitates monitoring of material availability in each unit, and accelerates access to the required information. In addition, integration with the SAP system also supports data accuracy and increases efficiency in material management. With the SCM Marketplace, the material procurement and management process can run more effectively so as to support smooth operations in the Commerce and Customer Management Division of PT PLN (Persero) West Java Distribution Unit.

title: A GenAI-assisted Privacy Gateway for Secure Third-party Data Processing

detail.title: A GenAI-assisted Privacy Gateway for Secure Third-party Data Processing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is currently employed by Wipro Limited, however, this work was undertaken independently in the author’s personal capacity and does not represent the views of Wipro Limited, its clients, or any affiliated organization. The author declares no personal or financial conflicts of interest that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work did not involve human participants, patient data, clinical procedures, or experiments requiring institutional ethics approval. The evaluation was conducted using prototype-based system testing and non-human sample data, therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding. The research, prototype development, and manuscript preparation were carried out independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Today, there is a diverse range of services available outside enterprise boundaries that can augment enterprise capabilities to fulfill business needs. These include infrastructure offerings (e.g., cloud platforms), domain-specific services (e.g., fraud detection), and specialized business workflows provided by third-party vendors (e.g., finance or recruitment services). However, using these services often requires sharing internal data with external processors, which raises significant privacy, compliance, and data-governance concerns. 

Organizations frequently handle sensitive data, including personally identifiable information (PII) and other confidential enterprise attributes, which cannot be freely transmitted to external systems due to regulatory frameworks, contractual obligations, and internal governance policies. Conventional anonymization techniques are primarily applied in one-way data publishing and do not adequately address controlled re-identification following external computation. In addition, rule-based PII detection methods often fail to identify contextual or implicit identifiers, particularly within unstructured text. 

This paper proposes a GenAI-assisted Privacy Gateway that enables secure, policy-driven data exchange between enterprises and external processing services. The architecture introduces a reversible transformation workflow in which sensitive values in outbound data are replaced with deterministic placeholders prior to external transmission, while inbound results can be selectively rehydrated using securely stored identifier mappings. This approach allows organizations to leverage external processing capabilities while ensuring that external systems operate only on transformed representations of sensitive data. 

The gateway combines rule-based detection with GenAI-assisted contextual analysis to identify sensitive information across heterogeneous enterprise datasets. Anonymization, mapping management, and rehydration remain deterministic and policy-driven. A dual-pipeline architecture supports both structured datasets and unstructured data flows, enabling consistent anonymization while preserving structural relationships required for meaningful external computation. 

The reference implementation was evaluated using synthetic structured and unstructured datasets containing 1,000, 5,000, and 20,000 records. For the evaluated workloads, the system achieved 100% placeholder restoration fidelity with zero unresolved placeholders, while LLM-assisted contextual detection accounted for the majority of anonymization processing time. These results demonstrate the feasibility of meaningful external computation on transformed data while maintaining deterministic round-trip restoration and architectural safeguards against direct exposure of sensitive information.

title:
The user side of AI Model Lifecycles: 
Evidence from the Keep4o Movement

detail.title:
The user side of AI Model Lifecycles: 
Evidence from the Keep4o Movement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
AI model lifecycles are commonly understood as a series of technical and organizational processes. Yet once a model enters sustained use, subsequent changes can also affect established user practices and user value. Using the Keep4o movement around GPT-4o as a case, this study examines post-deployment AI model lifecycle issues from the user side. We collected 61,846 public original posts on X from August 2025 to March 2026 and, using a systematically developed coding framework and LLM-assisted content analysis, analyzed discussion themes, users’ reasons for wanting to keep GPT-4o, and the specific claims they made.

Findings show that the Keep4o discussion extended well beyond continued access to the model itself. It covered concrete experiences of use, model behavioral characteristics and how they changed, and management issues across different stages of the model lifecycle. Reasons for keeping GPT-4o reflected interactional and relational value formed through long-term use, as well as judgments about the adequacy of replacement and the reasonableness of related decisions. The corresponding claims further reflected users’ specific expectations for model lifecycle arrangements and governance. Overall, the call to “keep GPT-4o” brought together different judgments about user value and governance concerns.

These findings suggest that technical version succession does not necessarily amount to effective replacement on the user side. Post-deployment AI model lifecycle management therefore needs to consider whether established user value can be carried forward and how model changes affect actual use. This study thus provides user-side empirical evidence for AI model lifecycle management. It further shows that user experience can provide important information for identifying post-deployment impacts and should be incorporated into lifecycle evaluation and decision-making.

title: Commercial Residual Control and Prudential Authority: Bank versus Platform Governance of Stablecoin Issuers
affiliations: Hanyang University

detail.title: Commercial Residual Control and Prudential Authority: Bank versus Platform Governance of Stablecoin Issuers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This theoretical study involved no human participants, animals, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A payment stablecoin is a digital token that promises a fixed value in a national currency. Its issuer must both keep that promise and make the token useful. Banks can safeguard reserves and redeem tokens; commerce platforms can build wallets, recruit merchants, and create payment services. Yet two important tasks—platform innovation and bank readiness for cyber incidents or financial stress—are hard to measure in advance. This paper uses a stylized formal model and a reproducible numerical illustration to ask who should control a company that issues one currency-backed stablecoin. Platform control encourages investment when the value the platform creates is neither fully portable nor fully captured under bank control. Bank control encourages safety effort unless contracts and economic exposure fully align the bank under platform control. Platform control is socially better only when its innovation benefit, after accounting for other governance costs that may favor either arrangement, outweighs greater-use risk, unsafe decisions, lost bank safety effort, and veto costs. Defined rights to stop unsafe decisions can help, but wider powers also add delay and invite misuse. Portability reduces dependence but need not favor platform control. When the threshold favors platform control, the proposed arrangement lets the platform direct commerce while banks provide contracted safety services; ring-fenced reserves and defined powers protect issuance, redemption, and recovery. South Korea's unresolved bank-consortium debate and rules abroad motivate the design; they do not test the model or establish an enacted ownership rule.

publicationDetails.detailsText: American Journal of Business Science Philosophy, volume 3, issue 1, 2026[10.70122/ajbsp.v3i1.8]

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital payment systems has transformed financial transactions in the Philippines, with mobile wallet platforms becoming central to everyday economic activities. This study examines the market dominance of GCash within the Philippine digital payment ecosystem using a secondary data analysis approach. Data were synthesized from official statistics, industry reports, and fintech market analyses to examine trends in digital payment adoption, mobile wallet usage, merchant integration, and market growth. Findings indicate an increase in digital payment adoption, with the share of digital retail payments rising from approximately 1% in 2013 to 57.4% in 2024. Concurrently, GCash experienced user expansion, growing from 20 million registered users in 2019 to more than 81 million in 2023, alongside a merchant network exceeding 2.5 million partners nationwide. Comparative analysis also shows that GCash maintains the most comprehensive service ecosystem among Philippine e-wallet platforms, contributing to its widespread adoption among consumers and small businesses. The results suggest that platform accessibility, trust, convenience, and network effects contribute to the platform's dominant position. This study provides empirical insight into the structural and behavioral factors shaping digital payment adoption in the Philippines and highlights the role of fintech platforms in supporting the country's expanding digital economy.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: AI agents can originate instructions that cross participant, ledger and settlement-system boundaries between accountable checks. This paper asks how a central securities depository (CSD) can connect evidence for those transitions without deciding customer assent, manufacturing cash finality or treating execution as a rights-effective transfer. Extending JFMI research on message-induced value changes, DLT coordination and legal finality, it develops an evidence-gated framework from a prospective public-document analysis of Korea's 2026-27 transition, contrasted with DTC, Project Agorá and Swiss designs. A proposed action precedes six states: participant-accepted, technically executed, rights-effective, securities-final, cash-final and exception or remedy. Without authoritative evidence for the next state, processing must not progress automatically. From February 2027, Korea's amended Act on Electronic Registration of Stocks and Bonds will preserve registration and issue-integrity controls while permitting specified account books to use a distributed ledger together with an electronically linked ledger. The paper assigns KSD only a conditional interface role and specifies matched simulation or pilot tests using state error, mismatch, detection and resolution time, false rejection, delay and asset reservation. It offers a pre-production decision protocol, not evidence that KSD centralization is superior.

detail.title: Towards Inclusive Governance: Blockchain in Citizen Representation

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency and was conducted as an independent Master's thesis at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Germany in 2024.

detail.abstract: Drawing on philosophical theories of justice, sociological critiques of surveillance and institutional trust, and political frameworks of polycentric governance, this study examines how blockchain technology can restructure public administration to foster inclusive citizen representation. By analyzing longitudinal datasets, including a decade of Democracy Radar Waves (DRW) surveys, the Global Corruption Barometer, OECD governance indicators, and Freedom House indices, alongside qualitative assessments of municipal smart city initiatives (such as Vienna’s public sector blockchain projects), this thesis investigates whether decentralized technologies can help strengthen inclusive governance paradigms. It seeks to bridge the gap between theoretical frameworks of decentralized ledger technology and the practical demands of contemporary democratic administration.

title: FLAP-X: A Dual-Leaf Attestation Protocol for Cross-Agent Regulatory Governance with Retrospective Cryptographic Verification

detail.title: FLAP-X: A Dual-Leaf Attestation Protocol for Cross-Agent Regulatory Governance with Retrospective Cryptographic Verification

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded - no funding received.

detail.abstract: Cryptographic verification presupposes determinism: a hash either matches or it does not, and a signature either holds or it fails. Agentic AI systems violate this precondition-identical inputs may produce different outputs, so there is no fixed expected value against which behaviour can be verified, and the naive application of cryptographic audit to AI fails at the first step. This paper takes a different route: separate what can be held invariant from what cannot. Credentials, delegation chains, prompt-template versions, access profiles, and controlexecution records are invariant by construction; model output is not. FLAP-X anchors the invariant set cryptographically and governs the variable residual with a calibrated tolerance, making non-deterministic multiagent systems retrospectively auditable. The dual-leaf attestation structure follows from this separation: Leaf 1 at the decision layer captures clause discharge, controls fired, and output hash; Leaf 2 at the workflow layer captures orchestration, delegation, and template version; the leaves are cross-linked and hash-bound to a principal chain rooted in a human agent owner. A four-check verification protocol operates across both surfaces. We parameterise a 15-condition test protocol in four parts-core verification (8), adversarial (3), governance lifecycle (3), and a comparative experiment (1) demonstrating two fault classes a single-surface record cannot handle: output substitution, which the single-surface record passes as a false negative, and surface attribution, which it cannot distinguish. We report honest negatives: adjacent-agent collusion producing mutually consistent false attestations passes verification, and a stolen signing key defeats signature checks; both are stated trust-boundary limitations addressed by the lifecycle layer, not the attestation layer. Effectiveness of the lifecycle controls at production scale remains future work; the author is actively seeking an empirical validation partnership.

title: Libby Care Dies Quietly

detail.title: Libby Care Dies Quietly

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract: The federal model for occupational disease care collapsed in Montana. Workers’ compensation inherits the wreckage. After a century of struggle, the United States had embarked on a new course for occupational medical care. That was written in good faith about a real statutory innovation. The innovation was sound. The delivery vehicle was a single nonprofit clinic in a town of three thousand people, funded by a renewable grant, exposed to hostile qui tam litigation by a party it had every reason to expect would be adverse, and dependent on an executive designation that has never been repeated. The more durable lesson is that occupational disease will not be solved one town at a time. The delivery of medical care to exposed workers belongs in a universal, non-litigious system coordinated with CMS, where entitlement does not depend on the employer, the chemical, the county, or the appropriations cycle.

title: How NFT Transaction Networks Structure Digital Market Participation: Ecosystem-Level Evidence from Ethereum and Polygon
affiliations: Telkom University, Telkom University and Telkom University

detail.title: How NFT Transaction Networks Structure Digital Market Participation: Ecosystem-Level Evidence from Ethereum and Polygon
detail.abstract: Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs) have emerged as a new organizational layer of digital exchange, raising questions about how participation, concentration, and community formation are structured within on-chain markets. Understanding whether these structures differ systematically across blockchain ecosystems with distinct asset orientations requires examining ecosystem-level interaction patterns. Most studies focus on specific collections or single platforms, offering limited insight into how connectivity, concentration, and community structure vary across markets with different NFT use cases. This study compares Ethereum and Polygon, two major NFT platforms with distinct dominant asset orientations (investment-oriented vs utility-oriented), to examine how their transaction networks differ at the ecosystem level. Using 3.9 million NFT transactions from May 2022 to May 2024, we apply network analysis to assess connectivity, centralization, community structure, and temporal dynamics. The findings show highly skewed interaction patterns in both ecosystems, with a small subset of addresses accounting for a disproportionate share of activity. Polygon networks exhibit higher modular segmentation and sharper upper-tail dominance, with communities aligning near-perfectly with application-specific boundaries, whereas Ethereum networks display comparatively more integrated, crosscollection interaction structure. These contrasts are interpreted as ecosystem-level structural patterns conditional on each chain's market composition and dominant NFT use cases, offering socio-technical insights into how participation concentrates and communities form across blockchain-based digital markets.

title: Customer Identity Resolution and Unification in Omnichannel Retail: A Descriptive Evidence Map

detail.title: Customer Identity Resolution and Unification in Omnichannel Retail: A Descriptive Evidence Map

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial or non-financial interests that could have influenced the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a literature-based descriptive evidence map using published scholarly sources and did not recruit human participants, collect identifiable private information, or involve animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Customer data quality and unification architecture concerns the systems and controls that make fragmented customer observations fit for trusted cross-channel use in omnichannel retail. Customer identity resolution is a central part of that architecture because records cannot be reliably unified when the identity object, identifiers, source conditions, or linkage evidence remain unclear. This study presents a descriptive evidence map of reported customer-identity conditions, matching and unification approaches, governance controls, and evidence characteristics. Two counted search routes were executed in OpenAlex and Dimensions Free for literature published from 2000 through the final formal-search date in August 2026. Four post-freeze exports contained 530 records; deterministic DOI/title deduplication and version adjudication produced 312 active title/abstract candidates. Full-text and source verification yielded a frozen formal corpus of 16 studies, comprising 12 Direct and 4 Contextual studies, from which 106 source-near evidence rows were extracted. Formal normalization produced 44 items and 148 raw-to-normalized mappings. Seven descriptive dimensions were then locked: source and identity fragmentation; customer-record quality and matching uncertainty; identity matching mechanisms; customer-profile unification and integration architecture; governance controls; evidence design and validation basis; and provenance, reproducibility, and reporting limitations. The contribution is integrative and methodological rather than algorithmic: it connects identity-resolution conditions and mechanisms with profile unification, governance, evidence design, and provenance in one source-traceable map. Supplemental Google Scholar/Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex sensitivity, and three bounded citation rounds were used as challenge routes and did not produce an out-of-structure finding. The map shows that reported retail customer-identity work spans both matching and profile-integration mechanisms, while governance and evidence-quality constraints materially shape what can be inferred from published claims. The evidence base is heterogeneous: the frozen layer contains Measured, Derived, Asserted, and Cited claims, but no post-threshold evidence row was classified as Measured. Findings are therefore bounded to the retrieved and eligible corpus. They do not establish field prevalence, literature exhaustiveness, causal relationships, comparative method superiority, or field-validated effectiveness.

title: Wealth Inequality, Financial Intermediation, and Institutional Risk in Albania
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Wealth Inequality, Financial Intermediation, and Institutional Risk in Albania
detail.abstract: This paper examines the development of wealth inequality in Albania through a macroeconomic, econometric, statistical, and political-economy framework. It treats wealth concentration neither as an automatic sign of productive success nor as sufficient evidence of institutional failure. Instead, it asks under what conditions concentrated wealth is transformed into domestic investment, productivity, employment, exports, tax capacity, social opportunity, and financial stability, and under what conditions it becomes associated with rent-seeking, restricted mobility, weak capital formation, and institutional exposure (Galor and Zeira 1993; Banerjee and Newman 1993; Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson 2005; North, Wallis, and Weingast 2009). The empirical benchmark is the World Inequality Database top 10 percent wealth share for adults under equal split, supported by bottom 50 percent wealth share, wealth Gini, and top 1 percent wealth share robustness indicators (Piketty, Saez, and Zucman 2018; World Inequality Database 2025, 2026). The macro-financial core uses World Bank and governance indicators, while the institutional-political economy layer uses descriptive Productive Concentration Score and Institutional Exposure Screen indicators (World Bank 2026; Hellman, Jones, and Kaufmann 2000; Shleifer and Vishny 1993). A compact UECM(p=2, q=2) is used as the preferred exploratory dynamic specification for the relationship between top wealth concentration and private credit, with ARDL retained as an appendix comparison (Pesaran, Shin, and Smith 2001). Companion evidence from a Bank Lending Channel paper is used to argue that private credit should not be interpreted mechanically as capital formation: in the Albanian case, credit may also reflect liquidity pressure, refinancing, debt-service stress, and balance-sheet repair (Bernanke and Blinder 1988; Bernanke and Gertler 1995; Kiyotaki and Moore 1997). The paper's central contribution is to frame Albania's wealth inequality not only as a distributional outcome, but as a test of the country's capacity to convert private accumulation, savings, and credit into broad-based economic development (Levine 2005; Beck, Demirguc-Kunt, and Levine 2007). All econometric results are interpreted as exploratory dynamic associations, not as legal findings or final causal proof (Granger 1969; Pesaran, Shin, and Smith 2001).

title:
The Sovereign Gateway Doctrine: Constitutional Control of Algorithmic Evolution in Public Power: 
A Doctrinal Framework for Algorithmic Sovereignty, Temporal Legitimacy, and Human Operational Control

detail.title:
The Sovereign Gateway Doctrine: Constitutional Control of Algorithmic Evolution in Public Power: 
A Doctrinal Framework for Algorithmic Sovereignty, Temporal Legitimacy, and Human Operational Control
detail.abstract:
Algorithmic governance creates a constitutional problem that cannot be resolved solely by regulating the
quality of algorithmic outputs or the speed with which those outputs acquire legal effect. A further
question is prior to both: who possesses the authority to change the computational rules by which public
power is exercised? The Sovereign Gateway Doctrine addresses this third dimension. It argues that where
a public authority relies on an algorithmic system to produce legally consequential decisions, the state
must retain effective control over the system's evolution, deployment substrate, update pathway, and
emergency isolation mechanisms. Algorithmic evolution is therefore treated as a matter of public-law
authority rather than as a purely contractual or technical issue.

The paper develops a three-vertex constitutional architecture: AEM addresses the substantive and risk
profile of the decision; Infrastructural Constitutional Timing addresses the temporal capacity of the
affected person to obtain explanation, contestation, and remedy; and the Sovereign Gateway Doctrine
addresses authority over changes to the algorithmic system itself. These three vertices are
supplemented—not replaced—by a cross-cutting operational safeguard for human officials.

The framework introduces K_trace (evolutionary traceability), K_veto (institutional veto effectiveness),
and K_iso (architectural isolation). K_iso is expanded to include logical isolation, substrate binding, and
an infrastructure-level veto. The paper also introduces Justified Operational Disagreement, K_sim
(Simulation Index), and K_trust (cross-border data trust). These mechanisms are deliberately limited to
public systems producing legally binding effects under conditions of substantial information, power, and
temporal asymmetry.

The Post Office Horizon scandal, SyRI, and Robodebt are used as doctrinal stress-tests rather than
empirical validation. The paper concludes with a legislative pathway for integrating the doctrine into
public-sector AI governance while preserving the anthropocentric character of public law.

title: Index-Demand Measurement under Float Scarcity: A Selection–Weighting–Absorption Architecture

detail.title: Index-Demand Measurement under Float Scarcity: A Selection–Weighting–Absorption Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This methodological and documentary study involves no human participants, patient data, personal data or animal research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Index inclusion changes provider-determined weights and can alter the target exposures of benchmark-linked portfolios. Measuring the resulting index-linked demand against the supply available to meet it is difficult when tradable supply is unusually limited. This note develops a six-position measurement architecture across three institutional domains: provider construction, tracker implementation and market absorption. It maps eligibility, selection or ranking, weighting transformations and final outputs for the Nasdaq-100 and Russell US methodologies, with the S&P 500 included as an institutional comparator only. The architecture distinguishes an observable or potentially observable final index weight, an estimated target-exposure benchmark and latent, implementation-dependent incremental demand. The position-by-position mappings imply that no single provider scalar represents all architectural positions within or across the three examined families. The note also distinguishes market-value D/F_t, which yields value per floating share, from a dimensionless shares-over-shares measure, which requires an explicit dated price conversion; effective tradable supply remains conceptually distinct and proxy-dependent. The SPCX institutional record is used only as a worked illustration. The architecture and measurement extensions are ex post relative to the provider announcements examined. No realised return, price path, abnormal return, volume or market-response outcome is analysed, and H4 remains unchanged and untested.

title: Digital Colonialism, AI, and the Cross-Border Migration of African Knowledge: Rethinking Intellectual Property Justice in the Global South

detail.title: Digital Colonialism, AI, and the Cross-Border Migration of African Knowledge: Rethinking Intellectual Property Justice in the Global South
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether existing intellectual property and data governance regimes adequately regulate the cross-border extraction and use of African knowledge in artificial intelligence (AI) systems. As generative AI technologies increasingly depend on large datasets collected across jurisdictions, African cultural expressions, legal materials, indigenous knowledge, languages, educational resources, and creative works are being incorporated into global AI infrastructures, often without meaningful consent, attribution, compensation, or equitable benefitsharing. The paper argues that current copyright and related intellectual property frameworks are insufficient to address the legal and structural inequalities created by transnational AI data practices, and it proposes a reform-oriented framework built on transparency, cross-border benefitsharing, recognition of collective knowledge interests, and equitable participation in AI governance.

title: What Does "7 Downloads" Mean? Metric Blindness and the Cold Start of Scholarly Attention After the SSRN Rankings Sunset

detail.title: What Does "7 Downloads" Mean? Metric Blindness and the Cold Start of Scholarly Attention After the SSRN Rankings Sunset

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author develops non-commercial multi-model orchestration systems for research (no product, pricing, or sales). The orchestration-layer design sketched in Section 8.10 is conceptual, and no diagnosis, result, or recommendation in the article depends on it. The author declares no competing financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable: this article reports no new empirical data and involves no human participants. The prospective human-subjects studies proposed in Section 8 would proceed only under prior IRB approval and informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: On 15 July 2026, the Social Science Research Network (SSRN) retired its public Rankings (the paper, author, and institutional league tables that had long supplied the platform's only widely accessible comparative frame) while download counts and citation statistics remained on individual papers and author profiles [144]. The result was an asymmetric measurement event: authors kept the numbers and lost the norm. SSRN's counters did not become meaningless; they became unreadable. Every download count became a number without a scale. This article argues that the question "What does 7 downloads mean?" is scientifically ill-posed until a paper's reference class is specified: a raw cumulative usage count cannot be interpreted without paper age, field, posting cohort, distribution exposure, and prior author visibility. The problem is most acute for new papers and low-visibility authors, whose early attention is shaped less by scholarly interest than by platform architecture, email-alert distribution, search indexing, author prestige, and the heavy-tailed dynamics of attention. We name this condition the cold start of scholarly attention. The available evidence shows why simple averages mislead. In the only recent large-sample study of an SSRN network (2,361 marketing working papers), mean downloads were 221.3 while the median was 87, the mean exceeding even the 75th percentile (206) [81]; download distributions are quasi-lognormal with extreme upper tails, and average downloads differ by roughly a factor of eight across subfields. Benchmarking a new paper against any platform-wide mean is therefore calibrating against a fiction of aggregation. A count such as 7 downloads from 40 abstract views is not, on the available conversion evidence, a sign of failure; it is a wide-interval screening result that must be read through reach, conversion, age, and field. From this we build an interpretation framework for post-rankings SSRN metrics. It separates exposure, abstract view, full-text download, and downstream use; introduces a reach-by-conversion diagnostic that distinguishes invisibility from rejection; proposes the Cold-Start Scholarly Attention Benchmark (CSAB) as a multidimensional alternative to a single vanity number; and offers a dossier protocol in which every reported metric carries its source, time window, reference class, and limitations. We then specify a preregistration-ready agenda for rebuilding the missing scale: a prospective panel of new SSRN papers observed from day 1 to day 180, quasi-experiments using curated email-alert distribution and the Rankings retirement itself, a community-built percentile benchmark, and an audit of preprint visibility in AI answer engines. The article reports no new empirical results; it specifies how the missing benchmark can be rebuilt, and why no download count should travel without its context.

title: DPACT: A Framework for Identity, Accountability, and Task-Scoped Authority in Autonomous AI Agent Systems

detail.title: DPACT: A Framework for Identity, Accountability, and Task-Scoped Authority in Autonomous AI Agent Systems
detail.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed as operational actors that read data, call tools, update systems, and communicate with users. Traditional identity and access management assumes that actors are either human users or deterministic service accounts. Agents violate this assumption: they act under delegated authority, compose actions at runtime, and may retain credentials beyond the task that justified them. This paper introduces DPACT, a five-dimensional framework for governing agent identity: Delegation, Policy, Audit, Context, and Time. DPACT provides a formal model of task-scoped authority, a taxonomy of identity failures, a maturity rubric, a reference architecture, an implementation profile, and an evaluation method for public incidents and representative agent patterns. The framework is mapped to deployable controls such as OAuth token exchange, capability tokens, policy decision points, short-lived workload identity, continuous authorization, structured audit logs, and revocation mechanisms. We apply DPACT to OpenClaw-style personal agents, the McHire AI hiring workflow incident, indirect prompt injection, multi-agent systems, autonomous coding agents, attended command-line coding assistants, and the Air Canada chatbot ruling. The analysis shows that agent trust is not a property of a model alone. It is an outcome of verifiable delegation, bounded policy, accountable audit evidence, contextual authorization, and time-limited authority.

title: What and Whom Does Short-Sale Regulation Affect? Evidence from 183 Policy Changes
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance

detail.title: What and Whom Does Short-Sale Regulation Affect? Evidence from 183 Policy Changes
detail.abstract: Financial regulators frequently restrict short selling without knowing how much activity they suppress or which traders they constrain. We study 183 tightenings and relaxations across 38 markets using global securities-lending data. Strikingly, most regulations have little effect on short selling. Even covered bans reduce shares on loan by only about 13%. Reexamining the 2008-2009 bans, we find that the widely cited spread increase is entirely driven by the United States and does not reverse when bans are lifted. Market effects instead depend on whose trading a rule constrains. Covered bans that exempt market makers reduce directional shorting but leave liquidity and market stability unchanged. Rules that primarily bind market makers worsen liquidity and stability while leaving shorting largely unchanged. Short-sale regulation therefore matters through the trading function it disrupts, not through its formal stringency.

title: One Frame, Many Rights: Mapping the Intellectual Property Architecture of Photography

detail.title: One Frame, Many Rights: Mapping the Intellectual Property Architecture of Photography
detail.abstract: A photograph is often treated, in both public discourse and casual legal commentary, as a single, undifferentiated object of ownership. This paper argues that a photograph is better understood as a site at which several distinct intellectual property (IP) regimes converge: copyright in the image itself, trademark where the image signals commercial source or goodwill, design where its visual elements are industrially applied to an article, patent in the imaging technology that produced it, geographical indication (GI) where it depicts a protected regional product, and traditional knowledge (TK) considerations where it captures cultural heritage. The paper further examines the distinct but related interests of the photographer and the photographic subject, and closes with an examination of how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is unsettling the human-centred assumptions on which photographic authorship has traditionally rested. Anchored in Indian statutory provisions and illustrated through decided cases-including Naruto v Slater on non-human authorship and Fairmount Hotels Pvt Ltd v Bhupender Singh on the misconception that visibility online amounts to public domain status-the paper develops a composite framework, described here as the photograph's IP 'X-ray', for identifying which of these regimes is engaged, and by whom, in a given photographic work. The paper concludes that the multiplicity of rights latent in a single image calls for greater public and professional literacy in distinguishing these overlapping but legally distinct claims.

title: The Continuity Threshold: Tipping Point Dynamics in the Degradation of Institutional Reasoning

detail.title: The Continuity Threshold: Tipping Point Dynamics in the Degradation of Institutional Reasoning
detail.abstract: Interpretive Entropy-the degradation of reasoning coherence in fragmented systems (Mayoh, 2026)-is a real, directional, and cumulative phenomenon. This paper extends that argument by proposing that fragmented systems do not degrade linearly. They may enter a self-reinforcing high-reconstruction regime in which reducing fragmentation is no longer sufficient, by itself, to restore the prior capacity for coherent accumulation. We call the transition into that regime the Continuity Threshold. Its economically consequential expression is a condition in which reconstruction cost grows faster than new value is created; this paper treats that crossover as a consequence that may occur at or beyond the transition rather than assuming that the two boundaries are necessarily identical. The paper draws on established tipping point theory, systems dynamics, and institutional economics-including direct empirical measurement of organisational knowledge depreciation and transfer, and a direct empirical test of early-warning-signal theory against real economic data-to establish the structural plausibility of this threshold, proposes observable indicators and diagnostics for its approach and possible crossing, and argues that-consistent with the navigational validity standard established in Paper 2-the threshold need not be precisely locatable to be practically significant. The case for hysteresis is supported by established critical-transition theory, an institutional account of asymmetric collapse and recovery, a formal AI model that explicitly produces a hysteresis gap, and empirical AI evidence of irreversible path-dependent degradation. A standalone companion piece adds independent phenomenological convergence, treated here as conceptual support rather than as an empirical evidentiary pillar.

title: Financial Development and Foreign Direct Investment: The Case of Middle East and North African (MENA) Developing Nations
affiliations: Institute of Management Studies, University of Peshawar

detail.title: Financial Development and Foreign Direct Investment: The Case of Middle East and North African (MENA) Developing Nations
detail.abstract: This research paper studies the likely effect of financial development on inward Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Middle East and North African (MENA) nations. Making use of yearly data for ten MENA developing countries from 1988 to 2015, the study finds significant positive influence of financial development on overseas investors' investment decision. The empirically established FDI determining factors such as market size, development level, trade liberalisation, macroeconomic stability, trade agreements, bilateral investment treaties and infrastructure & skilled labour availability, were also taken into consideration. Moreover, to sift purely the effect of financial development devoid of any time variant phenomenon equally affecting all the MENA nations I have also controlled for a time trend. Hence, it is expected that the results of the research shall be free of any omitted variable bias. Using various proxies for financial development through random effects panel estimation method the findings of the study suggests that financial development is a robust predictor of FDI inflows in the MENA region.

affiliations: and Independent

declarations.ethicsApproval: No interest relationship

keywords: Employment of Chinese female university graduates

detail.abstract: Millions of female university graduates in China face a severe shortage of standardized "two-day-office office jobs" each year, a structural mismatch that exacerbates employment pressure. Based on empirical data from the Anhui provincial civil service examination, this paper proposes a "dignity-defense-oriented reproductive decision-making model": Faced with the gap between high career expectations and reality, female university students, out of dignity defense and risk aversion to maternal punishment, prefer survival strategies such as "slow employment" and the "civil service exam craze" to marriage and childbearing, thus significantly suppressing the overall birth rate. To address this dilemma, it is recommended to reconstruct the university employment quality evaluation system and disciplinary structure, introduce national policies to reduce maternal punishment, and promote a shift in the macro-market towards women's self-indulgent consumption.

title: AI Adoption, Hospital Throughput, and Employment
affiliations: Brown University, RAND Corporation and Brown University

detail.title: AI Adoption, Hospital Throughput, and Employment
detail.abstract: We combine 2021-2024 data on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption across U.S. shortterm general hospitals with national measures of hospital finances, volume, employment, and measured quality. Using synthetic difference-indifferences , we find that AI adoption is followed by approximately 3% higher net patient revenue, 3% higher total paid hours, and 7% higher patient volume. Total and clinical expenses also rise. By contrast, estimates for administrative expenses, administrative hours, and employee full-time equivalents are imprecise under inference clustered at the hospital-system level. Measured risk-adjusted mortality declines for several conditions, but unadjusted mortality and claims-based clinical-process measures do not show corresponding improvements, while documented severity increases. The results therefore point most clearly to operational expansion, throughput, and richer documentation; they do not establish administrative cost savings, per-unit productivity gains, or lower underlying mortality.

title: Modelling the Transition towards Climate-Friendly Agriculture: A Simulation-Based Analysis
affiliations: Government of India - Department of Statistical Analysis and Computer Services

detail.title: Modelling the Transition towards Climate-Friendly Agriculture: A Simulation-Based Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a comprehensive framework to analyze sustainable transition finance in agriculture, beginning with a review of international efforts and modeling the transition using a partial equilibrium framework that incorporates firm dynamics and financing needs under different scenarios. Farmers face climate-induced productivity losses, prompting shifts to more sustainable crops that require upfront investments and cause temporary income declines, affecting loan affordability. While larger farmers can access formal credit, smaller ones depend heavily on government support. The model is then extended to a Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) framework, building on Jermann and Quadrini (2012), to capture forward-looking behavior, financial frictions, and the interactions among households, farmers, banks, and government in navigating climate shocks and policy responses. In this paper, calibration is based on empirical findings from the Making Agriculture Trade Sustainable (MATS) project, which promotes environmentally and socially sustainable agricultural trade. The MATS project provides valuable data by identifying trade policies, standards, and practices that support low-carbon, biodiversity-friendly farming while ensuring smallholder market access, thereby offering a robust basis for parameter selection in modeling sustainable agricultural transitions.

title: Market Incentives and the Obesity Economy: Fast-Food Density and Pharmaceutical Demand in Texas
affiliations: University of Houston and University of Houston

detail.title: Market Incentives and the Obesity Economy: Fast-Food Density and Pharmaceutical Demand in Texas
detail.abstract: Obesity is a leading driver of chronic disease and healthcare spending in the United States, yet little research has examined whether the local fast-food environment translates into greater demand for prescription medication. This study investigates the relationship between fast-food restaurant density and pharmaceutical demand across all 254 Texas counties from 2019 to 2023, using a panel of 1,270 county-year observations. Fast-food density is measured as the number of fast-food restaurants per 1,000 residents (USDA Food Environment Atlas), and pharmaceutical demand is proxied by the share of adults taking blood pressure medication (CDC PLACES). Pooled OLS, year fixed-effects, and county-and-year fixed-effects models are estimated, controlling for unemployment, income, education, age structure, rurality, food access, and physical inactivity. Fast-food density is positively and significantly associated with blood pressure medication use under pooled OLS and year fixed effects, but this relationship loses statistical significance once county fixed effects are added, indicating that cross-county differences, rather than within-county changes in fast-food access over time, drive the raw association. Unemployment remains a robust positive predictor of medication use across all specifications. Diagnostic checks (VIF, residual analysis) support the reliability of the estimates. The findings suggest that policies targeting fastfood availability alone are unlikely to meaningfully reduce pharmaceutical demand, and that broader economic and structural conditions deserve greater attention in efforts to address the health and financial burden of obesity.

title: Gaze-Regularized Low-Rank Adaptation of Swin Transformers for Dental Panoramic Lesion Detection: A Rigorously Controlled Negative Result
affiliations: Daffodil International University and Macquarie University

detail.title: Gaze-Regularized Low-Rank Adaptation of Swin Transformers for Dental Panoramic Lesion Detection: A Rigorously Controlled Negative Result
detail.abstract: Background/Objective: Panoramic dental radiographs are read under time pressure, and deep learning systems proposed to assist this task are typically opaque. Expert eye-tracking data, which is available for a small number of publicly released datasets, has been proposed as a training signal that could both improve detection and anchor model attention to clinically meaningful regions. We test this hypothesis for dental lesion detection using a rigorously controlled design rather than a single-arm accuracy claim. Methods: We adapt an ImageNet-pretrained Swin-Tiny transformer with rank-8 LoRA adapters and a convolutional spatial decoder in a two-phase protocol: domain pre-training on OralXrays-9 (12,688 images, no gaze), followed by gaze-regularized fine-tuning on the Tufts Dental Database (TDD, 1,000 images with paired expert eye-tracking heat maps). A Kullback-Leibler gaze regularizer aligns the model's final-stage self-attention to normalized expert gaze density. Four experimental arms Phase-1 transfer, gaze fine-tuning (λ = 0.05), a matched λ = 0 ablation, and an external ImageNet ResNet-50 baseline are compared under identical five-fold cross-validation on a 900-image development pool, a 100-image held-out test set, and the DENTEX corpus (1,005 labeled images) as an out-of-distribution probe. Faithfulness (area over the perturbation curve, AOPC), human alignment (normalized scanpath saliency, NSS; Pearson correlation, CC), and an adapted false-positive/false-negative error taxonomy are computed for the gaze and ablation arms and compared as paired differences. matched cross-validation, an external non-gaze baseline, out-of-distribution testing, and a faithfulness/error-taxonomy audit that we argue should be a minimum standard for future gaze-supervision claims in medical imaging.

title: Beyond the level of genuine saving: regime risk and the interpretation of sustainability
affiliations: University of Versailles Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines (UVSQ)

detail.title: Beyond the level of genuine saving: regime risk and the interpretation of sustainability
detail.abstract: Adjusted Net Saving (ANS) is among the few operational monetary indicators of macroeconomic sustainability, yet it is usually read as a yearly level and criticized for incomplete natural-capital coverage. We ask what the same accounts reveal when read as a regime: whether measured comprehensive wealth is rising or falling, for how long, and through which transitions. Using 133 countries over 1996–2021, we contrast ANS levels with deficit incidence, duration and transitions. The distinction changes the empirical picture. Macroeconomic fundamentals, notably investment and income, are associated with both higher ANS levels and lower deficit risk. By contrast, structural conditions largely silent in level regressions emerge in regime dynamics: better institutions and trade openness reduce deficit risk, with human capital less consistently so. Resource dependence is weakly related to levels but more clearly linked to deficit entry and persistence. Negative ANS remains state dependent after accounting for initial conditions and country heterogeneity; annual exit probability falls from about 29\% in the first observed deficit year to 13\% by the tenth. Biodiversity, unpriced by ANS, is associated within countries with higher ANS and lower deficit incidence. Yet among deficit countries, greater biodiversity is cross-sectionally associated with longer spells but not within-country recovery, an apparent paradox between ecological endowments and recovery dynamics explored in the paper. ANS thus contains information its conventional level reading obscures. Read as a direction of travel rather than a sustainability score, it connects an operational weak-sustainability indicator to institutional and ecological conditions central to strong-sustainability concerns.

title: The Feasibility of Sustainable Dietary Transitions in Developing Countries under Nutritional, Environmental, and Acceptability Constraints
affiliations: Waseda University

detail.title: The Feasibility of Sustainable Dietary Transitions in Developing Countries under Nutritional, Environmental, and Acceptability Constraints
detail.abstract: Sustainable dietary transitions are widely promoted as a strategy to reduce the environmental impacts of food systems. However, most global assessments estimate the environmental benefits of dietary change under the implicit assumption that sustainable diets are broadly feasible across populations. This assumption overlooks substantial heterogeneity in income, existing consumption patterns, and dietary preferences, particularly in developing countries. This study quantifies the feasibility of sustainable dietary transitions by jointly considering nutritional, environmental, and acceptability constraints. We develop a global optimization framework integrating detailed food consumption data for 91 developing countries, disaggregated into four income groups, with consumption-based environmental footprints derived from the FABIO multiregional input–output database. Rather than identifying environmentally optimal diets alone, the framework evaluates whether sustainable dietary transitions are simultaneously achievable for each country–income group.,Results reveal substantial heterogeneity in transition feasibility. Feasible dietary transitions exist for approximately 71.7% of the population covered by the analysis (3.77 billion people), while universal feasibility is rare. Lower-income groups generally require increases and diversification of food consumption to satisfy nutritional requirements, whereas higher-income groups require larger reductions and broader dietary reallocation to satisfy environmental constraints. Even where transitions are feasible, optimized diets require substantial restructuring, with 35–50% of total food intake reallocated on average. These findings demonstrate that the environmental potential of dietary change is constrained by socioeconomic and behavioural feasibility. Rather than supporting uniform global dietary targets, the results highlight the need for differentiated transition pathways that reflect heterogeneous constraints across populations.

title: Pesticide Residues in Vegetables from Accra Markets: Occurrence, MRL Compliance, and Exploratory Health Risk Assessment of Organochlorines and Synthetic Pyrethroids
affiliations: Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, Ghana Standards Authority, Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR)-Ghana - Food Research Institute, Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Environment and Sustainable Development, Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, Ghana Atomic Energy Commission and Accra Technical University

detail.title: Pesticide Residues in Vegetables from Accra Markets: Occurrence, MRL Compliance, and Exploratory Health Risk Assessment of Organochlorines and Synthetic Pyrethroids
detail.abstract: Pesticide contamination of fresh vegetables poses major food safety risks in low- and middle-income countries with limited regulatory enforcement. This exploratory surveillance study evaluated 24 pesticide compounds (15 organochlorines [OCPs] and 9 synthetic pyrethroids [SPs]) in carrot, cauliflower, beetroot, and lettuce from four Accra markets. Sixty-four composite samples were analyzed using GC-MS. Residues were detected in all samples, with OCPs accounting for 62.5% of the 18 detected compounds. Critical Maximum Residue Limit exceedances occurred for dieldrin (33.0×), β-HCH (10.3×), bifenthrin (8.83×), and δ-HCH (8.5×). Under adult exposure scenarios (61.3 kg body weight, 0.187 kg/day consumption), β-HCH (HQ = 3.14), δ-HCH (HQ = 2.59), and dieldrin (HQ = 1.01) yielded hazard quotients ≥1.0, with β-HCH showing consistent concern across all markets (HQ: 1.07–1.53). Class-specific cumulative hazard indices exceeded 1.0 in most combinations. Worst-case paediatric scenarios (20 kg, 0.35 kg/day) produced upper-bound HQs reaching 5.78 for dieldrin (5.3-fold increase). Principal component analysis revealed OCP-dominated (42.1%) and SP-dominated (26.3%) components, with hierarchical clustering identifying vegetable type as the primary determinant of residue profiles. These findings underscore the persistence of banned OCPs in Ghana's food supply and highlight urgent needs for enhanced monitoring, enforcement, and farmer education. Given the exploratory design (n = 4 per combination; power ≈ 42%), validation through larger surveillance programmes is essential.

title: Adherence Determinants and Intervention Priorities for Non-pharmaceutical Interventions Against Respiratory Infectious Diseases: A Modelling Study Using Real-world Survey Data

detail.title: Adherence Determinants and Intervention Priorities for Non-pharmaceutical Interventions Against Respiratory Infectious Diseases: A Modelling Study Using Real-world Survey Data

detail.abstract:
Background: Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) remain important strategies for reducing respiratory infectious disease transmission, particularly when vaccines or effective therapeutics are unavailable or insufficient. We aimed to compare willingness and adherence across six major NPIs, identify behavioural factors associated with adherence, and evaluate potential intervention priorities.

Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we analysed data from 10,065 participants in mainland China collected between December 2024 and February 2025 to assess adherence to six NPIs, including mask-wearing, respiratory etiquette, handwashing, avoiding gatherings, social distancing, and self-isolation. An integrated theory of planned behaviour framework, structural equation modelling, multinomial regression, and Bayesian network simulations were used to identify behavioural determinants and estimate potential intervention gains.

Findings: Mean willingness to adopt the six NPIs was consistently high (4.19–4.40 on a five-point scale), whereas reported adherence was substantially lower. Mask-wearing (39.47%), respiratory etiquette (20.66%), and handwashing (19.37%) showed the highest adherence, whereas the remaining three NPIs showed substantially lower adherence (6.11–11.02%). Although adherence differed substantially, the underlying behavioural determinants were broadly consistent. Attitudinal factors were the most consistent predictors across behaviours, whereas perceived barriers exerted the strongest constraining effect among both high-willingness (relative risk ratio 0.66–0.80; all P≤0.01) and low-willingness non-adherers (relative risk ratio 0.19–0.34; all P≤0.01). Bayesian network simulations indicated that targeting modifiable behavioural factors could produce the largest modelled gains in adherence for mask-wearing (+7.9%; 95% CI, 6.1–8.6%), handwashing (+5.5%; 95% CI, 5.1–7.2%), and respiratory etiquette (+5.2%; 95% CI, 4.7–6.4%).

Interpretation: A substantial willingness–adherence gap exists across NPIs. Perceived barriers were the most consistent factor associated with non-adherence. Improving NPI adherence may require not only effective communication but also practical support and enabling environments that help translate willingness into action.

title: Food Security Outcomes and Their Drivers among Participating and Non-Participating Households in Integrated Rice–Fish Farming Systems in Nigeria
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Ibadan, University of Ibadan and University of Ibadan

detail.title: Food Security Outcomes and Their Drivers among Participating and Non-Participating Households in Integrated Rice–Fish Farming Systems in Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study examines household food security outcomes and their drivers among farmers participating in integrated rice–fish farming systems and those not participating in Nigeria. Data were collected from 458 rural households (178 participants and 280 non-participants) across Ebonyi and Kebbi States using a multistage sampling approach. Food security status was assessed using the Foster–Greer–Thorbecke (FGT) food insecurity indices, and an ordered probit model was used to identify key determinants of food security. Results show that participating households had lower incidences (41.6%), depths (13.9%), and severities (7.0%) of food insecurity than non-participating households (44.1%, 16.3%, and 7.9%, respectively). Participation was associated with higher food expenditure thresholds, reflecting improved dietary quality and welfare. Access to credit, extension services, agricultural training, cooperative membership, household size, age, and mobile phone ownership significantly influenced food security outcomes. Despite persistent food insecurity across both groups, integrated rice–fish farming contributed to improved resilience and reduced vulnerability. The findings underscore the potential of integrated rice–fish systems as a sustainable pathway to enhance household food security and inform policies to scale up adoption across diverse agro-ecological settings in Nigeria.

detail.abstract: In sub-Saharan Africa, traditional biomass cooking imposes substantial health and time costs on women, yet the role of women's bargaining power in cleaner-fuel adoption remains unclear. Using three waves of the Ghana Demographic and Health Survey (2008-2022), we estimate the effect of women's bargaining power on households' choices among biomass, transitional, and modern clean fuels. To address endogeneity, we instrument a household decision-making index with wives' attitudes toward intimate partner violence. We find that greater bargaining power shifts households toward cleaner cooking fuels-primarily from firewood to charcoal among poorer households and from firewood to LPG among wealthier households. These findings suggest that women's bargaining power is an important factor to consider alongside policies that expand access to clean cooking fuels.

title: Should We Biopsy or Survey an Irregular Z-line? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of 33,000 Patients

detail.abstract:
Background: Guidelines advise against biopsy or surveillance of an irregular Z-line or columnar-lined esophagus less than 1 cm (CLE <1 cm), but its neoplastic risk relative to Barrett’s esophagus (BE) ≥1 cm remains unquantified.

Methods: PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library were searched from January 2000 to November 2025 for studies reporting dysplasia or esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) by segment length in adults with biopsy-confirmed intestinal metaplasia (IM). Annual progression rates, cumulative risks and random-effects relative risks (RRs) were calculated, with a further analysis restricted to incident cases detected after the index diagnostic endoscopy. Two investigators independently extracted summary data from published reports and assessed quality with an adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.

Findings: Of 1,395 records identified, 27 studies (16,731 patients with CLE <1 cm and 16,590 with BE ≥1 cm) were eligible; 11 compared both segments. Incident high-grade dysplasia (HGD) or EAC occurred in 0.13% (15/11,802) with CLE <1 cm and 3.31% (475/14,344) with BE ≥1 cm (pooled RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.05–0.43), one case per 787 patients surveyed versus 30, a 26-fold difference, with 97% of incident neoplasia in BE ≥1 cm. Including prevalent cases, risks were 1.08% and 5.29% (RR 0.46, 0.31–0.69). Annual progression in matched cohorts was 0.011 versus 0.559 per 100 person-years (IRR 0.131, 0.042–0.408); for EAC alone, 0.007 versus 0.197 (IRR 0.159, 0.063–0.399), against 0.004 in the general population.

Interpretation: Although irregular Z-lines are routinely biopsied and confirmed IM prompts surveillance, progression to HGD or EAC occurred at only 0.011% per year, and to EAC alone at a rate within twofold of the general population. Routine biopsy and surveillance are not warranted and should be reserved for an endoscopically abnormal or previously dysplastic Z-line.

title: Interest Rates and Consumer Financing in Pakistan: What Monthly Bank Data Tell Us, 2019-2026

detail.title: Interest Rates and Consumer Financing in Pakistan: What Monthly Bank Data Tell Us, 2019-2026

detail.abstract: This paper studies the relationship between interest rates and consumer borrowing in Pakistan. It uses monthly data from the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) from June 2019 to May 2026. The data cover five types of consumer finance: housing, car finance, credit cards, consumer durables, and personal loans. Over this period, the SBP first cut interest rates during COVID-19, then raised them sharply between 2021 and 2023, and later reduced them again. The five types of finance did not react in the same way. Car finance and personal loans grew more slowly when rates were high. Housing reacted more gradually. Credit-card balances continued to grow. The relationship was often strongest after a delay of several months. However, the paper does not claim that interest rates were the only cause. Inflation, banking rules, car-import restrictions, and changes in household demand also mattered. The main lesson is simple: the total amount of consumer finance can hide important differences between its parts.
