declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding and was conducted as part of the author's Pre-Master Finance/Financial Management program at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance and corporate capital structure in listed Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) firms, as well as whether government ownership moderates this relationship. Using an unbalanced panel of 138 non-financial firms (484-552 observations) from the seven MENA countries between 2022 and 2025, the study employs firm fixed-effect regressions of book leverage and debt-to- equity ratios based on ESG scores, government ownership, and the interaction of these two variables. Findings reveal no relationship between ESG scores and book leverage but do find that within-firm ESG performance has a negative association with debt-to-equity ratio; this relationship is statistically significant only at the 10% level. Random effects analysis finds that firms with government ownership have significantly lower leverage; however, the interaction between government ownership and ESG score is statistically indistinguishable from zero across all model specifications. Overall, it is concluded that ESG performance and government ownership are independent rather than interacting influences on firms' financing decisions. Thus, capital structure formation in MENA's state-capitalist economies supports a coexistence model rather than a transformation or entrenchment model.

title: Pricing European Options under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic Volatility Frameworks: An Application of Alan Lewis's (2001) Fourier-Transform Approach to the Merton Model
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Pricing European Options under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic Volatility Frameworks: An Application of Alan Lewis's (2001) Fourier-Transform Approach to the Merton Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or sensitive data. Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was conducted independently as part of the MSc Financial Engineering program at WorldQuant University.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the pricing of European options under advanced nonGaussian asset dynamics, focusing on the Merton jump-diffusion model within the context of Alan Lewis’s (2001) Fourier-transform framework. While standard BlackScholes assumptions fail to capture empirical anomalies such as the volatility smile and heavy tails, jump-diffusion and stochastic volatility frameworks (such as Heston and Merton models) provide the necessary mathematical flexibility. We review the analytical derivation of the log-price characteristic function, address numerical integration nuances including direct complex contour versus Gil-Pelaez risk-neutral probability representations, and apply the framework to a controlled parameter set. Using a specific benchmark configuration, we evaluate the resulting European call option price and discuss the implications of Fourier inversion techniques in financial engineering. The practical relevance of this work lies in the growing demand for models that reconcile theoretical tractability with empirical realism. In markets characterized by sudden news events, liquidity shocks, and regime shifts, asset returns frequently deviate from normality. Standard diffusion models underestimate tail risk and misprice deep out-of-the-money options. By embedding jumps and allowing for richer distributional properties through Fourier methods, practitioners can achieve more accurate hedging and risk management, particularly for portfolios exposed to event risk.

title: Renewable Curtailment and Grid Integration: Evidence from Vietnam's Solar Boom and Lessons for Malaysia

detail.title: Renewable Curtailment and Grid Integration: Evidence from Vietnam's Solar Boom and Lessons for Malaysia
detail.abstract: Rapid solar deployment can outpace grid capacity, forcing curtailment of clean generation. This paper is a structured comparative case study that sets Vietnam's realized 20182021 solar boom, during which installed capacity grew by roughly two orders of magnitude in two years and, on at least one credible data series, reached several times the numerical magnitude of a World Bank grid-integration study's 2018 planning reference for southern Vietnam, against Malaysia's current trajectory under its National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR). Vietnam's reported 20202021 curtailment implies foregone feed-in-tari-equivalent generation revenue of tens to low hundreds of millions of US dollars a contractual-revenue gure, not a welfare-cost estimate. The Malaysia comparison requires correcting two mismatches in how the country's solar trajectory is typically read against its own published Peninsular Malaysia grid-penetration thresholds: a geographic mismatch (Malaysia's national capacity gures versus Peninsular-only thresholds) and a unit mismatch (the published thresholds are expressed in instantaneous generation-output MW, while Malaysia's capacity and policy targets are expressed in installed-capacity MW). Correcting for both, and testing the output-to-capacity conversion against a sourced annual-capacity-factor reference case, two named scope-consistency scenarios, and a deliberately extreme, non-empirical outer bound, this paper nds that Malaysia's estimated 2024 solar capacity sits substantially below the capacity-equivalent 20 percent threshold under the sourced annual-CF reference case and the two scope-consistency scenarios; for 2035, a 72-cell sensitivity analysis over the comparison's remaining assumptions nds no threshold crossings under any of those three scenarios (0 of 18 combinations each), against 11 of 18 under the non-empirical outer bound alone. Malaysia's estimated current capacity, and its 2035 target under the tested demand scenarios, appear to retain materially more grid-integration headroom than a supercial, unit-mismatched reading of the published thresholds would suggest. The comparison also illustrates a broader measurement point: grid-penetration thresholds expressed in generation-output terms cannot be read directly against installed-capacity policy targets without risking a materially distorted picture of system headroom. Data and estimation limitations are treated transparently throughout, including a material discrepancy between two credible Vietnam capacity series; Vietnam's experience is best read as an illustration of the risks of rapid solar deployment amid constrained grid exibility, not a precise predictive template for Malaysia's own trajectory.

title: Determinants of Patent Applications across European Regions: Evidence from Panel Estimators, K-Means Clustering and Predictive Validation
affiliations: Dyrecta Lab - Istituto di Ricerca - IT research Laboratory, eCampus University, Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro and Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l.

detail.title: Determinants of Patent Applications across European Regions: Evidence from Panel Estimators, K-Means Clustering and Predictive Validation
detail.abstract: Europe measures the innovative performance of its regions largely by counting patents, and allocates public resources accordingly. This paper asks what regional patenting actually reflects, drawing on Regional Innovation Scoreboard data for 245 European regions observed annually between 2016 and 2023. Three candidate drivers are considered: the research effort of firms, the intensity of formal collaboration between the research base and industry, and the propensity to protect intangible assets through trademarks. Business research effort emerges as the dominant correlate throughout, scienceindustry collaboration as a weaker but consistent one, and trademark activity as a positive one, suggesting that firms which protect brands are not forgoing patents but exercising a single appropriation capability across several instruments. Two findings carry implications beyond measurement. Regional innovative capacity proves remarkably immobile: differences between regions account for roughly 95 per cent of the variation in the data, and differences within a region over the eight years for the remainder, so the short-run movements on which policy evaluation typically relies carry very little information, and the returns to innovation investment should be sought over horizons far longer than a programming cycle. And when the 245 regions are grouped into four innovation profiles rather than treated as a single population, the relationship that holds on average holds almost nowhere in particular: it is strong among leading and lagging regions, statistically absent in the largest group, and displaced by brand-led appropriation in a fourth group of 27 regions whose innovation is real but largely non-technological. Uniform innovation policy prescriptions and uniform managerial benchmarks are correspondingly difficult to justify.

title: The Sixth Person in the Room: Formalizing the Coding Engineer as an Independent Verification Function in AI Governance

detail.title: The Sixth Person in the Room: Formalizing the Coding Engineer as an Independent Verification Function in AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports no conflict of interest related to the argument presented.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual paper does not report human-subject research. Social-media engagement and private communications were not analyzed as data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: AI governance committees increasingly combine legal, compliance, risk, product, domain, privacy, security, and ethical expertise. Yet a committee may still approve an AI system without any participant being able to translate a governance claim into an executable test against the deployed technical system. This paper names that condition the governance-verification gap and proposes the “Sixth Person” as a corrective design: a code-capable engineer serving as an independent verification function within, or directly accountable to, the AI governance structure. The number is metaphorical rather than a universal team count. The role is defined by function, not title: converting policies and system claims into testable assertions; obtaining proportionate access to code, configurations, data lineage, evaluation scripts, permissions, dependencies, and logs; reproducing material claims; documenting discrepancies; and escalating unresolved failures before authorization. The argument synthesizes the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the NIST Secure Software Development Framework, the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, OECD accountability principles, and research on algorithmic auditing, documentation, organizational responsible-AI practice, and sociotechnical systems. The literature supports the need for multidisciplinary governance, technical test and evaluation, access to evidence, and reviewer independence, but it does not establish that a single engineer can resolve legal, social, or ethical questions. Accordingly, the proposed role is necessary in technically consequential contexts but explicitly insufficient on its own. This paper focuses on internal organizational governance, not external regulatory audits. The paper offers a role charter, an evidence chain, five testable propositions, counterarguments, and a controlled experiment for evaluating whether the role improves detection of seeded governance deficiencies. The contribution is not the invention of technical AI governance. It is the formalization of a missing interface between governance assertions and reproducible technical evidence.

title: Reality Control in Nineteen Eighty-Four
affiliations: Phenikaa University

detail.title: Reality Control in Nineteen Eighty-Four
detail.abstract: In The Orwellian Calculus (2026), Professor Vuong Quan Hoang formalized five mechanisms from Animal Farm, among them a shifting-baseline ratchet for gradual record revision. Applied to George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), that ratchet fits the Ministry of Truth's daily rectification of the past closely, but it does not cover the novel's more extreme case: a single, total, openly witnessed reversal of recorded fact (the mid-speech switch of Oceania's enemy from Eurasia to Eastasia during Hate Week) that goes undetected not because it is small, but because the checking act itself is suspended. This note states and proves a comparisonsuspension proposition that extends the ratchet's setup to cover this case, together with a partition-axis corollary showing the graduated and single-jump cases as dual extremes of one construction rather than points on a common limiting sequence. A second, independent extension reuses the entropy-based value-formation apparatus of The Sage's Empty Purse (Vuong & Nguyen, 2026) to formalize two further mechanisms: Newspeak's vocabulary contraction as a reduction in the maximum entropy a mind-state can achieve, and a partial formalization of doublethink as an exogenously imposed, rather than endogenously filtered, concentration of belief probability. That formalization is explicitly partial, and the note treats the gap itself as a result worth stating rather than a defect to excuse: because the model represents the mindstate as a single random variable, as the entropy apparatus itself requires, it can be shown directly that the probability of the two contradictory claims being held at once is exactly zero at every modeled instant, which means the model formalizes only successive near-certain commitment, not doublethink's requirement of genuinely simultaneous contradictory belief. Each proposition is proved in full and paired with a computational worked example (a numeric table or a plotted curve) tying the mathematics to a specific, cited passage of the novel; each application is anchored to that passage. None of the four results is mathematically novel, and the note states plainly, from its first page, what it does and does not establish.

title: Governing Poland's Public Healthcare System: A Strategic Management Framework for NFZ Performance, Accountability, and Resource Allocation

detail.title: Governing Poland's Public Healthcare System: A Strategic Management Framework for NFZ Performance, Accountability, and Resource Allocation

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available secondary sources and does not involve human participants, patient data, personal data, or experimental interventions. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Poland's public healthcare system faces persistent challenges related to waiting times, workforce constraints, regional disparities, hospital financial pressures, and the allocation of limited healthcare resources. Within this system, the National Health Fund (Narodowy Fundusz Zdrowia, NFZ) performs a central financing and purchasing role, yet resource allocation, performance measurement, institutional accountability, and strategic feedback are not always examined within a unified management architecture. This study develops the NFZ Strategic Governance Framework (NFZ-SGF) to integrate these functions within a single conceptual model of public healthcare governance. The study applies a structured conceptual-analytical design combining institutional analysis, secondary indicator mapping, policy benchmarking, and synthesis of literature on strategic purchasing, health-system performance, resource allocation, and public-sector accountability. The resulting framework connects population health needs, needs-sensitive resource allocation, strategic purchasing, healthcare delivery, multidimensional performance assessment, diagnostic accountability, and strategic feedback. Five performance domains-access, efficiency, quality, equity, and sustainability-are incorporated into the model, while resource allocation is conceptualised as a function of population, demographic structure, morbidity, socioeconomic need, workforce capacity, and utilisation or accessibility pressure. A central contribution of the study is the concept of diagnostic accountability, defined as the assignment of corrective responsibility to the institutional level possessing both the authority and practical capacity to influence the mechanism underlying an identified performance problem. NFZ-SGF consequently reframes performance information from a primarily retrospective reporting function into an input for subsequent purchasing, allocation, and corrective decision-making. The framework is conceptual rather than empirically validated and does not constitute an operational NFZ funding algorithm or establish causal effects on healthcare outcomes. Instead, it provides a testable strategic governance architecture and an empirical research agenda for evaluating regional allocation, purchasing performance, institutional accountability, and adaptive resource governance within Poland's public healthcare system. The study argues that the strategic effectiveness of public healthcare purchasing depends not simply on the availability of financial resources or performance data, but on the institutional capacity to connect healthcare needs, resources, purchasing decisions, performance evidence, accountable decision-makers, and subsequent corrective action.

title: Production Networks, Default Risk and Contagion
affiliations: and Georgia State University

detail.title: Production Networks, Default Risk and Contagion
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic structural model to show how an economy's production network affects firms' financial decisions, default risks and contagion. We analytically characterize the equilibrium and derive novel implications for the impacts of network characteristics. A higher network concentration lowers default probabilities and raises leverage for firms in the largest industries, which absorb profit share, and does the reverse for firms in smaller industries; because leverage and default lie on a common frontier, the two always move in opposite directions. Network sparsity has far smaller and more heterogeneous effects. Our calibrated model shows that these effects are quantitatively significant. The propagation of productivity shocks through the network depends on whether firms can adjust their capital structures: contagion is contained when leverage is free to re-optimize, but is amplified several-fold when leverage is held fixed. We exploit our calibrated model to explore the susceptibility of the U.S. production network to default contagion.

title:
When Machines Think for Us
Artificial Intelligence and the Quiet Erosion of Independent Thought

detail.title:
When Machines Think for Us
Artificial Intelligence and the Quiet Erosion of Independent Thought

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has made work faster, information easier to access and knowledge available in ways that were unimaginable only a few years ago. This paper does not argue against that progress. Rather, it examines what may happen when the use of artificial intelligence gradually becomes dependence upon it. The problem is not using AI. The problem begins when assistance becomes dependence. This paper examines excessive reliance on artificial intelligence across professional practice, law, medicine, education, business and human relationships. It considers whether repeated dependence on AI may weaken independent thought, critical reasoning, professional judgment and confidence in human decision-making. It also examines a wider concern: whether widespread reliance on similar generative AI systems could gradually make human ideas, language and creative expression more alike, thereby reducing the diversity of independent thought. The paper further considers the growing place of AI in human relationships, including its use as an adviser, confidant and companion, and asks whether technological convenience may gradually begin to replace intentional human communication and connection. The central argument of this paper is simple: artificial intelligence should make human beings more capable, not less willing to exercise their own capabilities. AI can assist us. It can research with us. It can help us create, communicate and make better decisions. But machines may think with us. They should never think for us.

title: Collective Intelligence Index (CII): A Multi-Capital Framework for Assessing National Intellectual Potential in the Era of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Development

detail.title: Collective Intelligence Index (CII): A Multi-Capital Framework for Assessing National Intellectual Potential in the Era of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it relies exclusively on publicly available, anonymized secondary aggregate data and contains no primary data collection involving human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant or financial support from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI), digital technologies, and knowledge-intensive production has increased the importance of measuring national intellectual capacity beyond conventional economic indicators such as gross domestic product (GDP). Building on an earlier conceptual working paper by the author (Nurmanbetov, 2026), this study develops a substantially refined empirical and methodological version of the Collective Intelligence Index (CII), a multi-capital framework for assessing national intellectual potential. The revised framework incorporates ten interrelated forms of capital - scientific, technological, innovation, information technology, environmental, creative, investment, economic, human, and socio-cultural- operationalized through 23 internationally comparable quantitative indicators.
A central methodological contribution is the explicit distinction between two complementary dimensions of national collective intelligence. CII-Intensity measures the relative efficiency of national systems in transforming intellectual, human, technological, and institutional resources into measurable knowledge and innovation capacity. CII-Absolute, in contrast, measures each country's proportional contribution to Global Collective Intelligence (GCI) by incorporating the aggregate scale of national intellectual and economic resources. This distinction makes it possible to separate intellectual efficiency from systemic scale and to identify countries in which high efficiency does not necessarily translate into a large global contribution, and vice versa.
The empirical application covers 40 countries using internationally comparable data for 2024 -2025 from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, UNESCO Institute for Statistics, World Bank, United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and other established international sources. The methodology employs theoretically informed weighting, z-score standardization, weighted aggregation, and linear rescaling, complemented by sensitivity and robustness analyses. The results reveal substantial cross-country heterogeneity. Small and medium-sized advanced economies achieve the highest CII-Intensity scores, whereas large economies account for substantially larger shares of CII-Absolute. The findings also identify a pronounced efficiency-scale asymmetry among several emerging and post-transition economies, particularly in Central Asia, where relatively low intellectual efficiency is accompanied by limited contributions to global collective intelligence.
The study demonstrates that national intellectual potential cannot be adequately characterized by either efficiency or economic scale alone. By integrating these two dimensions within a unified measurement framework, the revised CII provides a complementary diagnostic tool for comparative analysis of national innovation systems, knowledge-based development, AI-era competitiveness, and sustainable development. The findings offer a basis for identifying structural strengths and constraints and for designing policies aimed at strengthening national intellectual capacity and participation in the global knowledge economy.

title: Europe's AI Innovation Wave: Who Gains, Who Decides, Who Governs?
affiliations: The New School, The New School - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Europe's AI Innovation Wave: Who Gains, Who Decides, Who Governs?
detail.abstract: This paper asks how Europe should respond to the current wave of artificial intelligence. It argues that AI is best understood, at least for now, as a rapidly developing cluster of technologies within the wider information revolution rather than as a separate industrial revolution. The evidence on its economic effects remains unsettled. Productivity estimates vary widely, investment has moved ahead of what can yet be justified by measured gains, and the labour-market evidence points more towards the reorganisation of work than towards mass unemployment. These outcomes will depend less on the technology alone than on how firms deploy it, how the gains are distributed and what institutions shape adoption. Europe enters this transition from a weak position in frontier models, compute, cloud infrastructure and private investment. A credible response therefore requires more than regulation. It should combine conditional support for European firms, public investment in data and compute, stronger administrative capacity, labour force participation in deployment decisions and procurement rules designed to limit long-term dependence on foreign platforms. The paper also argues that part of any productivity gain should reach the workforce, through shorter working time and wage growth, rather than being captured only as lower labour costs and short-term capital gains. The central claim is that Europe's AI future will be decided not only by technical progress, but by ownership, institutional design and political choice.

title: Carbon Pricing and Development: Reconciling Decarbonization, Competitiveness, and Economic Growth

detail.title: Carbon Pricing and Development: Reconciling Decarbonization, Competitiveness, and Economic Growth
detail.abstract:
Carbon pricing has emerged as the central economic instrument for confronting what the report calls “the greatest market failure in human history”—the unpriced externality of greenhouse gas emissions . This report argues that the effectiveness of carbon pricing depends not on whether governments choose a carbon tax or an emissions trading system (ETS), but on the broader policy architecture surrounding it: revenue recycling, competitiveness protections, and international coordination.

The analysis identifies a core policy trilemma: nations must simultaneously decarbonize rapidly, preserve industrial competitiveness, and sustain economic growth. Empirical evidence from more than 70 global initiatives shows that well‑designed carbon pricing systems can reconcile these objectives. Leakage risks—where production shifts to jurisdictions with weaker climate policies—are concentrated in energy‑intensive, trade‑exposed sectors such as steel, cement, aluminum, and chemicals. Tools like free allocation and, increasingly, Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM) mitigate these risks by equalizing carbon costs between domestic producers and foreign competitors .

Revenue recycling is shown to be decisive for macroeconomic outcomes. When carbon revenues—now exceeding $100 billion annually—are used to reduce distortionary taxes or fund household dividends, economies can achieve a “double dividend”: lower emissions and higher economic efficiency. Equity considerations are essential; without compensatory transfers, carbon pricing can be regressive, as illustrated by France’s Yellow Vests protests. The report highlights growing global trends toward channeling revenues into green technology investment, innovation funds, and just‑transition programs.

Case studies of the EU, China, Canada, and California demonstrate divergent but converging pathways toward robust carbon pricing. The EU’s Phase 4 ETS and CBAM represent a shift toward global standard‑setting; China’s intensity‑based system reflects developmental priorities; Canada’s hybrid model balances federal stringency with provincial autonomy; and California’s system exemplifies price stability and equity‑focused reinvestment.

The report concludes that carbon pricing, when embedded within a coherent strategy of border adjustments, predictable price trajectories, dividend transfers, and international market linking, becomes not a punitive tax but a catalyst for industrial modernization and long‑run economic resilience. As carbon prices rise toward the $75–$100/tCO₂ range needed for Paris alignment, coordinated global action will be essential to prevent leakage and accelerate the transition to a low‑carbon economy.

title: Toward A Problem-Based Theory of Economic Development A Manifesto-Monograph Version 1.07

detail.title: Toward A Problem-Based Theory of Economic Development A Manifesto-Monograph Version 1.07

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a conceptual paper involving no new data collection. The fieldwork it draws on was conducted under ethics approval obtained at the time of data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This project received no funding. The empirical fieldwork drawn on here was conducted for previously published studies, in which the relevant funding is acknowledged; those papers are cited in the text.

detail.abstract:
Development economics has accumulated powerful and mutually compatible theories of institutions, capabilities, innovation systems, networks, and value chains – and no principle for deciding which applies when. This monograph argues that the absence is structural rather than accidental, and proposes a way to repair it.

The field characterizes solutions in enormous detail and barely characterizes problems at all. This is not the complaint that development scholarship ignores problems: every appraisal document begins with one. It is that naming a problem and characterizing one are different acts, and only the first is routinely performed. The result is a discipline fluent in remedies and largely silent on the diagnostic act that should precede them – which is why institutions transplanted whole die on arrival, capability programs arrive before the problems they answer, and industrial policy copied line for line misfires anyway. These are not failures of solution design. They are architecture without diagnosis.

The primitive proposed here is the productive problem: a gap between a purpose and a combination of existing components that would serve it and does not yet exist. Because a routine is a technology in Arthur’s sense, institutions, capabilities, and chain positions are one species of object individuated by purpose. What the field has been missing is an aspect of reality, not a better model of what it already sees. The position is therefore realist about the structure and anti-realist about the representation: the gap is mind-independent and prior to its discovery, while any actor’s characterization of it is lossy.

The argument is developed through a documented comparison. Two Argentine provinces faced the same productive problem at the same moment with comparable component stocks; both acted with public resources; one built a participatory architecture matched to a problem of coordination over socially distributed knowledge, the other delivered incentives top-down, and outcomes diverged. What had to be diagnosed in advance was not which solution would work but where the required knowledge sat – an observable feature of the situation rather than of the outcome.

Five falsifiable propositions and a seven-question research program follow. The claim is integrative rather than totalizing: the existing traditions are relocated as theories of solution architecture, not displaced. Nothing on the shelf is discarded; each account gains a statement of what it is for.

title: Tax Code Philosophy on Manufacturing as seen in the last 3 Finance Bills
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs Kenya

detail.title: Tax Code Philosophy on Manufacturing as seen in the last 3 Finance Bills
detail.abstract: Kenya's Medium-Term Revenue Strategy targets a tax-to-GDP ratio of 20 per cent by 2026/27, while industrial policy promises to arrest a premature retreat from manufacturing. This paper argues that the Finance Acts 2023–25 and the Finance Bill 2026 finance the first promise out of the second, and that they do so without moving a single headline rate. Resident corporate income tax remains at 30 per cent and standard VAT at 16 per cent; the adjustment has come through the effective schedule instead. Using the Hall–Jorgenson user cost of capital, the Diamond–Mirrlees production-efficiency result, and Feldstein's revenue-maximising rate as benchmarks, the paper shows that capping loss carry-forward and spreading allowances cut the present value of relief and raise the effective marginal tax rate on long-gestation investment; that an unfunded refund float of some Ksh 35 billion, reclassification of goods from zero-rated to exempt, and technology gates on input-tax recovery turn VAT into a levy on working capital; and that excise has drifted onto intermediate inputs and, for spirits, past the revenue-maximising rate. A further exposure is legal: Clause 36(a) of the Finance Bill 2026 would tax EAC-origin goods, as the East African Court of Justice has already suspended it once. The failures share one modelling error, namely, treating the tax base as a fixed stock rather than an endogenous flow. Because the statutes themselves are sound, the corrections are largely matters of appropriation and administration: fund the refund line, integrate the revenue authority's systems, and hold the rule set still.

title: From Prompt to Organization Delegated Construction in Exploratory AI Work

detail.title: From Prompt to Organization Delegated Construction in Exploratory AI Work
detail.abstract: Exploratory work cannot be fully planned in advance, yet AI agents depend heavily on written instructions. We study a sixteen-hour mathematical research run in which Shanmu Jin's one-page prompt led to a thirteenagent organization and a candidate proof of Crouzeix's conjecture. The prompt was neither a general request nor a detailed operating plan. It specified a dynamic multi-agent search: a diverse portfolio of initially independent routes, explicit tracking of approach families, grounded rules for blocking and reopening work, delayed sharing, adversarial checking, concrete reporting, and repeated synthesis by the first agent. It left the realized structure and procedures-headcount, hierarchy, assignments, timing, allocation, communication channels, and audit sequence-to that agent. Comparing the prompt with the public event record shows how these open choices were filled and how additional compatible practices appeared. We call this arrangement precise principles plus delegated construction. It is more viable when candidate components are much easier to check than to find, and less reliable when nominally separate agents share correlated errors.

detail.abstract: Supply chains are central to food security modeling, particularly in famine-prone settings, yet traditional analyses rarely adopt a system-wide perspective that accounts for their influence. One reason is that conventional predictive approaches used in supply chain analysis and systems modeling are difficult to calibrate and validate in contexts marked by sparse data and rapidly changing conditions. Drawing on a 6-year collaboration with USAID in Uganda, we argue that in such settings, an adapted system mapping approach can enable system-level analysis and produce actionable insights. We present our approach and examine its application to the Karamoja region of Uganda, where USAID sought to strengthen household resilience. We demonstrate the value of descriptive and prescriptive models in contexts where prediction is not feasible. In Karamoja, this approach highlighted the central role of supply chains in resilience outcomes and supported collective sense-making and collaboration among practitioners.

detail.abstract: Traditional after-school jobs like flipping burgers or folding clothes at the mall are fading out because, frankly, they do not pass the vibe check anymore. Today, high school and college students are pivoting to the gig economy for ultimate flexibility and autonomy. This paper explores the shift from standard part-time employment to app-based gig work among Gen Z students. I analyze how digital platforms allow students to balance academic stress and severe burnout with financial needs. Through a survey of peers and a literature review, this paper highlights why side hustles are completely replacing hourly shifts and what this means for the future of work.

title: Capacity Portfolio Optimization for EV Battery Swapping Stations: Coordinating Normal and Fast Charging
affiliations: Soochow University - Business School, , Soochow University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Capacity Portfolio Optimization for EV Battery Swapping Stations: Coordinating Normal and Fast Charging
detail.abstract: Battery swapping enables rapid electric vehicle energy replenishment, but economic viability of this business model hinges on coordinating capacity investments with dynamic charging operations. This task is complicated by heterogeneous charging technologies: normal charging is slower but less costly, whereas fast charging provides quicker replenishment but requires greater investment and accelerates battery degradation. In this paper, we formulate a two-stage stochastic optimization model that determines the capacity portfolio and optimizes subsequent dynamic dual-mode charging decisions. We prove that the transformed dynamic charging value function is L ♮-convex and that the capacity-planning cost is jointly convex under continuous relaxation. We further characterize how the two charging modes respond to inventory shortages across battery-availability horizons and establish their substitutability. Because solving the stochastic dynamic program directly is intractable, we develop a tractable Central Limit Theorem-based robust optimization approximation and a real-time Dual-Balancing Safety Stock Charging heuristic. Calibrated with real-world data, numerical experiments show that normal charging serves as an off-peak reservoir for low-cost replenishment, whereas fast charging acts as a critical shock absorber during demand surges. Our results yield three key insights: (i) The robust-optimal number of normal chargers varies nonmonotonically with normal-charging duration, with its decline occurring earlier when normal chargers are more expensive; (ii) Fast-charging degradation cost has a threshold effect on the capacity portfolio, with the largest adjustments occurring when the cost rises from negligible to positive; (iii) Electricity-price patterns favor parallel normal charging when batteries and normal chargers are inexpensive but greater reliance on fast charging when they are costly.

title: A New Social Contract: How an AI Sovereign Wealth Fund Could Boost Economic Security
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC) - Department of Psychology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: AI is driving record investment while Canada's income gap reaches its widest measured level, a pairing that we treat as the technology's signature, since AI substitutes for labour and concentrates capital. Rather than compete with the U.S. on compute, Canada should build on its comparative advantage in research talent, public trust, and distributive institutions by creating an AI sovereign wealth fund that pays every citizen a dividend, not one that merely finances AI firms. The paper proposes capitalizing it through equity warrants on compute subsidies and procurement, a data-centre energy levy, and an annual dilution levy paid in newly issued shares; governing it at arm's length on the CPP Investments model, with payouts capped at long-run real returns; and distributing proceeds as a basic income paired with personal AI-skills accounts. Canadian evidence from Mincome, Ontario's pilot, and the New Leaf Project supports the dividend's design.

title: From Signal to Substrate: Architecture, Irreversibility, and the Capital Economics of Custom Silicon
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Signal to Substrate: Architecture, Irreversibility, and the Capital Economics of Custom Silicon
detail.abstract: Hardware partitioning is commonly treated as an engineering decision: identify a computational bottleneck, estimate the performance or energy benefit of specialization, and determine whether the function belongs in software, programmable logic, or fixed silicon. That framing is incomplete. Moving computation toward dedicated hardware converts flexibility into commitment. Algorithms, dataflows, security assumptions, workload forecasts, interfaces, manufacturing dependencies, and supplier choices begin accumulating non-recurring engineering cost, verification effort, package constraints, capacity reservations, inventory exposure, and lifecycle obligations. Architecture is therefore also a capital-allocation discipline. This paper proposes a framework for deciding what deserves to become hardware by examining four questions: whether specialization creates measured technical advantage; whether the underlying computation is sufficiently persistent; whether risk-adjusted lifetime economics justify greater irreversibility; and whether the resulting implementation is manufacturable, supplyable, trustworthy, and deployable. The resulting question is not simply what can become silicon. It is what deserves to become irreversible.

title: When Text Becomes Tradable: Financial-domain Language Models and the Asymmetric Absorption of News in Agricultural Futures Markets
affiliations: University of Kent - Kent Business School,  and University of Kent, Kent Business School

detail.title: When Text Becomes Tradable: Financial-domain Language Models and the Asymmetric Absorption of News in Agricultural Futures Markets
detail.abstract: We ask whether large-language-model (LLM) embeddings of media news predict agricultural commodity futures returns and, if so, where the predictability resides. Using daily news on fourteen CBOT and ICE contracts from 2009 to 2023, we estimate a two-stage textual regression that maps pre-trained transformer embeddings to next-day returns via ridge regression, benchmarking against other text-based methods and non-text commodity-factor predictors across thirteen vectorisation models, including parameter-matched general-purpose baselines. The strongest text-based long-short portfolio, Araci's FinBERT on full news stories, attains an annualised Sharpe ratio near 2.5, and the tradable edge is sharply localised. First, it is concentrated in financially specialised pretraining: only the finance-domain (FinBERT) encoders retain economically large, statistically significant long-short Sharpe ratios after transaction costs, and only on full stories rather than headlines. Second, its informativeness is asymmetric and state-dependent across the portfolio legs: the short-leg Sharpe ratio is significantly higher on high-volatility days (around 3, versus about 1.4 unconditionally), confirmed by a block-bootstrap test, consistent with news predicting downside risk. Third, predictability accrues at the daily horizon (sub-daily strategies underperform), consistent with staggered absorption of dispersed news. These signals are not spanned by known commodity factors: after controlling for price, momentum, and carry benchmarks, the FinBERT long-short portfolio retains an annualised alpha of about 23% (t ≈ 5.9). Predictability is also materially stronger for grains than soft commodities.

title:
What Problems does the Theory Solve? 
An Applied Meta-theory for Strategic Management Working Paper Version 1.04

detail.title:
What Problems does the Theory Solve? 
An Applied Meta-theory for Strategic Management Working Paper Version 1.04

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual and theoretical work based exclusively on published literature and the author's scholarly analysis. It did not involve human participants, personal data, patient data, experiments, surveys, interviews, or case-study subjects requiring ethics approval or informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Strategic management has accumulated several powerful and mutually competing theories of the firm and no principle for deciding which applies when. This paper argues that the absence is structural rather than accidental, and proposes a way to repair it.

The field's founding object was the general manager's diagnostic act – the characterization of a situation prior to any response. That object is also the one most resistant to the identification standards through which the field earned its scientific standing, and so the field migrated away from it one defensible step at a time, toward phenomena downstream of diagnosis that could be estimated cleanly. The diagnostic act is still taught in every strategy classroom and performed by every executive. It has no cumulative theory.

The primitive proposed here is the productive problem: a gap between a purpose and a combination that would serve it and does not yet exist. Because a routine is a technology in Arthur's sense, governance, growth, and coordination problems are one species of object individuated by purpose – which is why the classes the field already studies can be dimensioned by type, boundary, and residence rather than filed under the theory that named each one.

The central claim is a level inversion. Existing theories explain how firms solve problems; none says what problems the theory itself solves. The mechanism of selection is boundary conditions: a theory's assumptions are the outer edge of its competence, and the first task is not a problem-to-theory mapping but an audit of where each theory's predictive power deteriorates. The objective is not which theory is universally true, but which exhibits the greatest predictive competence for a diagnosed class of problem.

The overlaps are where this begins, and the evidence is already collected. Comparative "horse race" studies have tested rival theories against each other on the same problems for thirty years and reported the draws as inconclusive – because a tournament has only one output, a ranking. Read as jurisdiction findings instead, that literature is a partial and unintended audit that requires no new data to reinterpret.

What follows is therefore an applied meta-theory: its object includes the field's own theories, and its output is a decision a manager can act on. It replaces nothing. Esto no es una invención; es una sistematización – an ordering of what the field already knows around the primitive that makes it usable.

title: Convergence as a Mitigation Strategy: How Synchronized Global Adoption of Clean Technologies Reduces Systemic Risk

detail.title: Convergence as a Mitigation Strategy: How Synchronized Global Adoption of Clean Technologies Reduces Systemic Risk
detail.abstract: Climate commentary treats a world cost collapse and a world generation share as synchronized adoption, and treats synchronized adoption as systemic-risk mitigation. Neither step survives a country file. Solar photovoltaic levelised cost in the IRENA world series fell 90 percent between 2010 and 2024. Solar-plus-wind reached 15 percent of world electricity, from 1.8 percent. World fossil CO2 rose 16 percent in the same window, to 38.6 gigatonnes. In a balanced reading of Ember and Energy Institute generation files, Global Carbon Budget territorial emissions, IRENA capacity, and the IEA Global EV Data Explorer via Our World in Data, we score 202 countries on two clocks. Power: solar-plus-wind at or above 8 percent of electricity, on a grid that already reaches 80 percent of the population. Fossil-exit: an 8-point fall in the fossil share of electricity since 2010 with the residual at or below 75 percent, or a fossil share already at or below 55 percent. Share-sync is both clocks on a lag of seven years or less. Twenty-one countries clear it, covering 2.35 billion people and 53 percent of scored territorial CO2. Drop China and the same cell holds 19 percent of the tonnes. Deep exit-fossil electricity at or below 40 percent-holds 9 percent of the tonnes. The tonne club of seventeen countries that each hold at least 1 percent of scored CO2 accounts for 81 percent of the file. Four of them are share-synced: China, the United States, Germany, and Australia. India is powerahead, at 10.5 percent solar-plus-wind and 77.5 percent fossil electricity. Russia, Iran, and Indonesia are absent. Sub-Saharan Africa has one share-sync country in forty-eight. Crosscountry dispersion of solar-plus-wind shares rose from 2.6 points in 2010 to 14.7 in 2024. The club clustered. The tail did not join. A cheap module is not a retired tonne. A mix clock that China and Germany close in the same decade is not a mitigation of the residual-tonne geography.

title: Wildfire Smoke, Recreation Losses, and Gateway Community Revenue
affiliations: , University of Wyoming, University of Wyoming, University of Wyoming, University of Wyoming and University of Wyoming

detail.title: Wildfire Smoke, Recreation Losses, and Gateway Community Revenue
detail.abstract: Wildfire smoke now accounts for roughly one quarter of all fine particulate matter (PM 2.5) in the United States and conditions are expected to worsen, yet smoke's consequences for outdoor recreation and recreation-dependent local economies remain poorly understood. We estimate the causal effect of wildfire smoke on daily visitation to national parks across the continental United States and on consumer spending at gateway community businesses surrounding those parks. Leveraging plausibly exogenous variation in park-level smoke-attributable PM 2.5 , combined with high resolution mobile phone-derived visitation counts, we find that smoke reduces park visitation at all but the most modest pollution levels, with declines as large as 42.4% on Very Unhealthy or Hazardous air quality index days. Smoke on a given day also suppresses future visitation, consistent with anticipatory trip cancellations. Travel cost modeling suggests that mean annual consumer surplus losses amount to approximately $13.6 million in foregone recreation. High-resolution business-level spending data show that severe smoke at nearby parks reduces gateway community revenue, while moderate smoke may increase it. We decompose these effects by their central mechanisms: park visitation losses, park visitor within-day substitution, and spatially correlated local smoke exposure. Revenue losses are not offset by subsequent increases in spending at later dates. These findings reveal significant disruptions to outdoor recreation demand and the tourism-dependent communities that rely on it.

title: Cameroon’s First WAFCON Title and the Sports Diplomacy Conversion Gap: From Symbolic Capital to Institutional Execution

detail.title: Cameroon’s First WAFCON Title and the Sports Diplomacy Conversion Gap: From Symbolic Capital to Institutional Execution
detail.abstract: Cameroon's 3 - 0 victory over Malawi in the final of the 2026 CAF Women's Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) in Rabat delivered the country's first continental title. It secured direct qualification for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup. Beyond its sporting significance, the result provides a timely case study through a recurring public policy problem can be examined: the conversion of high-visibility sporting success into durable diplomatic, institutional, and gender development outcomes. This paper introduces the Sports Diplomacy Conversion Gap, defined as the distance between the symbolic, reputational and diplomatic value generated by sporting achievement and the institutional, financial and organizational capacity mobilized to convert that value into sustained outcomes. It further distinguishes symbolic gender signaling, referring to narratives of visibility, recognition, and empowerment, from institutional gender transformation, referring to changes in financing, professional pathways, coaching systems, safeguarding, youth development, infrastructure, competition structures, and governance. Cameroon's journey is analytically instructive, especially as they had initially been eliminated by Algeria in the conventional qualifying pathway, Cameroon subsequently entered the expanded 16-team WAFCON field following CAF's decision to enlarge the competition and provide additional places to qualifying teams eliminated in the final round. The team then converted institutional access into competitive performance, reached the semi-finals and secured World Cup qualification before eventually winning the continental championship. This paper argues that the policy significance of the title should be assessed not through celebration or visibility alone, but through the institutional conversion that follows. Sporting achievement generates symbolic capital; institutions determine whether that capital becomes durable capacity.

reference: ZEW – Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-035
title: When Facts Fail: Experimental Evidence on Perceptions and Preferences toward Chinese Investments in Germany
affiliations: , City University of New York (CUNY) - CUNY Graduate Center, German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin) and ZEW Mannheim

detail.title: When Facts Fail: Experimental Evidence on Perceptions and Preferences toward Chinese Investments in Germany

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW – Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-035

detail.abstract: Can correcting large misperceptions about foreign economic exposure change preferences over economic integration? We study this question in a high-stakes setting, Chinese direct investment in Germany, with a survey experiment embedded in the German SocioEconomic Panel (N = 2,365) and a comparative survey in China (N = 2,000). Germans overestimate Chinese FDI more than 30-fold (perceived 33% vs. actual 1%) and evaluate it far less favorably than EU or US investment, while Chinese respondents view German FDI positively. We test the effects of three randomized interventions on attitudes: a factual correction and two narrative framings. Factual information improves stated perceptions of the economic benefits of Chinese FDI by about 0.2 standard deviations, positive narratives produce smaller gains, and negative narratives leave these perceptions unchanged, consistent with already-low baseline beliefs. Yet these changes in perceptions do not translate into changes in preferences over foreign investors. In conjoint choices between hypothetical investment proposals, Chinese investors are 40 percentage points less likely to be chosen than otherwise identical EU investors, and respondents require a Chinese acquirer to save about 40% more jobs than an EU or US acquirer before viewing the offers as equivalent; both estimates remain statistically unchanged across all treatment arms. These results demonstrate that brief informational interventions cannot reshape entrenched attitudes toward investment from geopolitically distant partners, though they can improve assessments of its instrumental benefits.

reference: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series No. 248
title: The Proprietary Cost of Machine-Readable Financial Reporting: Evidence from ESEF
affiliations: Paderborn University, Paderborn University and TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency

detail.title: The Proprietary Cost of Machine-Readable Financial Reporting: Evidence from ESEF

publicationDetails.detailsText: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series No. 248
publicationDetails.journalName: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The European Single Electronic Format (ESEF) requires issuers to tag annual reports with the IFRS Taxonomy and to anchor each firm-authored statement concept extension to a standard IFRS concept since 2020. This anchoring requirement distinguishes the European regime from the U.S. XBRL setting. Using 6,496 ESEF filings from 27 EU and EEA countries over 2020 to 2024, we study corporate disclosure informativeness and proprietary cost implications under this regime. Disclosure-period return volatility rises more with earnings news in filings that carry more anchored statement extensions, consistent with these firm-specific extensions being informative. More profitable firms use fewer anchored statement extensions compared to their industry peers, consistent with high economic-rent firms reducing their proprietary disclosure costs. The results are stronger where national regulatory quality is higher, where the national filing infrastructure makes the report machine-accessible, and where the firm is more exposed to China. As the European Single Access Point (ESAP) is scheduled to make ESEF annual reports centrally accessible across the EU from July 2027, our evidence on the proprietary costs of disclosure speaks directly to the policy implications of machine-readable financial reports in the EU.

title: Institutional Coordination and the Making of Corporate Value: A Nested Valuation Framework for China's A-Share Market

detail.title: Institutional Coordination and the Making of Corporate Value: A Nested Valuation Framework for China's A-Share Market
detail.abstract: Financial economics possesses well-developed theories of how investors price corporate fundamentals, but comparatively little to say about how those fundamentals themselves come into being in economies where industrial development is coordinated through sustained state and institutional action. This paper develops the Nested Valuation Framework (NVF), an analytical architecture linking institutional coordination, productive capability, corporate fundamentals, investor expectations and market capitalisation. Two operational concepts, Institutional Visibility and the Fractal Investment Clock, explain respectively how institutionally generated productive capability becomes incorporated into investor expectations, and why this incorporation proceeds asynchronously across sectors. The framework is illustrated, rather than tested, through three episodes in China's A-share market: semiconductor industrial policy, the 'new quality productive forces' strategy, and renewable energy. The paper argues that the NVF extends, rather than displaces, established valuation theory, and it closes by specifying the operational definitions, propositions and falsification conditions required to convert the framework into a testable research programme.

title: Passive Investors are Indeed Passive Monitors
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business, University of Miami Herbert Business School, The University of Hong Kong and University of Utah - Department of Finance

detail.title: Passive Investors are Indeed Passive Monitors
detail.abstract: The rise of passive investing raises the question of whether passive funds monitor management as effectively as active funds.  Gormley and Kim (2026) argue that Heath et al. (2022)'s methodology for answering this question is biased and propose four changes. Three are econometrically invalid. Two share a flaw with Appel, Gormley, and Keim (2016, 2019): they condition on ex-post information about how firms respond to treatment—one selects the sample on post-treatment index assignments, the other controls for post-treatment market capitalization. The third imposes an unsupported symmetry restriction. The fourth, already proposed by Wei and Young (2025), does not change the conclusions. Even after adopting all four, their governance estimates largely agree with Heath et al. (2022) and contradict Appel et al. (2016). Furthermore, their headline claim that passive ownership has not displaced active ownership is contradicted by third-party data showing near one-for-one displacement; thus, either their specification is biased, or it cannot identify the governance effects of passive ownership.

title: Reform of Financing for the Merah Putih Village and Urban Village Cooperatives in West Papua to Achieve Transparency and Economic Justice in West Papua Province
affiliations: , Universitas Musamus Merauke, Papua, indonesia, STIM Publik Makassar and Wira Bhakti College of Economics

detail.title: Reform of Financing for the Merah Putih Village and Urban Village Cooperatives in West Papua to Achieve Transparency and Economic Justice in West Papua Province
detail.abstract: Merah Putih Village/Kelurahan Cooperatives (Koperasi Desa/Kelurahan Merah Putih KDKMP) are intended to strengthen community-based economic institutions in Indonesia. This study examines financing governance in KDKMP in West Papua, focusing on institutional capacity, information transparency, regulatory alignment, digital governance, and member participation. A descriptive qualitative case-study design is employed using interviews, observation, documentation, and policy review. The empirical material covers government actors, cooperative managers, Business Assistants (BA), Project Management Officers (PMO), community representatives, and cooperative stakeholders. The analysis follows data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicate a gap between formal institutional expansion and substantive governance capacity. Across 831 cooperatives reported in the 2025 SIMKOPDES data, 202 had NIB, 667 had NPWP, and 213 had conducted RAT in 2025. Field evidence further indicates geographic and logistical constraints, incomplete administrative requirements, regulatory uncertainty, limited managerial capacity, uneven information disclosure, weak connectivity, and incomplete digital reporting. The study argues that digital governance should complement not substitute for institutional capacity. Based on the findings, a transparent financing framework is proposed combining policy alignment, proportional financing, transparent funding flows, digital reporting, capacity building, member participation, oversight, and local adaptation. The contribution is an empirically grounded policy framework for understanding how a national cooperative program is translated into local institutional practice in a geographically complex region.

reference: 115 California Law Review __ (forthcoming 2027)
title: Anti-Coercion Beyond the Spending Clause
affiliations: New York University School of Law

detail.title: Anti-Coercion Beyond the Spending Clause
detail.abstract:
NFIB v. Sebelius announced a constitutional anti-coercion principle: the federal government may neither directly commandeer state capacity, nor indirectly coerce states to give that capacity up. Yet, for all the headlines the opinion generated, the conventional understanding remains that anti-coercion applies only to exercises of the spending power. The federal government, however, offers a variety of inducements to states beyond conditional spending. And under the second Trump administration (though not exclusively in it), Washington has innovated novel methods of inducing state cooperation, including criminally investigating state and local officials who refuse to cooperate with its immigration enforcement agenda, refusing to deliver ballots in states that will not hand over voter data, and even surging armed agents into cities with disfavored policies.

This Article provides a systematic account of the broader federal inducement toolkit and reinterrogates both the scope and measure of anti-coercion. As to scope, it challenges the conventional understanding that NFIB’s anti-coercion rule is a Spending Clause constraint and argues instead that it is a federalism constraint. The principle is best understood as one manifestation of a more general anti-circumvention principle immanent in states’ structural entitlements under the Tenth and Eleventh Amendments. Relocating anti-coercion means that it applies beyond conditional spending legislation, covering executive conditions, non-spending inducements, and potentially inducements that indirectly target states.

As to measure, I argue that drawing the line between permissible pressure and impermissible coercion requires accounting for the institutional particulars of federal-state bargaining rather than, as current doctrine and scholarship do, analogizing states to private bargainers. States are not private individuals, but public representative institutions; the constitutional entitlements they trade are structural safeguards rather than individual rights; and they bargain within a constitutional matrix of both horizontal and vertical separation of powers. 

These two interventions do not solve every coercion puzzle, but they situate debate about federalism's rules of engagement on firmer conceptual terrain that is also more faithful to the institutional realities of our federalism. And they bring into view inducements that conventional coercion theories have difficulty evaluating.

title: Why Cultural Care in Out-of-Home Care Depends on Systems - Not Goodwill: Strengthening Cultural Identity for Multicultural Children Through Practice, Supervision, and Leadership
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Western Sydney University - Translational Health Research Institute, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Australian Catholic University

detail.title: Why Cultural Care in Out-of-Home Care Depends on Systems - Not Goodwill: Strengthening Cultural Identity for Multicultural Children Through Practice, Supervision, and Leadership
detail.abstract: Children’s sense of belonging, identity, and wellbeing are shaped by their cultural experiences and connections, yet how out-of-home care systems support the cultural identities of multicultural children is limited. This study addresses this gap by examining how organisational structures, leadership behaviours, and knowledge-building processes strengthen cultural care and uphold children’s cultural rights, drawing on international comparison across five national systems.A qualitative, interpretive design combined two sequential stages. Stage 1 was a secondary analysis of knowledge artefacts from an international Churchill Fellowship; Stage 2 comprised six follow-up interviews with seven senior leaders from out-of-home care sector organisations across the same five jurisdictions. Reflexive thematic analysis examined how organisational conditions shape the translation of cultural knowledge into practice.Findings show that cultural care is widely valued but structurally fragile, sustained more often by individual commitment than by organisational capability. Four key patterns emerged: cultural care depends on individual practitioners as conduits; risk-aversion silences cultural inquiry; organisational machinery (leadership, supervision, accountability) determines whether cultural intent becomes embedded; and cultural data infrastructure is essential for accountability. Strengthening cultural care as a safeguarding responsibility requires clearer role expectations, shared accountability, and leadership-driven system approaches rather than reliance on individual goodwill.

title: The Same Distribution, a Different Direction: Temporal Irreversibility in Global Equity Returns

detail.title: The Same Distribution, a Different Direction: Temporal Irreversibility in Global Equity Returns

keywords: Global Equity Markets Show more lines

detail.abstract: Reversing a return series leaves its empirical distribution unchanged. Its mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, quantiles, and Wasserstein distance from the original sample are therefore identical. Yet the risk process need not be unchanged, because negative returns may precede volatility expansions more often than volatility expansions precede negative returns. We use this exact distribution-preserving transformation to study daily S&P 500, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225, and Hang Seng returns from January 2000 through June 2026. Temporal direction is measured by the difference between two mixed third moments, averaged over lags one through five. The forward-time statistic is positive in all four markets-0.339, 0.317, 0.320, and 0.364-and remains significant after Holm correction across the four primary tests. Reversing each series changes the statistic's sign while leaving marginal Wasserstein distance exactly zero. Randomizing return signs while preserving the magnitude sequence centers the statistic at zero in 2,000 replications (p = 0.0005 in every market). The direction remains positive across bandwidth, bootstrap, past-only standardization, lag, episode-deletion, subsample, and winsorization checks. Of 36 prespecified robustness tests, 31 pass a 5% Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate threshold and 13 survive the stricter Holm family-wise correction. Distributional risk measurement is therefore incomplete without an ordering-sensitive layer: the same return distribution can encode a different direction of risk propagation.

title: Buy Box and Price Parity: Competitive Effects and Consumer Welfare in Online Marketplaces
affiliations: , Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and New York University (NYU) - Department of Information, Operations, and Management Sciences

detail.title: Buy Box and Price Parity: Competitive Effects and Consumer Welfare in Online Marketplaces
detail.abstract: Amazon's Buy Box (now the Featured Offer) grants selected sellers prominent placement that substantially increases visibility and sales. Buy Box eligibility partly depends on whether a seller's Amazon price is no higher than the product's rival-platform price, effectively imposing an implicit price parity rule. This practice has drawn regulatory scrutiny: the FTC argues that it stifles competition and harms consumers by compelling sellers to raise prices on rival platforms to maintain eligibility. We develop a game-theoretic model of a dominant platform enforcing the eligibility-linked price parity rule. Unlike contractual Most-Favored-Nation clauses, implicit parity lets sellers opt out when compliance is costly, generating an endogenous response absent from standard parity models. Analyzing both single-seller and two-seller market structures yields the following findings. First, where parity binds, its price effects depend on market structure: under a single seller, it lowers the dominant platform's price but raises the rival's, whereas under competing sellers, it lowers both prices. Second, under multi-homing, welfare effects hinge on seller compliance rather than on the direction of prices: parity raises consumer welfare when Buy Box eligibility is retained, but lowers it when compliance costs induce opt-out, even as both prices fall; welfare also falls when the seller single-homes on the dominant platform. Third, parity never raises the dominant platform's commission revenue under competing sellers. Our findings challenge the view that parity rules uniformly harm consumers. Eligibility-linked price parity can improve welfare when the seller complies while multi-homing, but backfires when the seller opts out or single-homes. Blanket prohibitions therefore risk suppressing the rule where it is pro-competitive.

title: A Data Eligibility Protocol Screens Curb Records for Queue Priority Decisions
affiliations: Hanyang University

detail.title: A Data Eligibility Protocol Screens Curb Records for Queue Priority Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses openly available transportation records and does not involve human participants or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of this paper.

detail.abstract: Transportation agencies collect curb occupancy and event records, but these records may not identify the queue required by a priority rule. This paper develops an auditable data-eligibility prescreen for nonpreemptive next-berth priority among transit, freight, and ride-hailing vehicles. The method tests whether data identify one opening and an eligible request queue. Conditional on that gate, a single-server priority index, a first-come, first-served (FCFS) activation test, and interval uncertainty classify policy activation. Domain incompatibility, measurement incompleteness, and decision indeterminacy are distinguished. Two datasets demonstrate the protocol. At two Barcelona loading areas, multiple vehicles appear in 96.0% and 69.3% of occupancy observations, so whole-facility occupancy cannot validate one opening. In Seattle, a minimum of two events per class retains seven marked-space-days and 212 focal service completions. Minimums of one, three, and five retain 20, two, and zero space-days. Complete-event dwell occupies 13.3% of monitored time. Completion-based dwell ratios imply cost-ratio thresholds of 0.288 for transit/freight, 0.894 for transit/ride-hailing, and 3.108 for freight/ride-hailing. Exact site-day deletion makes one threshold cross the equal-cost boundary, while a class-coding change reverses part of the equal-cost order. Neither archive observes attempted arrivals, waits, social cost weights, implementation costs, or policy effects. Consequently, these data cannot support deployment. The protocol assigns unsupported geometry, incomplete measurement, and uncertain appraisal to a changed model, additional request data, or pilot evaluation.

title: The Unarmed Mind and the Armed Mind: A Philosophical Concept of Power, Naivety, and Psychological Armament

detail.title: The Unarmed Mind and the Armed Mind: A Philosophical Concept of Power, Naivety, and Psychological Armament
detail.abstract: This paper proposes two related philosophical concepts: The Unarmed Mind and The Armed Mind. Both begin from a realist premise: power is a persistent feature of human relations, whether or not an individual chooses to acknowledge it. The Unarmed Mind is a condition in which an individual fails to adequately recognize power as a persistent force within human relations and, consequently, lacks sufficient understanding of the mechanisms through which power is acquired, exercised, preserved, and used against them. By contrast, the Armed Mind is a condition in which an individual recognizes power as a persistent force within human relations, understands the mechanisms through which it is acquired, exercised, preserved, and lost, and deliberately develops the capacity to navigate those mechanisms. The distinction rests not on intelligence or morality, but on awareness and capability. Drawing from the political realism of Niccolò Machiavelli, Friedrich Nietzsche’s treatment of power and human motivation, later thought on power and strategy, and findings from psychological research, this paper examines how naivety toward leverage, dependency, incentives, status, perception, persuasion, and competing interests can leave individuals vulnerable within ordinary human relationships. It further argues that ignorance of power does not place an individual outside power relations; it merely limits their ability to participate in them deliberately. The Armed Mind is therefore presented not as a doctrine of universal distrust or ruthlessness, but as a form of psychological armament: the ability to recognize power, protect against its exercise by others, cultivate it where advantageous, and employ it deliberately in pursuit of chosen ends. The paper ultimately advances a Machiavellian proposition at the center of the framework: to remain ignorant of power is not to remain outside of it, but to participate in it at a disadvantage.

title: Beyond Autonomy: The Role of Millennial Leadership, Job Crafting, and Mentorship in Transforming Corporate Culture to Retain Gen Z Talent

detail.title: Beyond Autonomy: The Role of Millennial Leadership, Job Crafting, and Mentorship in Transforming Corporate Culture to Retain Gen Z Talent
detail.abstract:
At present, the global corporate workforce is grappling with immense challenges brought on by rapid advancements in technology and shifting workplace norms, and the presence and emergence of Generation Z (Gen Z)—those born between 1997 and 2012—as a significant workforce demographic is undeniable (Pew Research Center, 2019). While previous generations have faced their share of corporate workplace challenges and transformations, there is a lack of empathy towards the younger generation workforce, who face scepticism regarding their work ethic, commitment levels, and inability to adapt to long-established ways of working (Deloitte, 2024). This perception can diminish an organisation’s ability to retain emerging talent, and MNCs need to adapt their organisational cultures more holistically. Unlike older generations, Gen Z workers—who have grown up and been socialised in a digital landscape—bring unique expectations and values to the workplace. Their natural predilection for autonomy, authenticity, career growth, and social responsibility calls for a revaluation of traditional management practices (Deloitte, 2024) (Kwartawaty, Ismail, & Martadi, 2024). 

This paper posits that the successful retention of Gen Z employees isn’t brought about solely by meeting their demands for a more hands-on approach, but by fostering an environment that elicits job crafting and mentorship as integral aspects of an organisation’s culture.

title: Division of Labor and the Survival Value of PnL per Token

detail.title: Division of Labor and the Survival Value of PnL per Token
detail.abstract: A model can be more capable than every competitor and nevertheless disappear from most economic production.
