We formalize this claim in a competitive economy of prediction tasks in which standardized units of compute ("tokens") are itinerant: at zero switching cost they may move between tasks and may instantiate whichever available algorithm they choose. Mobility generates a no-arbitrage condition under which marginal profit-and-loss per token is equalized across all active uses of compute, and any technology offering a strictly smaller return on the same subcontractible task receives zero execution share. As the division of labor becomes progressively finer, execution is therefore selected by task-conditional marginal economic productivity per standardized unit of compute-not by generic capability. We exhibit an explicit equilibrium in which a generalist that is strictly more capable than every specialist on every task nonetheless has compute market share tending to zero, and we give sufficient conditions, in both directions, relating asymptotic execution share to membership of the active productivity frontier. Measurement follows from the same accounting: a market-scoring-rule prediction mechanism pays each entry its marginal contribution at the state it faced, and for a sole frontier supplier on one task at its competitive scale, average PnL per token equals the shadow price of compute divided by the elasticity of task value with respect to effective compute, so at a common shadow price it ranks task-level productivity exactly when that elasticity declines with crowding, as it does under log production; administered deployment or mixed scarcity regimes can invert the unconditioned quotient, and an arbitrary model-level lifetime quotient has no such representation without additional structure. The model supplies no canonical taskinvariant scalar quality: any aggregate PnL-per-token ranking embeds a task distribution and deployment weighting, measuring the economic niches a model occupies.

title: Governing Beyond the State: Customary Authority and the Co-Production of Political Order in Africa
affiliations: African Research Network (ARN)

detail.title: Governing Beyond the State: Customary Authority and the Co-Production of Political Order in Africa
detail.abstract: African political systems are frequently evaluated through the institutional architecture of the modern state, with bureaucratic capacity, statutory law, administrative reach, and centralized authority serving as primary indicators of governance effectiveness. Such an approach, however, risks overlooking the institutional plurality through which political order is actually produced. Across much of Africa, customary authorities continue to exercise substantial normative influence over land, dispute resolution, community organization, social cohesion, and local development. Their persistence raises a fundamental question for political sociology: should customary authority be interpreted primarily as a substitute for weak state institutions, or can it constitute a complementary component of contemporary state capacity? This article develops a comparative argument through two contrasting institutional configurations in Africa: customary governance in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and constitutionalized chieftaincy in Ghana. Drawing upon the Dual-Legitimacy Institutional Interplay Model (DLII), the article conceptualizes eastern DRC as a case of Customary-Led Statecraft, in which limited formal state reach coexists with substantial customary normative authority, and Ghana as a case of Symbiotic Hybridity, in which comparatively strong formal institutions coexist with constitutionally recognized and socially embedded customary institutions. The comparison demonstrates that customary authority cannot be understood simply as an institutional residue or as evidence of state absence. Its political significance depends upon the institutional relationship established between customary legitimacy and formal state authority. The article argues that the central problem in African governance is therefore not the coexistence of formal and customary institutions but the absence, presence, and quality of mechanisms that connect them. These mechanisms include institutional recognition, epistemic translation, jurisdictional coordination, institutional arbitrage, constitutional accountability, and mutual adaptation. The article further argues that customary institutions can contribute to political order without necessarily becoming state institutions, while the state can strengthen its capacity without eliminating customary authority. The resulting conception of governance is one of institutional co-production, in which different sources of authority contribute distinct capacities to a common political order. The article concludes by proposing a new paradigm of African state-building based not on institutional substitution but on accountable institutional integration.

title: What Business Owes Democracy: Three Moral Grounds for Corporate Democratic Responsibility
affiliations: and Dresden University of Technology

detail.title: What Business Owes Democracy: Three Moral Grounds for Corporate Democratic Responsibility
detail.abstract: Democratic backsliding is on the rise, yet the role of corporations in defending democracy remains underexplored. In this paper, we develop a normative account of corporate democratic responsibility (CDR) as a distinct form of responsibility grounded in freedom understood as protection against arbitrary domination and in an understanding of democracy as institutionalized opposition to tyranny. We identify three moral grounds for CDR: leverage, arising from corporations' capacity to influence democratic discourse and institutions; complicity, resulting from silence or selective engagement amid democratic backsliding; and rectification, a backward-looking responsibility rooted in past harms or omissions. Together, these grounds form a context-sensitive framework that clarifies when and why firms in liberal democracies have moral reasons and, under non-ideal conditions of democratic erosion, pro tanto duties to actively support democracy. By shifting the focus from harm avoidance to context-dependent forms of engagement, our contribution reframes debates on corporate responsibility and advances normative scholarship.

title: AI-Driven Visual Testing for Reliable Enterprise Software: A Three-Layer Framework Integrating Perceptual Detection, Semantic Validation, and Adaptive Self-Healin
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of the Witwatersrand

detail.title: AI-Driven Visual Testing for Reliable Enterprise Software: A Three-Layer Framework Integrating Perceptual Detection, Semantic Validation, and Adaptive Self-Healin

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare the sole authorship of research paper
declarations.ethicsApproval: I declare the sole authorship of research paper
declarations.funderStatement: I declare the sole authorship of research paper

detail.abstract: Enterprise software teams increasingly rely on continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines that ship user-interface (UI) changes at a pace traditional visual quality assurance cannot match. Functional test suites routinely pass while users still encounter layout shifts, clipped elements, and rendering defects, failures that are structurally invisible to logic-only testing. This paper develops an integrative conceptual framework for AI-driven visual testing, synthesizing computer-vision-based visual regression research with the parallel literature on selfhealing test automation. Building on Rajaseakaran Nair's (2026) computer-vision and AI-driven framework for enterprise UI validation at scale, together with peer-reviewed research on deeplearning GUI testing, Vision Transformer-based visual comparison, and industry evidence on enterprise visual-testing platforms, the paper proposes a three-layer framework, Perceptual Detection, Semantic Validation, and Adaptive Self-Healing, describing how modern AI-driven visual testing systems move beyond brittle, pixel-diff-based validation toward context-aware, lowmaintenance UI quality assurance. The framework is illustrated through disclosed, non-empirical proof-of-concept scenarios spanning web and mobile enterprise applications. The analysis does not report primary experimental or production data. The paper discusses theoretical, engineering, and organizational implications for enterprise QA practice and proposes an agenda for empirical validation, including attention to unresolved research gaps such as the limited integration of semantic visual verification with DOM-based self-healing.

title: AI Ecosystem Interfaces as Orchestration Mechanisms for Public Value Creation

detail.title: AI Ecosystem Interfaces as Orchestration Mechanisms for Public Value Creation

declarations.ethicsApproval: The authors declare that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
Despite growing interest in AI-enabled governance and ecosystem coordination, existing public value frameworks provide limited explanation of how intelligent technologies orchestrate multi-stakeholder value co-creation across complex institutional environments. This study proposes the AI Ecosystem Interface as an intelligent socio-technical orchestration mechanism that facilitates communication, resource integration, and adaptive coordination among market actors, stakeholders, and policymakers within a shared valuecreation network.

 Drawing upon Marshallian value theory, Stakeholder Theory, Platform Ecosystem Theory, and Service-Dominant Logic, the study develops a conceptual framework that explains how AI-enabled coordination supports the creation, realisation, and perception of public value. The framework positions the AI Ecosystem Interface as an embedded orchestration layer that aligns stakeholder interests, facilitates ecosystem coordination, and supports adaptive governance processes. 

The study contributes to public value and ecosystem governance literature by conceptualising AI ecosystem interfaces as intelligent orchestration mechanisms for multistakeholder value co-creation. It further extends existing theories of value creation by integrating economic, stakeholder, ecosystem, and service perspectives within a unified model of AI-enabled public value creation.

title: Decision-Focused Observation Scheduling for Satellite Conjunction Assessment

detail.title: Decision-Focused Observation Scheduling for Satellite Conjunction Assessment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study used simulated conjunction data and involved no human participants or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: A conjunction warning must be resolved into a maneuver decision under finite tracking capacity: only a few of the available observation opportunities can be spent before closest approach. Standard practice selects the observations that most reduce orbital state uncertainty, a criterion indifferent to the decision the estimate will serve. We analyse the decision-focused alternative in the linearised encounter-plane model, where the posterior covariance and the covariance of the posterior mean are exact complements, and three results follow from it. The collision probability is a martingale in the observation filtration, so no schedule reduces expected risk and admissible objectives are dispersion measures. The first-order surrogate (the risk gradient contracted with the resolved covariance, equivalently c-optimal design) is an expansion in a parameter tied to the information collected, and performs worse than random selection. In the small-hard-body limit both moments of the future collision probability are available in closed form, and the resulting criterion decomposes into encounter-plane D-optimal design plus a risk correction that vanishes as the posterior tightens. Over 20,000 simulated conjunctions with an exhaustive combinatorial optimum, exhaustive selection under the closed-form criterion reduces expected Bayes loss by 3.8% to 4.1% relative to D-optimality and comes within 1.4% of the exact optimum at roughly a twelfth of its cost, while D-optimality improves on the best data-independent rule by 21% to 35%. The ordering is stable as the maneuver cost ratio is swept across the operational band. The advantage concentrates in conjunctions that appear safe and disappears under a mis-specified prior.

title: Venture Capital Syndicate Centrality and Follow-On Financing: Evidence from UK Fintech, 2019-2021
affiliations: and

detail.title: Venture Capital Syndicate Centrality and Follow-On Financing: Evidence from UK Fintech, 2019-2021
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the network centrality of a venture capital syndicate predicts follow-on financing outcomes for early-stage fintech companies in the United Kingdom. Using a dataset of 368 institutional seed and Series A rounds completed between January 2019 and December 2021, constructed from PitchBook and cleaned to retain only institutional investors, we build a bipartite VC-to-company co-investment network, project it onto a VC-to-VC adjacency graph, and compute degree, betweenness, and eigenvector centrality for each investor. Syndicate-average centrality scores are estimated against a binary follow-on funding outcome within 24 months using a Cox proportional hazards framework, with degree centrality specified as the primary measure. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in average syndicate degree centrality is associated with a 33 per cent higher hazard of raising a follow-on round (HR = 1.330, p = 0.016), after controlling for deal size, round stage, year, and foreign investor presence. Betweenness and eigenvector centrality, treated as secondary specifications given their high correlation with degree centrality, are directionally consistent but statistically underpowered. An exploratory test of foreign venture capital participation shows a positive but inconsistent association with follow-on speed, reaching only marginal significance in one of three specifications and constrained by incomplete investor nationality data; we treat this as motivation for future work rather than a confirmed finding. The paper provides the first empirical test of the Hochberg, Ljungqvist and Lu (2007) centrality-performance framework in UK fintech and introduces syndicate-average centrality as an alternative to lead-investor centrality in markets where deal leadership is diffuse.

title: Integrating the Svensson Model of the U.S. Treasury Yield Curve and the High Frequency VIX Microstructure for Systemic Risk Management

detail.title: Integrating the Svensson Model of the U.S. Treasury Yield Curve and the High Frequency VIX Microstructure for Systemic Risk Management
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a novel systemic risk management that integrates the daily-frequency Svensson model of the U.S. Treasury yield curve with the minutely high-frequency Svensson model of the VIX microstructure. By constructing a multi-layered, multi-timescale model—comprising a high-frequency layer (minute-level jump-diffusion and Kalman filtering), a medium-frequency layer (daily VAR with Johansen cointegration), and a low-frequency layer (weekly/monthly HP filtering and wavelet coherence analysis)—we capture risk transmission from short-term market sentiment fluctuations to long-term economic fundamental changes. We construct an Extended Systemic Expected Shortfall (Extended SES) indicator whose four components (Treasury term premium, VIX long-term volatility level, Treasury-VIX cointegration residual, and VIX jump intensity) are weighted via a dynamic mechanism. Empirical analysis demonstrates that this framework exhibits strong early-warning capabilities during historical crisis episodes. Finally, we design a stress-testing methodology that evaluates the likelihood of future systemic risk by simulating macroeconomic shocks of varying intensity, providing policymakers and market participants with a forward-looking risk management tool.

title: The Geography of Global Convergence, 2000–2025: Income, Productivity, Technology Adoption, and Structural Transformation across Developing Economies

detail.title: The Geography of Global Convergence, 2000–2025: Income, Productivity, Technology Adoption, and Structural Transformation across Developing Economies
detail.abstract: Developing economies closed a third of the income gap with high-income countries after 2000, and almost none of that closing is a developing-world fact. In a population-weighted reading of World Bank GDP per capita at PPP, low-and middle-income economies moved from 13.4 percent of the high-income level in 2000 to 23.0 percent in 2023. Drop China and the same ratio moves from 14.6 to 18.4. Drop China and India and it moves from 17.7 to 19.6. Sub-Saharan Africa ended where it began, at 8.4 percent of high-income income. Latin America fell back, from 34.8 to 32.6. East Asia, pulled by China, went from 11.4 to 34.3. The four clocks that development theory treats as one process-income, labour productivity, technology adoption, and structural transformation-did not move together. Agricultural employment in developing East Asia fell from 49 to 25 percent of jobs. In sub-Saharan Africa it fell from 58 to 50. Manufacturing's share of African GDP declined. African internet use reached 33 percent and electricity 53 percent; East Asian developing internet use reached 86 percent and electricity 98. Twenty-six developing countries clear all four clocks we define, covering 57 percent of developing-country population. One of them is in sub-Saharan Africa, Ghana, covering 2.7 percent of regional population. Unweighted β-convergence among 123 developing countries is weak. Population-weighted β-convergence is strong. That is the difference between a country count and a headcount, and it is the difference between a theory of catch-up and a China-India-Viet Nam industrialisation. Extreme poverty in the developing sample fell from 43 percent around 2002 to 12 percent around 2022. The sub-Saharan headcount rose, from 351 million to 517 million. A mean that is three countries is a map. It is not a convergence theorem.

title: When Arbitration Meets Insolvency: Party Autonomy, Automatic Stays, Arbitrability and Collective Creditor Interests in Cross-Border Disputes
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: When Arbitration Meets Insolvency: Party Autonomy, Automatic Stays, Arbitrability and Collective Creditor Interests in Cross-Border Disputes

keywords: UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency

detail.abstract: The collision between international arbitration and insolvency law exposes a structural tension between two forms of legal ordering. Arbitration is bilateral, consensual and decentralised: it protects party autonomy and the bargain to resolve defined disputes outside national courts. Insolvency is collective, mandatory and court-supervised: it centralises claims, preserves the estate and seeks an orderly distribution among creditors. The tension becomes acute when insolvency begins after an arbitration agreement has been made or after arbitral proceedings have commenced. This article develops a comparative framework for resolving that conflict. It examines the survival and enforceability of arbitration agreements after insolvency, the effect of automatic stays and moratoria, the distinction between pre-insolvency private rights and insolvency-created collective claims, and the limits of arbitrability where relief affects the general body of creditors. Particular attention is given to the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency, Regulation (EU) 2015/848, the United States automatic stay, the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Peace River Hydro Partners v Petrowest Corp, the Singapore WHEN ARBITRATION MEETS INSOLVENCY 2 authorities from Larsen Oil and AnAn to Sapura Fabrication v GAS, and the Privy Council's recalibration of English law in Sian Participation v Halimeda. The article argues that neither arbitration nor insolvency should enjoy categorical priority. A principled solution turns on the character of the claim, the stage and purpose of the insolvency process, the effect of arbitration on the estate and other creditors, and the distinction between determining a debt and exercising uniquely collective insolvency powers.

title: The Sour Apple Paradox: Why Organizations Struggle to Reform Competent but Harmful Managers
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Sour Apple Paradox: Why Organizations Struggle to Reform Competent but Harmful Managers
detail.abstract: This paper conceptualizes the "Sour Apple" as a manager who provides substantial functional value to an organization while repeatedly producing avoidable relational harm through anger, intimidation, public reprimands, excessive monitoring, or other modifiable managerial behaviors. Drawing on research on bad apples, abusive supervision, destructive leadership, psychological safety, employee voice, organizational silence, social learning, prestige bias, power dependence, and organizational defense, the paper develops the Sour Apple Paradox to explain why organizations may struggle to reform harmful behavior precisely when the manager is highly competent and valuable. The central argument is not that competence causes harmful conduct. Rather, competence, performance, expertise, site-specific knowledge, and concentrated responsibilities may increase Organizational Irreplaceability and organizational dependence. This dependence can create a Competence Shield that weakens corrective pressure on the manager. At the same time, anger may generate visible short-term compliance while suppressing employee voice, producing Feedback Starvation and reducing the manager's access to information about the relational costs of their own behavior. When correction is repeatedly deferred, the manager's competence, success history, and behavioral style may become increasingly fused. Corrective Voice can then be redefined as a threat not only to the manager but also to prior organizational judgments and legitimacy. Under such conditions, organizations may shift from reforming behavior to managing the messenger, thereby protecting harmful conduct while attempting to retain a valuable employee. As an alternative to the binary choice between removal and tolerance, this paper proposes Competence-Preserving Behavioral Reform, which separates the person from the behavior and seeks to retain expertise, responsibility, and operational value while replacing unnecessarily harmful managerial practices. The Sour Apple Paradox therefore reframes the problem of harmful leadership as a failure of organizations to reform valuable people without first devaluing or removing them.

title: Corruption and Illegality in International Commercial Arbitration: Evidentiary Standards, Arbitrability and the Public Policy Limits of Enforcement
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Corruption and Illegality in International Commercial Arbitration: Evidentiary Standards, Arbitrability and the Public Policy Limits of Enforcement
detail.abstract:
Corruption occupies an uneasy position in international commercial arbitration. Arbitration rests on consent, procedural flexibility, confidentiality and the finality of awards, but none of those principles can justify arbitral assistance in enforcing contracts obtained or performed through bribery, fraud or comparable illegality. The central difficulty is therefore not whether corruption matters, but how tribunals and courts should identify and respond to it without allowing an allegation of illegality to become a tactical device for delaying proceedings, avoiding contractual obligations or obtaining a disguised appeal on the merits.

This article examines three connected questions: the evidentiary standards applicable to corruption allegations; the arbitrability and jurisdictional consequences of illegality; and the public-policy limits governing annulment, recognition and enforcement. It argues that the older view that corruption necessarily deprives a tribunal of jurisdiction has largely given way to a more coherent model based on separability and kompetenz-kompetenz. A tribunal ordinarily has authority to decide whether the underlying transaction is corrupt, even though it must refuse relief where enforcement would give legal effect to prohibited conduct. On proof, the article rejects both a mechanically heightened standard and the proposition that suspicion or "red flags" alone may establish corruption. Because corrupt arrangements are deliberately concealed, circumstantial evidence, documentary anomalies and appropriate adverse inferences are indispensable; nevertheless, the ultimate finding must result from a disciplined evaluation of the whole evidentiary record and observance of due process.

At the post-award stage, the article proposes a calibrated public-policy model. The exception under the New York Convention must remain narrow enough to protect arbitral finality, but it cannot become so deferential that courts are required to enforce an award that directly gives effect to proven corruption or that was itself procured through fraud. Comparative decisions from England, Singapore and France demonstrate different points on this spectrum. The article concludes that the legitimacy of international arbitration depends upon institutional complementarity: tribunals bear primary responsibility for investigating credible illegality, while courts exercise exceptional but meaningful control where enforcement would compromise fundamental public policy or the integrity of adjudication.

title: Legal Privilege in International Commercial Arbitration: Choice of Law, Confidentiality and Equality of Arms in Cross-Border Evidence
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Legal Privilege in International Commercial Arbitration: Choice of Law, Confidentiality and Equality of Arms in Cross-Border Evidence
detail.abstract: Legal privilege presents a distinctive conflict-of-laws problem in international commercial arbitration. A tribunal may be seated in one jurisdiction, apply the substantive law of another, and receive evidence created by parties and lawyers subject to multiple professional regimes. The resulting differences are not marginal. They affect whether in-house counsel communications are protected, the scope of corporate legal advice and litigation privilege, waiver, settlement communications, and the obligations of counsel asked to disclose material. This article argues that privilege should be understood as a procedural-substantive hybrid rather than automatically governed by the law of the seat, the governing law of the contract, or each party's home law. It first distinguishes privilege from arbitral privacy and confidentiality, showing why protective orders cannot substitute for a rule determining whether evidence is producible. It then examines competing choice-of-law models and comparative divergences in English, United States, European Union and recent French law. Building on the 2020 IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence and the IBA Task Force on Privilege, the article proposes a structured LEGAL PRIVILEGE IN INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION 2 transnational model: party agreement should be respected; mandatory legal and ethical duties preserved; a uniform minimum protection applied to core legal-advice, litigation and settlement communications; residual privileges determined by closest connection; and equality-of-arms corrections used where national differences create material forensic asymmetry. The article concludes that transparent privilege protocols, privilege logs, clawback rules and proportionate confidentiality measures can reconcile evidentiary access with candid legal advice while reducing due-process risk at the set-aside and enforcement stages.

title: Who Guards the Guardians? Legal Accountability Gaps in Bangladesh's Federation Elections Process

detail.title: Who Guards the Guardians? Legal Accountability Gaps in Bangladesh's Federation Elections Process

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal accountability gaps in Bangladesh’s sports governance framework, with a particular focus on the powers of the National Sports Council (NSC) under section 21 of the National Sports Council Act 2018. It argues that the Council’s broad power to dissolve the executive committees of sports organisations and appoint ad hoc committees creates significant risks of unchecked administrative discretion, particularly where the legislation provides limited procedural safeguards such as prior notice, hearing, written reasons, or an effective appeal mechanism. The paper further identifies two related governance deficiencies in federation elections: the absence of clear restrictions preventing members of ad-hoc committees from contesting elections administered during their tenure, raising concerns under the principle of nemo judex in causa sua, and structural barriers that may restrict genuine and inclusive participation in federation elections. Drawing on Bangladesh’s statutory and constitutional framework, including judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution, the paper proposes legislative and institutional reforms to strengthen due process, transparency, electoral integrity, and accountability while preserving legitimate regulatory oversight. It concludes that effective sports governance requires not merely authority to regulate, but mechanisms capable of holding those exercising that authority accountable.

title:
Convergence as a Mitigation Strategy for the Polycrisis: 
Integrating Clean-transition, Climate-adaptation, and Cooling systems to Reduce Cascading Global Risks

detail.title:
Convergence as a Mitigation Strategy for the Polycrisis: 
Integrating Clean-transition, Climate-adaptation, and Cooling systems to Reduce Cascading Global Risks
detail.abstract: Climate policy treats three systems as three sectors: a clean-energy transition, a climate-adaptation programme, and a cooling-technology build-out. A polycrisis is not a sector problem. It is a cascade in which failure in one domain raises the cost of absorbing the next. This paper asks whether those three systems occupy the same countries. In a balanced reading of World Bank, ND-GAIN, Ember/Energy Institute electricity files, and ERA5 temperatures, 31 of 127 developing countries clear all three clocks we define-clean transition, adaptation readiness, and cooling capacity-covering 3.8 billion people. Forty-three countries clear none, covering 1.4 billion. None of the 41 developing countries that sit in three or four polycrisis-risk domains occupy all three systems. Three-quarters of that high-risk group occupy none. The correlation between the system count and the polycrisis-risk count is-0.67. Mean GDP per capita growth in 2019-23 was-0.43 percent a year in zero-system countries and +1.70 percent in threesystem countries; population-weighted, +0.29 against +3.57. Sub-Saharan Africa, where the cascade is thickest, has zero three-system countries. Solar and wind reached 15 percent of world electricity in 2024, from 0.2 percent in 2000, and solar's levelised cost fell 90 percent after 2010. Those are real clocks. They are not a map of the cascade. Kenya generates 18 percent of its electricity from solar and wind and still fails the access floor that would make that generation a cooling and production system. Nigeria sits at 172 kWh per person against 3,573 cooling degree days. The hardware is being built where absorptive capacity already exists. Joint occupation is the mitigation. Separate sector programmes are a ranking error.

title: Settlement within International Commercial Arbitration: Med-Arb, Arb-Med-Arb, Consent Awards and the Singapore Convention on Mediation
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Settlement within International Commercial Arbitration: Med-Arb, Arb-Med-Arb, Consent Awards and the Singapore Convention on Mediation
detail.abstract: Settlement is not external to international commercial arbitration. It increasingly operates within the arbitral process through mediation windows, Med-Arb and Arb-Med-Arb protocols, tribunalfacilitated settlement and consent awards. This convergence promises speed, cost savings, commercial flexibility and improved enforceability, but also creates difficult questions concerning impartiality, confidentiality, party consent and the legal character of settlement outcomes. This article examines the architecture of settlement within international commercial arbitration and argues that hybrid processes are legitimate only when procedural safeguards preserve the adjudicative integrity of arbitration. It distinguishes Med-Arb, in which mediation precedes arbitration, from Arb-Med-Arb, in which an arbitration is commenced, stayed for mediation and resumed if settlement fails. Particular attention is given to the SIAC-SIMC Arb-Med-Arb framework, the treatment of settlement under the UNCITRAL Model Law and the 2026 ICC Arbitration Rules, and the legal status of consent awards under the New York Convention. The article then analyses the United Nations Convention on International Settlement Agreements Resulting from Mediation (Singapore Convention on Mediation), including its scope, exclusions, formal requirements, grounds for refusing relief and relationship with arbitral SETTLEMENT WITHIN INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION 2 awards. It argues that the Singapore Convention reduces the historical need to convert every mediated settlement into an arbitral award merely for cross-border enforcement. Nevertheless, consent awards retain important functions where arbitration has already commenced, where parties require finality in award form, or where enforcement through the New York Convention is strategically preferable. The article proposes a safeguards-based model: informed consent, role separation as the default, strict protection of confidential mediation communications, tribunal scrutiny before issuing a consent award, and deliberate selection between Convention-based mediation enforcement and award-based enforcement.

title:
Decision Governance as a Candidate Field of Scientific Inquiry: 
A Research Proposition on the Measurement and Distinctiveness of the Evidence-to-Commitment Transition

detail.title:
Decision Governance as a Candidate Field of Scientific Inquiry: 
A Research Proposition on the Measurement and Distinctiveness of the Evidence-to-Commitment Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is affiliated with the EBR Institute (in formation), which is developing and stewarding the EBR Protocol referenced in this paper as a candidate operational artefact. The research proposition is explicitly designed to permit revision, integration, replacement or rejection of the Protocol's underlying assumptions. No commercial interest or external party has been granted influence over the research conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human participants, patients, animal subjects, or identifiable personal data. No ethics approval was required for the preparation of this research proposition.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for the preparation of this paper. The research proposition was developed independently.

detail.abstract: Biological research and development generates evidence continuously, while institutional commitment decisions occur at discrete points in time. Between the emergence of decision-relevant evidence and formal organisational action, there may exist an interval in which available evidence has become sufficiently informative to warrant reconsideration of an existing commitment, while institutional governance has not yet translated that evidence into a corresponding action. This paper examines whether that relationship constitutes a coherent and measurable object of scientific inquiry.

title: Shedding The Shackles of Legalese: Dismantling The “Symbolic System” and Maintaining Relevance of The Legal Profession in a Generative and Agentic AI Age
affiliations: University of Malaya, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia

detail.title: Shedding The Shackles of Legalese: Dismantling The “Symbolic System” and Maintaining Relevance of The Legal Profession in a Generative and Agentic AI Age
detail.abstract: There has been much discourse over the relevance of lawyers with the proliferation of artificial intelligence (‘AI’). Members of the legal profession continue with hard-won traditions: from legalese to that which is legalistic. Most conversations, scholarly or otherwise, surrounding AI within the profession, specifically, however, are fixated on the use of AI in law practice, its risks, liabilities, and challenges it poses. In short, how technology could play a part in the profession, the legal implications of the technology, but not how lawyers are to essentially redeem themselves when the technology is advancing at such a pace. That is not the context in which this article sits. This article will not delve into the risks or liabilities associated with AI. That is well-worn territory at this stage. Rather, this article focuses on the value that the profession has or could have if and only when young members of the profession break free from the shackles of legalese. Divisive though this could be, in this article, the author hypothesises that legalese is a relic of the past that has withstood the test of time, not merely because of self-preservation in a purely economic sense, but also because the presence of legalese in the legal profession serves to promote a deeper social status quo – the “symbolic power”. Legalese, this author aims to show, has been a flawed instrument of power. With the advent of AI, the author proposes that it is not legalese that will maintain the profession’s relevance, but rather skills that surpass the patternrecognition inherent in generative and agentic AI.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility: A Systematic Literature Review and Integrative Framework of Corporate Sustainability Silence and Greenhushing
affiliations: President University

detail.title: Corporate Social Responsibility: A Systematic Literature Review and Integrative Framework of Corporate Sustainability Silence and Greenhushing
detail.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) shapes corporate legitimacy not only through what firms communicate but also through what they reduce, selectively withhold, or leave entirely undisclosed. Existing Business, Management, and Accounting research explains this communicative restraint through multiple labels corporate sustainability silence, greenhushing, strategic silence, green blushing, sustainability muteness, and corporate commissive silencewhose definitions and theoretical relationships remain fragmented. This systematic literature review, guided by PRISMA 2020, integrates 34 peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 to clarify how these constructs are related. It distinguishes corporate sustainability silence from greenhushing by examining six construct labels across four analytical dimensions: communicative behaviour, intentionality, strategic orientation, and stakeholder orientation. The synthesis identifies a shared conceptual architecture in which firms restrain CSR-related communication despite substantive sustainability performance, commonly because of anticipated greenwashing accusations and associated reputational risks. Meaningful differences nevertheless remain in the scope of withheld communication, assumptions about managerial intention, stakeholder targets, and theoretical grounding. The proposed model positions corporate sustainability silence as an intentionality-neutral umbrella construct encompassing reduced, selective, or absent sustainability disclosure. Greenhushing forms its deliberate, performance-grounded subset, whereas corporate commissive silence operates as a distinct stakeholder-attributive overlay concerning uncommunicated commitments. This hierarchy explains how similar observable silence may arise from different intentions and strategic conditions while producing different stakeholder interpretations. The review contributes a parsimonious vocabulary and integrated construct model for CSR communication research while identifying conceptual standardisation and the operationalisation of intentionality as priorities for future empirical investigation.

title:
Beyond Synergy
Rethinking Failure in Cross-Border Mergers and Acquisitions

detail.title:
Beyond Synergy
Rethinking Failure in Cross-Border Mergers and Acquisitions
detail.abstract: When cross-border mergers or acquisitions fail, the usual explanation is "lack of synergy", idea that the combined firms simply didn't create the extra value they promised. This paper argues that while synergy does matter, it is only part of the picture. In many cases, deals fall apart not because the business logic was flawed, but because of legal and structural barriers that were underestimated from the start. This paper compares how major jurisdictions including the United States, European Union, China, and India regulate cross-border deals through foreign investment screening, competition law, and emerging tools like the EU's Foreign Subsidies Regulation. It also looks at how deal structures and contractual choices interact with these legal systems. Based on this comparison, the paper identifies recurring legal failure points and shows how they shape deal outcomes. It then proposes a "legal-structural" approach, arguing that regulatory design should be treated as a core part of deal strategy from the very beginning, rather than something addressed after the business case is already in place.

title: Transmission Immunity and Organizational Rigidity: Extending the Organizational Skeleton Framework
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Transmission Immunity and Organizational Rigidity: Extending the Organizational Skeleton Framework
detail.abstract: This paper extends the Organizational Skeleton Framework by introducing transmission immunity as a mechanism distinct from transmission loss. Whereas transmission loss describes the attenuation of organizational intent as signals move through hierarchical and structural interfaces, transmission immunity describes the selective acceptance, blocking, or rejection of signals at organizational joints. The framework distinguishes between two forms of transmission immunity. Malignant immunity occurs when organizational joints are occupied by actors whose self-interest overrides organizational purpose, allowing information shielding, selective filtering, and resistance to organizational intent to reinforce structural rigidity. Benign immunity occurs when professional judgment, organizational identification, or ethical commitment enables actors to resist flawed directives in order to protect the organization's legitimate purpose. The paper further distinguishes immune signal sources from organizational joints and separates immune activation from immune success. Corrective signals may originate from bottom-up participants or external actors who lack direct authority to determine or execute the relevant organizational decisions. Immune activation occurs when the aggregate intensity of such signals exceeds the response threshold of a decision-making joint, but activation does not necessarily produce organizational correction. The subsequent outcome depends on whether the organizational skeleton can receive, transmit, interpret, and implement the resulting corrective response. Building on case analyses of the CFMEU, Public Service Association of New Zealand cases, Toshiba, Enron, and Haier, the paper develops the concepts of the prosperity trap, structural replacement of judgment, and organizational self-correction. The prosperity trap explains how structural rigidity may accumulate during periods of organizational success as reduced 1 vigilance and dominant success narratives weaken responsiveness to corrective information. Self-correction provides the complementary mechanism through which detected deviations can generate local feedback, structural adjustment, and adaptive renewal. The resulting framework conceptualizes organizational resilience not as the absence of resistance or error, but as the preservation of corrective capacity within the organizational skeleton. A resilient organization is therefore one in which resistance remains connected to organizational purpose and corrective signals remain capable of entering, travelling through, and modifying the organizational structure.

title: Clean Transition Pathways for Developing Countries: Institutional Reforms, Distributed Renewables, and Policy Sequencing for Low-cost Decarbonization

detail.title: Clean Transition Pathways for Developing Countries: Institutional Reforms, Distributed Renewables, and Policy Sequencing for Low-cost Decarbonization
detail.abstract: The cheap-module thesis says developing countries can now decarbonise on a cost curve. Solar photovoltaic levelised cost in the IRENA world series fell from 42 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2010 to 4 cents in 2023. Solar's share of world electricity rose from 0.2 percent to 6.9 percent. That is a real clock. It is not a transition pathway. In a balanced reading of World Bank access and loss files, Worldwide Governance Indicators, and Ember/Energy Institute generation files, 18 of 127 developing countries occupy all three clocks we define-institutional reform, distributed solar, and an 80 percent access floor-covering 3.7 billion people. Thirty-two countries occupy solar without the reform-and-access pair. We call that cell an enclave. Median generation there is 239 kWh per person against 2,773 in the sequenced cell. Mean solar share is higher in the enclave (11 percent against 8). Sixty-four countries occupy neither distributed solar nor the reform-and-access pair, covering 1.7 billion. Sub-Saharan Africa has three sequenced cases-Mauritius, Senegal, South Africa-and sixteen enclaves. Among the 36 developing countries that eventually crossed both an 80 percent access line and a 3 percent solar line, 32 crossed access first, on a median lag of twenty years. Solar's correlation with government effectiveness is 0.04. Access's correlation with the same index is 0.54. Hardware went where the cost curve pointed. The system went where the offtaker and the wire already existed. Carbon prices, the instrument most often prescribed as the efficient first step, sat in 4 percent of developing countries in 2023 and 23 percent of high-income ones. Low-cost decarbonisation is a sequencing problem. Copying a late-stage instrument into an early-stage grid inverts the order that produced the cheap transitions we can actually observe.

title:
The Great Electrification: Pathways to a Post-Carbon Industrial Economy 

Quantifying Hydrogen, Electrification, and AI-Optimised Grids as Drivers of Mid-Century Stabilisation

detail.title:
The Great Electrification: Pathways to a Post-Carbon Industrial Economy 

Quantifying Hydrogen, Electrification, and AI-Optimised Grids as Drivers of Mid-Century Stabilisation
detail.abstract: Mid-century climate commentary treats hydrogen, electrification, and artificial-intelligence-optimised grids as three co-equal drivers of a post-carbon industrial economy. The public files treat them as an order. Electricity was 21 percent of world final energy in the IEA World Energy Outlook 2025, and 19.7 percent of primary energy in the Ember/Energy Institute series for 2024. The Net Zero Emissions path needs that share above 50 percent by 2050. Hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels reach about 10 percent of final energy in the same path, and only in residual uses. In the IEA Global Hydrogen Review 2025, world hydrogen demand was almost 100 million tonnes in 2024; new applications were less than 1 percent of that demand; low-emissions production was less than 1 percent of supply. Electrolyser capacity was 2 gigawatts. China held 65 percent of installed capacity and projects at final investment decision. Data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, 1.5 percent of world electricity, 45 percent of it in the United States. In a balanced reading of World Bank access, loss, and internet files and Ember/Energy Institute generation files, 19 of 129 developing countries occupy all three clocks we define-direct electrification, clean surplus, and matching capital-covering 2.1 billion people. Sixty-six occupy none, covering 1.8 billion. Sub-Saharan Africa has one three-clock country, South Africa, and a 91.5 percent share in the zero cell. Electricity's share of primary energy is uncorrelated with solar-plus-wind's share of electricity (0.02). Among 58 countries that eventually crossed both a 2,000 kilowatt-hour floor and an 8 percent solar-plus-wind line, 57 crossed intensity first, on a median lag of twenty-two years. Hydrogen is a residual-molecule technology. AI-optimised grids are matching capital. Direct electrification is the industrial-economy clock. Treating the three as interchangeable pathways inverts the order the files show.

title:
The Global Cooling Gap: 
Why Fans, not Air Conditioners, Will Define Human Survival in a Hotter Century

detail.title:
The Global Cooling Gap: 
Why Fans, not Air Conditioners, Will Define Human Survival in a Hotter Century
detail.abstract:
Climate commentary treats cooling as an air-conditioning story. The hardware file is an air-conditioning story. The
people file is not. In the IEA stock we retrieve, the world held 2.21 billion air-conditioning units in 2023. China
held 39 percent of them. The United States held 19 percent. India, with 1.45 billion people and a cooling-degree-day
load five times the high-income median, held 4 percent: 0.05 units per person against 1.23 in the United States. Sub-
Saharan Africa is not a named series. This paper asks where heat, electricity, and compressor cooling actually sit. In
a balanced reading of World Bank indicators, Ember/Energy Institute electricity files, and ERA5 temperatures, 89
of 122 developing countries are cooling-relevant (monthly-mean cooling degree days of at least 1,500, base 18 °C),
covering 4.72 billion people. Thirty of those countries clear an AC-capable floor — electricity access of at least 90
percent and generation of at least 1,000 kilowatt-hours per person — covering 2.88 billion, of whom 1.45 billion are
Indian. Thirty-six countries sit on a fan floor: hot, wired enough to run airflow, not intensive enough to run a
compressor. That cell holds 1.22 billion people and begins Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Tanzania, Kenya.
Twenty-three countries are unwired heat, 618 million people, beginning Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of
Congo, Uganda. Heat and kilowatt-hours are negatively correlated, at −0.47. Median generation is 640 kilowatt-
hours in hot developing countries and 2,346 in the rest. Sub-Saharan Africa’s AC club is Gabon and Mauritius, 4
million people. Its fan floor is 636 million. Its unwired heat is 554 million. A ceiling fan draws on the order of 70
watts. A room air conditioner draws 1 to 3.5 kilowatts. The survival technology for the hot side of that inversion is
airflow. The hardware catalogue is refrigeration. They are not the same map.

title: Trust-Calibrated Multi-Agent Decision Intelligence for Financial Risk Management under Market Regime Shifts
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Trust-Calibrated Multi-Agent Decision Intelligence for Financial Risk Management under Market Regime Shifts
detail.abstract:
Financial machine-learning models may exhibit unstable reliability when market conditions change, limiting the effectiveness of single-model systems and static ensembles. This study proposes a trust-calibrated multi-agent decision-intelligence framework for forward drawdown warning and downside-risk management under delayed feedback and market-regime shifts. The framework combines three specialized predictive agents representing market, volatility, and residual-stress information, while a separate VIX-based regime module provides contextual information for reliability assessment. Agent influence is updated dynamically using recent predictive discrimination, probability quality, and regime-conditioned reliability. Only fully matured historical outcomes are used in trust updates, and the resulting reliability evidence is smoothed and transformed into time-varying consensus weights. Trust calibration refers to the dynamic calibration of agent influence using observable reliability evidence rather than to perfect probabilistic calibration of the final consensus score.

The framework is evaluated using SPY, QQQ, eleven sector exchange-traded funds, the CBOE Volatility Index, and six macroeconomic indicators from 31 December 2014 to 30 April 2026. The prediction task identifies whether SPY experiences a decline of at least 5% during the following 21 trading days. Architecture and trust parameters are selected using chronological validation and frozen before one-time held-out test evaluation. The validation-selected trust consensus achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.881, PR-AUC of 0.486, recall of 0.818, and F1 score of 0.545. Its transaction-cost-adjusted allocation strategy produces a CAGR of 21.63%, Sharpe ratio of 1.859, Sortino ratio of 2.783, and maximum drawdown of -10.27%, compared with 20.60%, 1.238, 1.847, and -18.76%, respectively, for SPY buy-and-hold. Paired moving-block bootstrap analysis supports positive Sharpe-ratio differences relative to buy-and-hold, matched fixed exposure, and volatility targeting, whereas predictive superiority over the strongest unified baseline is not statistically established. The framework is therefore best interpreted as a transparent model-governance and decision-support layer for dynamically coordinating heterogeneous predictive models under delayed feedback and changing market conditions.

title: Choice Consistency in Symmetric Centrality Operators: The Smallest Loss Criterion Reconsidered
affiliations: National Institute for Space Research

detail.title: Choice Consistency in Symmetric Centrality Operators: The Smallest Loss Criterion Reconsidered

declarations.funderStatement: no funding

detail.abstract: Many decision rules select a single representative point from a finite set of alternatives evaluated on several conflicting criteria, without recourse to preferences, weights, or a pre-existing total order. Such rules are naturally modeled as choice correspondences C(A) ⊆ A on the family of nonempty finite subsets of R k. We study the class of configuration-dependent correspondences, in which the value assigned to an alternative depends not only on that alternative but on the configuration of the whole set, and we ask when this class can satisfy two standard consistency conditions on choice correspondences: Sen's contraction property α and expansion property β. We show that effective configuration-dependence (genuine reversal of the relative ranking of two alternatives as the configuration changes) is what drives inconsistency, and give a general sufficient condition, together with concrete verified examples, under which such reversal forces a violation of α or β. We also identify a class of operators, additively separable in the alternative and the configuration, that is formally configurationdependent yet always rationalizable by a fixed weak order and therefore always consistent. The Smallest Loss Criterion, a compromise rule from applied multiobjective optimization, instantiates both cases within a single family: its component-wise (Chebyshev) variant is effectively 1 configuration-dependent and violates both consistency conditions with non-negligible frequency, while its mean-aggregation variant is provably rationalizable and never violates either. This contrast, rather than a blanket impossibility result, is the structural content of the paper, and situates the Smallest Loss Criterion explicitly within the choice-function literature initiated by Arrow, Sen, and Aizerman and Malishevski.

title: Is Inflation Causally Monetary? A Global, Historical, Institutional, Balance-sheet, and Falsification Audit

detail.title: Is Inflation Causally Monetary? A Global, Historical, Institutional, Balance-sheet, and Falsification Audit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The research relies exclusively on publicly available, secondary, aggregate country-level data and does not involve human participants, interventions, personally identifiable information, or individual-level confidential data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Is inflation causally monetary, or do monetary aggregates primarily record endogenous accommodation of fiscal, exchange-rate, credit, supply, and expectations shocks? We conduct a layered adversarial audit rather than a single preferred regression. The global core covers up to 215 economies over 1960-2024, with 4,202 preferred country-years from 133 economies, and is replicated against independent price baskets, IMF central-bank balance sheets and government finance, legal central-bank independence, and the JST macrohistory panel beginning in 1870. The design combines two-way fixed effects, distributed lags, local projections, DML, dynamic-bias correction, weak-IV/GMM diagnostics, Anderson-Rubin inversion, multiplicity control, serial-preserving and spectral placebos, wild-cluster randomization, omitted-confounding sensitivity, low-frequency and first-difference tests, structural breaks, selection weighting and multiple imputation, SIMEX measurement-error stress, cross-sectional-dependence corrections, country-slope meta-analysis, equivalence tests, transition hazards, reverse local projections, specification curves, extreme-shock estimators, and strict space-time validation. Broad-money growth remains a highly robust reduced-form inflation signal: the preferred M2 coefficient is 0.243 and survives double clustering, Driscoll-Kraay inference, common-correlated-effects controls, country polynomial trends, wild-cluster randomization (p = 0.002), same-year foreign-money reassignment (p = 0.005), Fourier phase randomization (p = 0.005), and deletion of any single decade. Independent annual price outcomes and JST history reproduce the positive sign. Yet stronger claims fail. Post-2000 and post-2010 coefficients approach zero; first differences of annual inflation and money-growth rates yield only 0.036 (p = 0.053); country slopes are highly heterogeneous (I 2 ≈ 77%); modern monetary-base effects are statistically small; internal lag instruments fail validity diagnostics; and reverse local projections show inflation predicting future M2 for several years. The cumulative evidence therefore rejects both monetary irrelevance and a universal quantity rule. Monetary quantities provide robust, portable, state-and institutiondependent evidence of nominal propagation, but observed money growth is an endogenous proxy rather than a universally exogenous treatment, and no invariant structural monetary elasticity is identified.

title: Economic Co-Benefits of Labour Productivity Gains from PM2.5 Reductions
affiliations: CICERO Center for International Climate Research, , , CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Met Office Hadley Centre, , CICERO Center for International Climate Research and Australian National University (ANU) - National Centre for Epidemiology and Population Health

detail.title: Economic Co-Benefits of Labour Productivity Gains from PM2.5 Reductions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Stringent climate policies are associated with immediate economic costs, whereas the benefits from avoided adverse climate change impacts are largely long term. Near-term economic co-benefits from improved air quality may offset some mitigation costs. However, these benefits remain uncertain and not yet fully quantified. This study assesses the global economic benefits of increased labour productivity resulting from reduced PM2.5 exposure, achieved through reduced fossil fuel consumption and substitution with renewables. Specifically, we focus on productivity gains associated with reduced presenteeism. First, we conduct a meta-analysis to estimate novel PM2.5-labour productivity exposureresponse functions (ERFs). Second, using these ERFs, we quantify labour productivity responses under low-and high-emission scenarios (SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0). These future labour productivity responses are then integrated into a global multi-region, multi-sector computable general equilibrium model to assess the associated economic impacts. Results show that increased labour productivity from reduced PM2.5 exposure leads to substantial economic gains across all regions, particularly in East and South Asia. By 2050, global GDP is projected to rise by about 3%, with East and South Asia experiencing increases of about 5% and 4%, respectively. These near-term co-benefits can offset a large portion of mitigation costs for limiting global warming to below 2°C. Substantial economic co-benefits from increased labour productivity may help address concerns regarding the economic costs of stricter climate policies.

title: Talent Management and Employee Retention: Evidence from Academic and Non-teaching Staff of The University
affiliations: University of Ilorin, Ilorin, Nigeria

detail.title: Talent Management and Employee Retention: Evidence from Academic and Non-teaching Staff of The University
detail.abstract: Prior studies have shown that, after investing in recruitment, onboarding training/development, compensation, and other initiatives, organisations often experience high turnover among high-performing employees. Therefore, this study investigates the effect of talent management on employee retention of academic and non-teaching employees of the University of Ilorin, Kwara State, Nigeria. This was a cross-sectional survey study. The study participants are 3,391 University academic and nonteaching staff. Based on this, 358 samples were selected using the Taro The Yamane formula, and the valid responses were analysed. Simple regression with a significance level of 0.05 was used to analyse data collected via a structured questionnaire. The result indicates that recruitment transparency does not have a statistically significant effect on employee retention, with a coefficient value (R= –0.018; t= –0.320; p= 0.749). In addition, competitive remuneration does not affect employee retention statistically significantly with a coefficient value (R=0.038; t=0.690; p=0.491). The study concludes that, in the context of the study, the practice of talent management will help address employee engagement initially, but, alone, is not enough to guarantee long-term retention. Therefore, adopting a holistic talent management structure that incorporates equitable pay, transparent recruitment, systematic career management, professional learning and development, and enabling leadership is recommended to increase longterm retention of academics and non-teaching staff.

title: Innovation Strategies of Oil Pipeline Transport Companies: Digital Transformation and Technological Sovereignty in a Comparative Perspective
affiliations: MGIMO University

detail.title: Innovation Strategies of Oil Pipeline Transport Companies: Digital Transformation and Technological Sovereignty in a Comparative Perspective
detail.abstract: Oil pipeline transport occupies a strategic position within national energy systems, combining high capital intensity, stringent safety requirements, and growing exposure to geopolitical and technological pressures. This paper examines innovation strategies of oil pipeline transport companies through a comparative lens, drawing on the experience of a leading Russian operator alongside international counterparts in North America, Europe, and Asia. The analysis identifies core directions of innovative development, including digitalization of pipeline monitoring and flow management, high-precision in-line inspection combined with predictive analytics, robotic welding and construction technologies, advanced corrosion-resistant materials, and environmentally oriented leak-detection systems. The paper argues that sustainable innovative development in the sector is best achieved through an integrated approach that combines technological modernization, import substitution of critical equipment, and adoption of internationally proven digital practices, tempered by attention to the sector's specific capital intensity, regulatory constraints, and safety imperatives. The findings contribute to the broader literature on strategic management of innovation in capitalintensive infrastructure industries and offer a framework applicable beyond the oil pipeline sector to other energy transport infrastructures.

title: Handcrafted Graph Features and Temporal Validation for Operational AML Risk Scoring
affiliations: Morehouse College

detail.title: Handcrafted Graph Features and Temporal Validation for Operational AML Risk Scoring

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Anti-money laundering transaction monitoring is a rare-event problem in almost every sense that matters for model design. Laundering labels appear on the order of one case per thousand legitimate payments, false negatives and false positives carry asymmetric costs, investigator queues have hard ceilings, and regulators increasingly ask for scores that can be explained rather than merely computed. Accuracy and static rule thresholds, for all their familiarity, often misread what operations teams are trying to optimize. We describe an implementation-oriented risk-scoring framework trained on 5,078,336 cleaned transactions from the IBM HI-Small corpus (11 attributes). The workflow respects time: a 70/15/15 chronological split on Timestamp, integer risk scores on a 0-1000 scale with five business bands, and a daily alert simulation capped at 2,000 reviews. Twenty-four engineered features mix calendar behaviour, amount structure, channel encodings, bank frequency proxies, and graph centrality statistics computed only from the training period. Message-passing graph neural networks (MP-GNN) and temporal graph networks (TGN) appear here as design references; neither is trained end-to-end in this evaluation. On the held-out test slice (761,751 transactions; 1,561 positives; rate 0.2049%), ExtraTrees with balanced_subsample reached PR-AUC 0.1353 and recall@1% 0.4574. Adding NetworkX centrality features to XGBoost moved PR-AUC to 0.1488 and recall@1% to 0.4664, a modest but measurable lift from relational signal. At the F1-optimal threshold (t = 0.950), precision was 0.1027 (95% CI [0.0947, 0.1114]) and recall 0.3350 ([0.3121, 0.3588]). Under a 100:1 false-negative-to-false-positive cost ratio (t = 0.710), recall rose to 0.7168 ([0.6940, 0.7386]) while precision fell to 0.0506 ([0.0478, 0.0535]). A capacity simulation at 2,000 alerts/day shows qualitatively different behaviour on binding versus non-binding days: on the two high-volume test days (760k+ transactions), recall_under_capacity was 0.205-0.285; a day-weighted mean of 0.849 is inflated because eight low-volume days reviewed every transaction (recall = 1.0 by construction). Transaction-weighted recall under capacity was 0.561. Paired bootstrap on distinct score vectors (B = 1,000) yields ΔPR-AUC = 0.0135 with 95% CI [-0.0024, 0.0284] and P (Δ > 0) = 0.957. This study makes four primary contributions: (1) a temporally honest path from model score to band, threshold, and analyst queue; (2) on this synthetic IBM HI-Small corpus, handcrafted NetworkX centrality features merged with XGBoost suggest improved prioritization relative to the tabular ExtraTrees champion at fixed review fractions; (3) validation machinery spanning cost-sensitive thresholds, capacity simulation, calibration, and drift; and (4) explainability framed as decision support and audit material, not autonomous adjudication.

title: Cost-Efficient Deep Learning for IT Operations Using Model Compression and Edge AI Techniques

detail.title: Cost-Efficient Deep Learning for IT Operations Using Model Compression and Edge AI Techniques

detail.abstract: The growing dependence on power-consuming GPUs in centralized data centres for the deep learning models powering AI-driven IT operations (AIOps), such as for analysis and anomaly detection, capacity planning and intrusion detection. This method is expensive, unsustainable, hard to manage by ITOps teams and requires a high amount of latency. This review provides a consolidation of recent research which has tried to solve the problem of the cost of deploying deep learning for AIOps pipelines by compressing the models. It considers model size reduction principles such as pruning, quantisation, knowledge distillation and low-rank factorisation, as well as the edge / TinyLM deployment model that brings a company closer to the data source: in addition to model size reduction, latency becomes a factor. Additionally, federated and distributed learning are explored for the balance of efficiency on device and ongoing model improvements. The review sources over fifty peer-reviewed and archival sources, and concludes that key benefits of combining compression pipelines can be the reduction in model size by more than 60% and in inference times by approximately 50% with less accuracy loss (less than 3% for moderate compression ratios). Finally, important open challenges in the field are outlined, such as standardized benchmarking, proper security of compressed models and the environmental sustainability of supporting edge energy consumption, and the research challenges that can help achieve the goal of a cost-effective, sustainable AIOps are identified.

title:
Development Economics in the Age of Climate Constraints

Rethinking Growth Models When Environmental Limits Bind

detail.title:
Development Economics in the Age of Climate Constraints

Rethinking Growth Models When Environmental Limits Bind
detail.abstract:
Development economics must be rebuilt for a world in which environmental limits are no longer peripheral externalities but binding stock constraints. The report argues that the carbon budget—a finite, rapidly depleting stock of atmospheric capacity—and the planetary boundaries framework together redefine the feasible space for growth. As the document states, “The environment is no longer a residual. It is the binding constraint on the growth path itself.”

Three core insights follow.

First, climate change is fundamentally distributional. The temperature–growth relationship peaks around 13 °C and declines sharply beyond that point. Poor countries—concentrated in hot regions—sit on the wrong side of this curve and face disproportionate damages they did not cause. As the report notes, “The poorest economies sit…on the hot, declining side of that curve.”

Second, the central empirical question becomes decoupling: whether economies can grow while emissions fall fast enough to stay within the remaining carbon budget. Historically, the world has achieved only relative decoupling—emissions rising more slowly than GDP—while the climate constraint requires absolute and sufficient decoupling, roughly a 7% annual decline in emissions this decade. The report emphasizes that “Reaching a 1.5 °C‑aligned path requires emissions to fall roughly 7 percent per year to 2030.”

Third, measurement must shift from GDP to inclusive wealth, which accounts for produced, human, and natural capital. GDP can rise even as natural capital is depleted and the carbon budget consumed. Under a stock constraint, development must optimize wealth per capita within planetary boundaries, not income flows. As the report concludes, “GDP can rise while the natural capital that underpins future income is quietly liquidated.”

The report’s directive is clear: every growth projection must be evaluated against the carbon budget, and every development strategy judged by its decoupling rate and its impact on inclusive wealth, not by GDP alone.

title: From Hierarchies to Networks: Teaching Network-based Research Methods in Public Administration
affiliations: National School of Political Studies and Public Administration (NSPSPA) and National School of Political Studies and Public Administration(NSPSPA)

detail.title: From Hierarchies to Networks: Teaching Network-based Research Methods in Public Administration
detail.abstract: Public administration systems are increasingly characterized by complex networks of institutions rather than strictly hierarchical structures. This transformation is particularly visible in areas such as multilevel governance, digital administration, and inter-institutional cooperation. As a result, traditional approaches to teaching public administration often struggle to capture the dynamics of contemporary governance systems. There is a growing need for educational approaches that help students and practitioners understand institutional interaction through network-based perspectives. This paper explores the pedagogical potential of network-based research methods for teaching public sector governance in higher education. The study argues that network-oriented analytical frameworks can provide a valuable learning tool for understanding institutional collaboration, policy coordination, and digital interoperability within public administration systems. Using the case of prefect institutions in Romania, the paper illustrates how network-based research can be introduced as a methodological learning approach in public administration programs. Prefect institutions operate at the intersection of vertical, horizontal, and transversal institutional relations, connecting central government, deconcentrated services, and local authorities. This multi-level interaction provides a suitable context for applying network-based analytical methods in educational settings. The paper proposes a conceptual framework for integrating network-based research methods into teaching practices in public administration and governance studies. The approach combines policy network analysis, case-based learning, and institutional mapping to support students in understanding complex administrative ecosystems.
