title: The Economic Law of Autonomous Needs: A Law-Like Framework for Institutional Political Economy
affiliations: University of the Punjab

detail.title: The Economic Law of Autonomous Needs: A Law-Like Framework for Institutional Political Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial or personal relationships influencing the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human subjects, patient data, or empirical experiments. It is a philosophical and conceptual analysis based entirely on publicly available information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author as an independent scholarly contribution.

detail.abstract:
This paper formulates the Economic Law of Autonomous Needs, a law-like framework in the tradition of institutional political economy. The framework identifies a recurring pattern observable across multiple technological transitions and economic systems: human needs frequently emerge through decentralised adaptation, imagination, and experimentation before centralised institutions exist to recognise or govern them; private actors tend to respond through autonomous investment; and as these systems gain social indispensability, institutional intervention—while often delivering genuine welfare improvements—also tends to expand regulatory leverage, manage dependency, and consolidate administrative control.

The paper introduces three analytical principles to explain the mechanisms within this pattern. The Doctrine of Non-Mix argues that welfare functions and control-expansion functions within institutional interventions are analytically distinct and should be studied separately. The Autonomy Severance Principle identifies how institutional instruments applied through wrong causal diagnosis tend to suppress autonomous investment without resolving the original problem. The Induced Investment Dependency Principle states that follow-on private investment depends causally on the visible success of autonomous investment and tends to contract when that trigger is institutionally blocked.

The framework is applied to five historical cases—electricity, central banking, currency and energy systems, solar energy, and artificial intelligence—with explicit recognition that cases vary in the strength of evidence they provide. The paper acknowledges counterexamples, states boundary conditions, and specifies what evidence would weaken the framework. The paper invites editors, scholars, and intellectuals to refine the framework further through stronger case studies and broader comparative testing, with the aim of clarifying how autonomous needs generate autonomous investment and how autonomous investment can subsequently induce further investment within changing institutional environments. This framework identifies a recurring institutional pattern rather than a universal historical law.

title: Bilateral Geopolitical Tensions, Trade Linkages, and Tail Risk Spillovers across G20 Stock Markets
affiliations: , Chongqing University of Science and Technology, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics and Southwestern University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Bilateral Geopolitical Tensions, Trade Linkages, and Tail Risk Spillovers across G20 Stock Markets

keywords: Quantile Vector Autoregression with Common Factors

detail.abstract: Using a quantile vector autoregression with common factors to measure tail risk spillovers across G20 stock markets, we show that geopolitical tension from the source country toward the target country significantly amplifies left tail risk spillovers from the source stock market to the target stock market before 2022, but this effect becomes insignificant after 2022. Meanwhile, geopolitical tension has little effect on right tail risk spillovers. We interpret this pattern through trade linkages. Before 2022, geopolitical tension did not significantly reduce bilateral trade linkage intensity, allowing existing trade linkages to transmit and amplify adverse shocks. After 2022, geopolitical tension significantly weakened bilateral trade linkage intensity, limiting the real economic channel through which adverse shocks propagate across stock markets. For favorable shocks, geopolitical tension reduces the incentive to deepen trade exposure to geopolitically sensitive partners, and the post-2022 decline in trade linkage intensity further restricts the transmission of favorable shocks. Heterogeneity tests indicate that the pre-2022 effect on left tail risk spillovers is stronger among geographically proximate country pairs and when the source country has low trade dependence or is a major energy exporter. Overall, our findings suggest that geopolitical tension and recent global fragmentation reshape tail risk spillover networks across country stock markets.

title: The Greek National Climate Law in the Architecture of European Union Climate Governance
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: The Greek National Climate Law in the Architecture of European Union Climate Governance
detail.abstract: This study examines the Greek National Climate Law, Law 4936/2022, as a domestic framework law operating inside the binding and increasingly detailed architecture of European Union climate governance.1 The central thesis is that the Greek statute is not merely a declaratory text adopting the language of climate neutrality. It is a national reception mechanism for Union obligations, a coordination instrument for sectoral decarbonisation, and a legal platform for administrative planning, private compliance and judicial review. Its normative force must therefore be assessed against the European Climate Law, the 2030 Fit for 55 acquis, the 2040 Union target introduced in 2026, the Governance Regulation, and the emerging human-rights dimension of climate litigation.2345 The analysis proceeds in four stages. First, it identifies the structure and legal nature of the Greek Climate Law. Secondly, it places the Greek statute within the hierarchy and functional logic of EU climate law. Thirdly, it tests the domestic provisions against Union expectations on targets, carbon budgets, sectoral measures, adaptation, reporting, just transition and enforcement. Finally, it assesses the unresolved issues: legal justiciability, administrative capacity, the integration of climate planning into licensing and procurement, and the risk that national climate legislation remains programmatic unless connected with binding sectoral duties and effective remedies.

title: Sustainable AI Compute Infrastructure: Data Centers, Resource Demands, and Pathways Forward

detail.title: Sustainable AI Compute Infrastructure: Data Centers, Resource Demands, and Pathways Forward

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Provenance AI / Fact Protocol. This working paper was prepared independently and does not promote or evaluate any proprietary products, services, or systems of the author’s organisations.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work. The author declares no competing financial interests that could have influenced the analysis or conclusions presented.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving substantial growth in data center capacity and associated demand for electricity, water, land, specialised hardware, and skilled labour. This paper examines the resource profile of contemporary AI-oriented data centers and argues that human access to essential resources and the expansion of compute infrastructure should be treated as joint provisioning problems rather than competing claims. Rejecting both the rationing of basic human needs to accommodate AI growth and unconstrained build-out that externalises costs onto communities, the paper develops a practical orientation centered on expanding the sustainable supply of the relevant resources in parallel with demand. Drawing on the most recent International Energy Agency assessments and related evidence, it documents current consumption patterns and near-term projections, reviews sustainability practices already in use, and considers longer-term options. The analysis concludes with five orientations that follow from the joint-provisioning principle.

title: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Greece
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Greece
detail.abstract: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism constitutes one of the most technically complex and constitutionally significant instruments of the European Union climate acquis. It is designed to equalise the carbon cost borne by Union producers under the EU Emissions Trading System with the cost borne by importers of selected carbon-intensive goods, thereby addressing the risk of carbon leakage while preserving the Union's climate ambition. This study examines the CBAM as a legal mechanism rather than merely as an environmental levy. It analyses the structure of Regulation (EU) 2023/956, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2083, its interaction with Directive 2003/87/EC, the transitional and definitive regimes, the duties of authorised CBAM declarants, the calculation and verification of embedded emissions, the treatment of carbon prices paid in third countries, the phase-out of free allocation under the EU ETS, customs-law interfaces, Greek administrative implementation, sanctions, data governance, State aid implications, WTO compatibility and the particular significance of the mechanism for Greek importers, Greek industry and Greek climate law.

title: Technically Informed or Technically Naive? A Critical Gap Analysis of India's AI Governance Guidelines (2025)
affiliations: University of Rochester

detail.title: Technically Informed or Technically Naive? A Critical Gap Analysis of India's AI Governance Guidelines (2025)
detail.abstract: On November 5, 2025, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology released the India AI Governance Guidelines-the country's first comprehensive framework for artificial intelligence governance. Structured around seven guiding principles and six policy pillars, the Guidelines adopt a voluntary, non-binding approach that prioritises innovation enablement over regulatory constraint. This paper offers a critically-informed gap analysis of the Guidelines from a technically-grounded perspective. Drawing on comparative policy analysis against the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act 2024 and the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI Committee Report (2025), and on the machine learning and AI safety literature, the paper identifies four structural gaps: the adverse selection dynamics created by voluntary compliance; the technical infeasibility of proposed governance mechanisms including explainability mandates and deepfake watermarking; weaknesses in the proposed institutional architecture including the absence of a legally empowered cross-sectoral coordination authority; and the inadequate treatment of AI-mediated welfare delivery, where algorithmic failures are already causing documented harm to hundreds of millions of vulnerable citizens. The paper argues that these gaps, if unaddressed in the medium-term phase of India's AI governance action plan, risk producing governance that is more symbolic than substantive in the domains where it matters most. Four targeted directions for policy consideration are proposed that preserve India's innovation-enabling governance posture while addressing the most consequential gaps identified.

title: Impact of the Bitcoin Spot ETF Launches on Cryptocurrency Markets
affiliations: and

detail.title: Impact of the Bitcoin Spot ETF Launches on Cryptocurrency Markets
detail.abstract: SEC approval of spot Bitcoin ETFs was a seminal event for the cryptocurrency industry. The significance of this approval, offers a natural experiment to evaluate the impact of the introduction of spot Bitcoin ETFs on the cryptocurrency market. Considering this background, we explore the impact of the introduction of spot Bitcoin ETFs on the cryptocurrency market using an event study. We identify positive abnormal returns for the cryptocurrency market on the event day. However, this effect quickly fades. Findings suggest that the approval of spot Bitcoin ETFs did not significantly influence the longterm return structure of the cryptocurrency market. Findings have important implications for the legitimacy, efficiency, and liquidity of the cryptocurrency market.

title: Christus Solus
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: Christus Solus
detail.abstract:
What happens to language when a Name cannot be replaced?

Christus Solus is not a book about belief. It is a study of how one Name alters the grammar of every sentence that dares to contain it. From Koine Greek to ecclesiastical Latin, from creeds to confessions, from verbs to articles, the Name Christus does not behave like any other noun. It does not describe. It reorganizes.

In this groundbreaking linguistic inquiry, Agustin V. Startari traces a formal pattern: wherever Christus appears, substitution fails, equivalence collapses, and the sentence loses neutrality. Grammar tightens. Predicates align. Scope narrows. This is not theological rhetoric. It is structural analysis. Drawing on ancient texts, syntactic markers, and the refusal of plural or apposition, Christus Solus exposes the Name not as a symbol, but as a grammatical operator. The result is a sentence that declares, not negotiates.

This book is written for readers who want clarity without reduction, doctrine without simplification, and language without metaphor. It challenges linguistic conventions, bypasses dogmatic filters, and opens a new path: reading Scripture as a structure shaped by one irreversible word.

One Name. No replacement. No equivalence. Only grammar, altered.

title: Addressing the Pollution Cycle: A Systems-Dynamics Model of Environmental Degradation and Recovery

detail.title: Addressing the Pollution Cycle: A Systems-Dynamics Model of Environmental Degradation and Recovery
detail.abstract: The environmental problem is not a cycle. It is a set of loops that run on clocks five orders of magnitude apart, and the argument is lost or won on which clock the decision matches. We assemble the public record and a reduced-form model to quantify the feedback loops that connect emissions, ecosystem decline, and mitigation. The atmosphere now holds 425 parts per million of carbon dioxide, 53 percent above the pre-industrial level, and that stock has not paused even where the flow beneath it has: global emissions have been flat for a decade while the concentration keeps rising. The reason is persistence. Sinks absorb 58 percent of each year's emissions, so 42 percent accumulates, and of any tonne emitted today 41 percent is still airborne in a century and 28 percent in five hundred years. The growth loop that drives the flow is weakening at the margin-the short-run income elasticity of emissions has fallen to 0.50, and 48 of 185 countries now grow output while cutting territorial emissions-but it has not inverted. The balancing loops that close the problem are strong only where the stock adjusts fast. For fine particulates, which clear in days, 138 of 161 growing countries have already cut exposure; for carbon, which clears in centuries, 174 of 202 countries still levy no effective carbon price. The world turned off ozone-depleting substances, a slow stock, in a single generation because the sink existed before the law and the phase-out half-life was under five years. Applying the same stock discipline to carbon shows the operative cost of delay is not the small increment to 2100 temperature. It is the doubling of the abatement rate a later start demands: meeting a 2050 net-zero date after a tenyear pause requires removing 2.7 billion tonnes a year rather than 1.7.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Clean Transition: How AI Could Transform Energy Systems, Industrial Efficiency, and Decarbonization

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Clean Transition: How AI Could Transform Energy Systems, Industrial Efficiency, and Decarbonization
detail.abstract: Climate and technology commentary treats artificial intelligence as a decarbonisation technology. The public files treat it first as a new electricity load. In the IEA's Energy and AI assessment, data centres consumed 415 terawatthours in 2024, about 1.5 percent of world electricity, and are on course for 945 terawatt-hours by 2030. The United States held 45 percent of that 2024 load and 5.6 percent of the world's internet users. Emerging and developing economies excluding China held 55 percent of internet users and, in the IEA's capacity file, less than 10 percent of data-centre capacity. This paper asks whether the countries that can host that load are the countries that can use AI as an industrial-efficiency and clean-power technology. In a balanced reading of World Bank indicators and Ember/Energy Institute electricity files, 18 of 130 developing countries clear all three clocks we define-load capacity, a lever stack of internet-plus-industry, and a clean kilowatt-hour-covering 2.1 billion people. Fortyseven countries clear none, covering 1.3 billion. Sub-Saharan Africa has one three-clock country, South Africa, and a 77 percent share in the zero cell. Median generation in the neither cell is 172 kilowatt-hours per person against 3,304 in the lever cell. India's generation is 1,418: a wired, solar-and-wind-using, AI-services economy that still cannot host a hyperscale load without crowding out everything else on the grid. Kenya generates 18 percent of its electricity from solar and wind and still fails the access, internet, and surplus floors. Solar's levelised cost fell 90 percent after 2010. That is a real clock. It does not make a data centre a climate policy, and it does not make a language model a substitute for a tight wire. AI transforms energy systems where the three clocks already occupy the same country. Everywhere else it arrives as a load, or it does not arrive.

title: Crisis without Collapse: A Theory of Capitalist Persistence

detail.title: Crisis without Collapse: A Theory of Capitalist Persistence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human participants, patient data, or personal data; all data are public and aggregate.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The terminal crisis of capitalism has been predicted regularly since 1848. It has not occurred. We treat this 175-year forecasting record as a stylized fact in need of a model, and we supply one. The model unifies results from five literatures: adaptive systems, mechanism design and computational complexity, behavioral decision theory, global games, and the political economy of redistribution. Ten assumptions deliver twelve formal results and one theorem. Recurring shock classes have geometrically decaying collapse hazards, and the institutional response lag within the banking class alone has fallen from 816 days (1930-33) to 18 days (2008) to 2 days (2023). A centralized replacement of the price mechanism fails on at least one of two horns, computation or truthful input, and we are explicit about which horn survives modern algorithms. Revolutionary participation requires a reference-point break, and we derive Davies's J-curve from cumulative prospect theory together with a new result: the revolutionary window closes endogenously, with length inversely proportional to the speed of hedonic adaptation, roughly four to nine years at calibrated parameters, and with its perceptibility threshold derived from the participation constraint rather than assumed. Personalized media shift protest games, in the model, into the unique no-attack equilibrium of a global game. Redistribution is a dial, not an identity: countries with nearly identical market Ginis (0.505-0.512) sustain disposable Ginis from 0.273 to 0.395. We state seven testable predictions and six falsification conditions, and we map which assumption each rival school must deny.

title: Human AI Decision Hybrids in Middle Managements
affiliations: Lamar University, Lamar University, Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB), Students, University of Hertfordshire - University of Hertfordshire, University of Hertfordshire - University of Hertfordshire and Melbourne Institute of Technology

detail.title: Human AI Decision Hybrids in Middle Managements

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Engineering Technology Research & Management (IJETRM), Volume-06, Issue 03, Pp. 146-154

detail.abstract: Human-AI decision hybrids are emerging as one of the main characteristics of modern organizations, but the consequences of it on middle management are not specified. Middle managers are at the intersection between strategic intention and operational implementation, where they have to balance top-down priorities to coordinated action, to manage risk, people and performance. The article constructs an organized explanation of the way middle-management work is restructured to include the use of human-AI decision hybrids (algorithms plus human judgment, intuition, and contextual sense making) to formulate ideas about their environment. Our decision-rights/trust-calibration model outlines the situations in which middle managers ought to accept, challenge, override or defer to AI output as per uncertainty, explain ability, severity of consequences, and accountability criteria. Adoption frictions, which include, but are not limited to, resistance to algorithmic evaluation, loss of autonomy, or skill atrophy are also identified in the paper and are mitigated by transparencyby-design, human-in-the-loop auditing, competence development to be an effective translator of an AI, and mechanisms to govern actions to preserve accountability and enhance speed and consistency. The contribution represents a workable roadmap on how to design and manage human-AI decision hybrids that can improve performance without compromising managerial agency, integrity and organizational learning. Lastly, we specify testable results such as decision quality, cycle time, fairness, error recovery, and team climate as well as testable propositions to be empirically tested in the field.

title: The Correlation Between Popular Podcasts and Voting in Young Adults

detail.title: The Correlation Between Popular Podcasts and Voting in Young Adults
detail.abstract: This study examined whether political content embedded within popular non-political comedy podcasts correlates with the political beliefs and voting behaviors of young adults ages 18–29. Previous research has shown that traditional and social media can reinforce political beliefs, contribute to polarization, and create ideological echo chambers; however, little research has explored how non-political entertainment media may relate to political attitudes and voting behavior. To address this gap, this study used a mixed-method approach consisting of a content analysis and a correlational analysis. Four popular comedy podcasts — SmartLess, This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von, Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend, and The Giggly Squad — were randomly selected from Apple Podcasts’ comedy rankings. Three episodes per year from 2020–2025 were randomly chosen and analyzed for political mentions categorized as left-leaning, right-leaning, or neutral. These findings were compared with voting demographic data from the Pew Research Center using Pearson’s correlation and Spearman’s rank correlation analyses. The results indicated that each podcast demonstrated a relatively consistent political leaning over time, with most shows favoring either left-leaning or neutral political mentions. Across the podcasts analyzed, neutral political mentions generally increased over time. The correlational analysis identified several strong negative correlation coefficients between political mentions and Democratic voting margins among young adults; however, none of the relationships reached statistical significance at p < .05. While the findings do not establish a causal relationship between popular podcasts and voting behavior, they suggest that popular entertainment media may reflect broader political trends and contribute to ideological reinforcement within audiences. These findings support existing research on media echo chambers and political polarization while highlighting the need for further research on the political effects of non-political entertainment media.

title: Forecasting Asia's GDP Share to 2100: A Multi-Model Comparison Using Convergence Theory, Demographic Projections, and Capital-Formation Dynamics

detail.title: Forecasting Asia's GDP Share to 2100: A Multi-Model Comparison Using Convergence Theory, Demographic Projections, and Capital-Formation Dynamics
detail.abstract:
The uploaded paper constructs a multi‑model forecasting framework—a standard Solow‑Swan convergence model, a demographics‑augmented Solow model, and a capital‑constrained model—to project Asia’s share of global GDP (PPP) through 2100. The models integrate UN demographic projections, GFCF trajectories, TFP convergence estimates, and climate‑damage overlays.

Two key sentences from the document:

“Our central composite forecast estimates that Asia's GDP share will rise from approximately 49% in 2025 to a peak of 55‑56% around 2060‑2070…” “…Under severe climate‑damage scenarios (RCP 8.5), Asia's GDP share could fall below 40% by 2100…”

Core findings

  • Model A (optimistic convergence): Asia peaks near 61% of global GDP by 2100.

  • Model B (demographics‑adjusted): Asia peaks at 55–56% mid‑century, then declines to ~53%.

  • Model C (capital‑constrained): Asia peaks at ~53% around 2050, falling to ~47% by 2100.

  • Composite forecast: Inverted‑U shape, peaking ~2065, ending ~53% in 2100.

Drivers of uncertainty

  • TFP growth, working‑age population dynamics, and climate change account for >70% of inter‑model variance.

  • Severe climate scenarios (RCP 8.5) impose large downside risk, potentially reducing Asia’s share by 14 percentage points.

Contribution

The paper provides a transparent, replicable multi‑model comparison with explicit uncertainty quantification, offering a long‑run forecast horizon to 2100.

title: When the Scenario Outlives the Bond: Measuring Horizon Bias in Climate Credit Stress Tests

detail.title: When the Scenario Outlives the Bond: Measuring Horizon Bias in Climate Credit Stress Tests
detail.abstract: Climate stress tests translate scenario paths into portfolio losses, but the scenario horizon can outlive the instruments being stressed. This paper isolates one implementation choice: whether sector-level shocks are censored at each security's contractual exit. The frozen universe contains 822 Chinese interbank medium-term notes issued by 116 listed legal entities and outstanding at year-end 2025. Holding the NGFS CLIMACRED path, legal-issuer mapping, and portfolio weights fixed, a horizon-blind maximum-loss rule exceeds its maturity-aware counterpart by 0.081–0.253 percentage points across three short-term scenarios. The gap is concentrated in bonds exiting within two years, remains positive in all 5,000 issuer resamples and leave-one-issuer-out exercises, survives a conservative sector-remapping envelope, and can reorder sector rankings. Mean and cumulative variants preserve the positive maximum-loss direction. A terminal-year statistic, which compares different calendar years, is positive in two scenarios and negative in DIRE; the set-inclusion property guaranteeing a non-negative maximum-loss gap does not extend to that statistic. Legal-maturity and first-call variants form a separate modeling margin. For regulators, the result shows why runoff and reinvestment conventions should be explicit in climate stress templates. This is a measurement contrast, not a forecast, causal estimate, realized loss, or claim about market mispricing.

title: The Thermodynamics Of Global Growth: Surplus‑Energy Constraints And The Emerging Limits Of 21st‑Century Economic Expansion

detail.title: The Thermodynamics Of Global Growth: Surplus‑Energy Constraints And The Emerging Limits Of 21st‑Century Economic Expansion
detail.abstract:
Economic growth in the 21st century is increasingly constrained by the physical laws governing energy conversion, entropy, and spatial complexity. This report reframes macroeconomic expansion as an entropic process driven by the dissipation of dense hydrocarbon energy and bounded by declining global Energy Return on Investment (EROI). As the world transitions from high‑density fossil fuels to diffuse renewable energy systems, the margin of surplus energy narrows, exposing structural vulnerabilities across food, manufacturing, financial, and geopolitical systems. The document demonstrates that traditional production models omit the fundamental role of exergy, noting that “capital and labor are…mechanisms for transforming raw energy into ordered societal structure” and that “every dollar of GDP generated requires a precise, calculable throughput of physical energy” .

Using multi‑agent simulations built on the Fraktál engine and statistical‑mechanical modeling, the analysis maps how thermodynamic limits shape GDP scaling, urban geometry, supply‑chain resilience, and regional development trajectories. Declining EROI, rising spatial entropy, and the thermodynamic rigidity of heavy industrial processes collectively generate a global polycrisis, wherein shocks propagate across tightly coupled systems once buffered by cheap energy. The report argues that long‑term resilience and poverty reduction depend on aligning financial expectations, technological diffusion, and urban design with hard physical constraints. Growth in a bound universe requires a strategic pivot toward thermodynamically efficient architectures, complexity management, and physics‑grounded macroeconomic planning.

title:
Comparative PPP Wealth Benchmarks: 
When is a Crorepati a Millionaire?
A cross-country framework for India, Thailand, the United States, the United Kingdom, Mexico and China

detail.title:
Comparative PPP Wealth Benchmarks: 
When is a Crorepati a Millionaire?
A cross-country framework for India, Thailand, the United States, the United Kingdom, Mexico and China
detail.abstract: The terms "crorepati" and "millionaire" are commonly used as shorthand for substantial wealth, yet nominal currency conversion does not provide a meaningful crosscountry comparison of living standards. This paper develops a purchasing-power-parity (PPP) framework for comparing two benchmark wealth targets: (i) INR 10 million (₹1 crore) held in India and (ii) USD 1 million held in the United States. Using World Bank PPP conversion factors and crosscountry inequality evidence from the World Inequality Database / World Inequality Report 2026, the paper translates these wealth benchmarks into local purchasing-power equivalents for India, Thailand, the United States, the United Kingdom, Mexico and China. It then compares the resulting targets with income benchmarks at the national-average, top-10% and top-1% levels. A separate India-specific analysis uses income-distribution thresholds from the World Inequality Lab to distinguish the 90th-and 99th-percentile entry points from the average incomes of people already within the top 10% and top 1%. The paper finds that ₹1 crore has substantially greater domestic purchasing power than its market-exchange-rate dollar value suggests, but remains about half the purchasing-power value of a US$1 million American benchmark. The paper also shows why "years of income needed" must use an income denominator appropriate to the person being studied: the time required falls sharply as one moves from the median to the top 10% and top 1%.

title: Reaction versus Prediction in Trade Execution: A Risk-Management Examination of Regime-Conditional Lead-Lag Signals in XAUUSD-XAGUSD
affiliations: Independent Inventor

detail.title: Reaction versus Prediction in Trade Execution: A Risk-Management Examination of Regime-Conditional Lead-Lag Signals in XAUUSD-XAGUSD
detail.abstract: Prior work on the correlation structure among gold (XAUUSD), silver (XAGUSD), and Bitcoin (BTCUSD) has established that intermarket leadership between assets is regime-conditional rather than fixed: silver has been documented to lead gold during momentum and rally phases owing to its higher beta and more speculative order flow, while gold reasserts leadership during pure safe-haven shocks (Sulistyardi, 2026). This regime-dependence has a direct but underexplored consequence for trade execution and risk management: a signal generated from a lead-lag relationship is only informative conditional on the prevailing regime holding, and that condition cannot be verified in advance. Drawing on the market-microstructure literature on support and resistance (Osler, 2000, 2003) and the behavioral finance literature on overconfident, forecast-driven trading (Odean, 1998; Barber & Odean, 2000, 2001), this paper argues that the resulting uncertainty is best resolved not by predicting which asset will lead and by how much, but by treating the lead-lag relationship as a probabilistic filter that raises the odds of a favorable reaction once price independently confirms structure at an empirically motivated reference zone. We contrast this reaction-confirmation approach with prediction-contingent execution, which acts on the leading asset's signal before the lagging asset confirms, and argue that the former is structurally lower-risk because stop-loss placement is anchored to a confirmed structural invalidation point rather than to a hypothesized future price path. A concrete illustrative trade example is provided, together with an exploratory, scale-independent case illustration (win rate, profit factor, payoff ratio, and R-multiple drawdown, expressed as ratios and percentages rather than absolute currency amounts, with a 95% confidence interval reported for the win rate) drawn from a live trade log, and an agenda for controlled empirical validation using Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and per-trade risk (R-multiple) comparisons is proposed.

title: The Fractal Defense Model: Why Do Individuals and Organizations Retaliate in Similar Ways?
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Fractal Defense Model: Why Do Individuals and Organizations Retaliate in Similar Ways?
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Fractal Defense Model (FDM) to explain why individuals and organizations, despite operating at different levels and possessing different resources, may produce functionally similar defensive responses to criticism, dissent, or problem-raising. Previous research on employee voice, organizational silence, workplace ostracism, whistleblowing retaliation, threat-rigidity, and organizational defensive routines has clarified important mechanisms of silence, exclusion, retaliation, and defensive contraction. Yet less attention has been given to why interpersonal withdrawal and organizational marginalization can assume functionally self-similar forms across levels.

FDM proposes that when problem-raising is redefined as a threat to an existing order, defensive responses may emerge at multiple levels through reduced contact, information restriction, limits on voice and access, role contraction, exclusion, sanction, and subsequent justification. The term fractal is used here as a conceptual metaphor rather than a mathematical claim. It refers to functional self-similarity across organizational levels: different actors may use different resources while reproducing a comparable defensive grammar.

The paper distinguishes Relational Erasure, in which interpersonal recognition, response, information exchange, and relational access are progressively reduced, from Occupational Erasure, in which organizational roles, professional access, participation, skill utilization, and evaluative opportunities are progressively narrowed. It also distinguishes defense from retaliation. Defense describes the actor-side logic of preserving self, authority, order, or legitimacy, whereas retaliation describes the target-side or functional consequences of those actions. When defensive responses across multiple levels converge on the same individual and cumulatively restrict voice, role, access, and recognition, the resulting pattern is conceptualized as Fractal Retaliation.

Furthermore, this study treats defensive responses at the individual and organizational levels not as isolated phenomena, but as forms of functional self-similarity that recur across organizational levels. In doing so, the FDM provides a framework for understanding silence, exclusion, formal sanctioning, retaliation, and organizational defense within a common cross-level perspective. The central question posed by the FDM is not whether defense itself is inherently desirable or undesirable. Rather, the crucial issue is whether, after defensive order has been restored, the organization still preserves channels through which problems can be recognized, dissent can be heard, and its own judgments and institutional arrangements can be revised.

title:
The Next Wave of Convergence
Digital-Industrial Complementarities and the Rise of Mid-Tier Growth Economies

detail.title:
The Next Wave of Convergence
Digital-Industrial Complementarities and the Rise of Mid-Tier Growth Economies
detail.abstract: Following the theoretical foundations laid in previous frameworks analyzing global technology diffusion (Hughes, 2025), this comprehensive research report models the emerging macroeconomic paradigm of "digital-industrial complementarity." As legacy cost-curves in clean energy and artificial intelligence compress simultaneously, mid-tier economies (e.g., India, Vietnam, Mexico, Indonesia) are capturing unprecedented multi-system resilience. By integrating quantitative macro-systems analysis with network geometry, we demonstrate that the historical prerequisite of pure manufacturing-led development is obsolete. Instead, economies leveraging hybrid digital orchestration pipelines over traditional heavy-industrial bases are experiencing accelerated convergence, fundamentally altering global supply chain gravity and polycrisis mitigation strategies for the 2030s. This extended analysis provides a granular breakdown of the computational, energetic, and geometric forces driving this transition.

title: The Core Value of Public Policy Should be Equality
affiliations: University of Utah - College of Social & Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics, University of Utah - College of Social & Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics and University of Houston Law Center

detail.title: The Core Value of Public Policy Should be Equality

declarations.funderStatement: The authors are grateful to the Institute for New Economic Thinking for support

detail.abstract: Research in biology and anthropology shows that humans evolved in largely egalitarian small groups; occasional selfishness was punished. Aversion to inequality is thus an inherited human characteristic. In unequal societies, humans experience stress, leading to many social pathologies, as shown by extensive literature in epidemiology. Well-being can be increased by reducing inequality, independent of increases in GDP. This is obscured by current economic theories, which use unrealistic assumptions and an empirically completely unsupported "equity-efficiency tradeoff" to justify ignoring distribution. Finally, we show that public policy can have an enormous impact on income inequality and has done so in the past.

reference: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 251
title: Adam Smith and the Moral Foundations of Political Economy
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Adam Smith and the Moral Foundations of Political Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This Working Paper is a chapter from Alessandro Roncagli’s forthcoming study of the history of economic thought which will be published by Cambridge University Press

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 251
publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Adam Smith's political economy is best understood as part of a broader inquiry into human beings and society, rather than as a narrow theory of market self-regulation. This paper situates The Wealth of Nations within Smith's wider intellectual project, including his writings on moral philosophy, rhetoric, jurisprudence, and scientific method. It emphasizes the complementarity between selfinterest and sympathy, the centrality of the division of labor to Smith's theory of economic development, and the role of institutions, justice, and public action in sustaining commercial society. The paper also revisits Smith's theories of value, prices, distribution, and competition, arguing against interpretations that assimilate Smith to modern general equilibrium theory or reduce the "invisible hand" to a doctrine of automatic market optimality. Smith emerges instead as a theorist of social interdependence, historical development, and institutional complexity.

title: Free at One Store, $40,000 a Year at the Next: The Break-Even Basket for DC Fast Charging at U.S. Convenience Stores

detail.title: Free at One Store, $40,000 a Year at the Next: The Break-Even Basket for DC Fast Charging at U.S. Convenience Stores

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author operates RightSite, a commercial EV-charging site-selection service that uses the tariff library and pricing methodology described in this paper; this constitutes a financial interest in the subject matter.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract:
Standalone small-scale DC fast charging (DCFC) is not a viable business: the preceding study in this series found small operators cash-negative in effectively every scenario and year through 2036, concluding that small-format charging is rational only as a subsidized traffic amenity for a retail host. This paper quantifies that sentence for the host that matters most - the American convenience store, an industry of 151,975 stores that captures roughly 80% of U.S. consumer fuel purchases. A host does not need the charger to break even; it needs the charger's deficit to be smaller than the incremental in-store gross profit the charger recruits. We define the break-even basket - the dollars of in-store gross profit per charging session required to cover the charger's full cost - and compute it across the RightSite tariff library (332 encoded U.S. commercial rate schedules, 246 verified), at observed convenience-store utilization (about 12% port occupancy), under post-subsidy 2026 conditions: the federal 30C credit expired for property placed in service after June 30, 2026, while the restarted NEVI program still pays up to 80% of capital.

Results: at convenience-store traffic on a 350 kW port, the median conventional tariff prices electricity at $0.50/kWh - above the $0.49/kWh national average retail charging price before any capital or operating cost - against $0.27/kWh on EV-specific rates. The unfunded charger needs a median $9.67 of in-store gross profit per session on conventional tariffs and $3.36 on EV rates; with an 80% capital grant the median EV-rate charger needs $0.00 - it self-funds on charging revenue alone - while the median conventional-tariff charger still needs $4.80. Break-even occupancy is 9.5% on a granted EV rate, below today's convenience-store average, versus 23.5% unfunded on a conventional tariff - above today's national average and beyond all but the busiest U.S. markets. On the base-case utilization path the requirement worsens through a 2027-28 trough, then falls; by 2036 the median unfunded EV-rate requirement is $1.25 per session, while unfunded conventional-tariff sites still need $5.54. Whether a charger is free traffic or a paid amenity is knowable in advance from two documents: the utility tariff and the grant award.

title: Remittances, Household Consumption, and Financial Resilience During Economic Shocks
affiliations: Ulster University

detail.title: Remittances, Household Consumption, and Financial Resilience During Economic Shocks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses secondary, anonymised household survey data and did not involve direct recruitment or interaction with human participants. Therefore, additional ethics approval was not required for this analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how international remittance flows influence household consumption smoothing and financial resilience during periods of macroeconomic stress, using household survey data from remittance-dependent economies across two recent shock periods: the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2021) and the subsequent global inflationary episode (2021-2023). Comparing consumption volatility between remittance-receiving and non-receiving households, the analysis employs a differencein-differences framework alongside household fixed-effects regression to identify the causal effect of remittances on consumption stability and savings recovery. Results indicate that remittance-receiving households exhibit significantly lower consumption volatility and faster recovery in savings rates, suggesting remittances act as an informal insurance mechanism. The paper discusses policy implications for leveraging remittance channels as a complement to formal social safety nets in shock-prone economies.

title: Leading Under Uncertainty: Conviction Work and the Self-Regulation of Founder Confidence in Early-Stage Technology Ventures
affiliations: Duke Kunshan University

detail.title: Leading Under Uncertainty: Conviction Work and the Self-Regulation of Founder Confidence in Early-Stage Technology Ventures
detail.abstract: Founders of early-stage technology ventures face a tension that entrepreneurship research has documented on both sides but never theorized as such: their epistemic situation cannot warrant confident belief, yet their role demands the behavioral outputs of confidence-decisive action, persistent effort, emotional stability, and the skilled public performance of conviction to resource holders. This paper theorizes what happens in the middle. I define the epistemicbehavioral gap as the discrepancy between the confidence a founder's evidence warrants and the confidence the founder's functioning requires, and conviction work as the continuous, effortful self-regulatory process by which founders produce, repair, and perform a conviction state sufficient for decision and persuasion across that gap. I develop a dual-audience process modelthe conviction cycle-in which evidence events generate regulatory demands, founders deploy regulation strategies directed at the evidence, the self, the environment, or the audience, and the resulting performance of conviction recursively shapes private belief through audience responses that become new evidence. Building on this model, I derive a taxonomy of sixteen conviction work strategies, specify the characteristic pathology into which each strategy family tips when overused, and offer a principled account of the boundary between functional persistence and escalation of commitment: regulation remains functional while it operates on the founder's state and situation, and turns pathological when it begins to operate on the admissibility of evidence. Boundary conditions concerning uncertainty type, founder experience, team structure, and cultural display norms are specified, and an experience-sampling research agenda is proposed. The theory repositions founder confidence from a trait-like input to an ongoing, socially embedded regulatory accomplishment, and speaks beyond entrepreneurship to leadership under uncertainty generally.

title: The ASEAN Growth Gradient: Why Vietnam Accelerates, Indonesia Stabilizes, and the Philippines Oscillates Across the Convergence Path

detail.title: The ASEAN Growth Gradient: Why Vietnam Accelerates, Indonesia Stabilizes, and the Philippines Oscillates Across the Convergence Path
detail.abstract:
The report introduces the ASEAN Growth Gradient, a framework explaining why Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines—despite shared regional dynamics—follow sharply different macroeconomic trajectories. Drawing on structural data, institutional reforms, and export‑complexity trends, the study argues that emerging‑market convergence is no longer uniform but segmented into three developmental phases.

Vietnam occupies the Acceleration Phase, propelled by high‑value manufacturing FDI, rapid export‑complexity gains, and aggressive infrastructure expansion, though constrained by emerging energy bottlenecks. Indonesia sits in the Stabilization Phase, leveraging downstream industrial policies to transform volatile commodity sectors into integrated value chains and attract long‑term capital. The Philippines remains in the Oscillation Phase, where strong consumption and services growth coexist with manufacturing deficits and infrastructure gaps, producing cyclical volatility.

By mapping these economies along the gradient, the report provides a predictive lens for external‑shock vulnerability, optimal FDI strategies, and long‑run income trajectories. As global supply chains restructure and demographic dividends peak, the ASEAN Growth Gradient offers a more precise model for investors and policymakers seeking to navigate Southeast Asia’s increasingly divergent development paths.

title: The Perceptual Failure Resilience Doctrine: Adversarial Machine Vision, Autonomous Vehicle Threat Convergence, and the Duty to Detect Sensor Disagreement in the United States National-Security Architecture

detail.title: The Perceptual Failure Resilience Doctrine: Adversarial Machine Vision, Autonomous Vehicle Threat Convergence, and the Duty to Detect Sensor Disagreement in the United States National-Security Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This manuscript is offered as an independent work of legal, national-security, technical, and systems scholarship. Its purpose is to identify a consequential vulnerability arising from institutional reliance on artificial-intelligence-mediated machine perception and to propose a framework for evaluating and mitigating that vulnerability within constitutional and statutory limits. The Perceptual Failure Resilience Doctrine is not advanced as an accusation against any manufacturer, technology provider, law-enforcement agency, governmental institution, autonomous-vehicle developer, or critical-infrastructure operator. Nor does it presume that the failure mechanisms examined herein are universal. Its purpose is to determine whether a plausible, high-consequence architectural dependency warrants formal assessment and proportionate remediation. The manuscript rests on a foundational distinction: machine perception is an interpretation of physical reality; it is not physical reality itself. A system may remain operational while its interpretation becomes incomplete or unreliable. Where protective functions depend upon that interpretation, computational non-recognition may become a failure of institutional awareness. The doctrine does not require technological infallibility. It asks whether high-consequence systems should preserve uncertainty, recognize meaningful disagreement, maintain residual awareness during failure, and prevent a single computational pathway from converting non-recognition into presumed physical absence. This manuscript concerns resilience, not prediction. It does not forecast attacks, identify adversaries, prescribe offensive methods, or provide operational guidance for exploitation. Its concern is architectural dependency. The appropriate response is disciplined assessment: identify the dependency, test it, measure consequence, evaluate mitigation, prioritize according to risk, and reassess as technology evolves. The doctrine is equally bounded by constitutional law. Technical vulnerability does not create governmental authority. Greater sensing capability does not itself justify prolonged tracking, unrestricted aggregation, indefinite retention, generalized suspicion, or coercive action. Detection, identification, suspicion, probable cause, and lawful intervention remain distinct states. The doctrine therefore rejects both institutional blindness and institutional overreach. Artificial intelligence tools were used for research assistance, source identification, organizational support, editing, language refinement, and drafting support. Their role was auxiliary. Artificial intelligence did not originate, formulate, or independently develop the Perceptual Failure Resilience Doctrine, the Sensor-Classifier Disagreement Principle, Perceptual Failure Without Notification, the Perceptual Resilience Test, or the doctrine’s constitutional and systems architecture. The doctrine’s formation, conceptual development, analytical judgments, and substantive conclusions remain attributable solely to Nicolin R. Decker. Artificial intelligence functioned as a research and editorial instrument, not as an author, co-author, legal authority, institutional reviewer, or endorsing party. All responsibility and liability for this manuscript rest solely with Nicolin R. Decker, including responsibility for its formulation, factual assertions, legal analysis, citations, interpretations, omissions, conclusions, recommendations, and publication. No artificial-intelligence provider, developer, operator, or associated institution assumes authorship, endorsement, validation, responsibility, or liability for the doctrine. The governing intent is simple: to strengthen institutional awareness where machine perception may fail while preserving the principle that greater technological capability must never become greater governmental authority by default.

Accordingly, Institutional Review Board (IRB) or equivalent human-subject ethics approval was not sought because the research undertaken for this manuscript did not constitute human-subject research requiring such review. The manuscript nevertheless applies ethical constraints appropriate to national-security scholarship. The paper avoids unnecessary operational detail, distinguishes demonstrated evidence from inference, and does not treat technological capability as justification for expanded governmental authority. The author further recognizes that national-security necessity does not displace constitutional, legal, privacy, or civil-liberties obligations.
