detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates the relationship between physical reality and institutional awareness across automated license-plate recognition, vehicle classification, perimeter security, and related machine-perception systems. This paper identifies a distinct national-security vulnerability arising when computational non-recognition is treated as physical absence. It terms this condition Perceptual Failure Without Notification: a physically present object may fail to survive the machine-perception chain while the larger security architecture lacks an independent mechanism for recognizing that the failure itself is consequential.

The paper proposes the Perceptual Failure Resilience Doctrine (PFRD), which holds that no machine-perception system performing a high-consequence national-security function should possess unilateral authority to convert classifier failure into presumed physical absence when independent evidence of presence can reasonably be obtained. The accompanying Sensor-Classifier Disagreement Principle requires material contradiction between physical evidence and semantic non-recognition to become an observable security state rather than a silent null result.

PFRD develops a two-horizon resilience framework: software-based observability, telemetry, anomaly retention, disagreement detection, and human review in the near term; and risk-tiered independent sensing and multimodal fusion where consequence justifies additional physical redundancy. It further proposes a four-prong Perceptual Resilience Test based on Failure Observability, Independent Corroboration, Graceful Degradation, and Constitutional Constraint.

The doctrine is equally constitutional. Greater technical capability does not create greater governmental authority. Detection, identification, suspicion, historical aggregation, investigative use, and coercive action remain legally distinct. PFRD therefore incorporates Fourth Amendment limits, privacy-by-architecture, data minimization, bounded retention, access controls, auditability, lawful process, and accountable human judgment.

The paper ultimately advances bounded resilience as the appropriate national-security equilibrium: greater detection reliability + narrower information authority + accountable human judgment. Its central contribution is a systems doctrine for ensuring that machine-perception failure becomes observable, institutional awareness survives degraded conditions, modernization proceeds according to consequence, and technological resilience remains subordinate to constitutional law.

title: Economic evaluations of interventions for youth at risk: A critical literature review
affiliations: University of Sussex, School of Education and Social Work, University of Sussex and University of Sussex

detail.title: Economic evaluations of interventions for youth at risk: A critical literature review
detail.abstract: In recent years, constraints on the public purse have led to greater recognition of the importance of allocating social care resources based on rigorous research and evaluation. Despite an increase in experimental and quasi-experimental research into the impact of children's social care interventions over this period, there has been little attention to the development of robust methodologies for economic evaluation. This paper reports a critical review which identified, classified, and synthesized existing economic evaluations of interventions for young people aged 15-24 years. Only 12 articles met the inclusion criteria.Two costing approaches were identified: top-down and bottom-up. Bottom-up was potentially more accurate, since the costs could be linked to participants in the interventions. The most common outcomes were costings for reductions in criminal behaviour and improvement in quality of life. However, there were no outcomes related to employment, educational attainment, or housing, even though they are monetisable.Significant methodological limitations were identified which need to be addressed in future studies. The nature of control groups needs specification beyond ’service as usual’. The process by which outcomes are monetised needs to be explicit as there was a reliance on prior research or estimates without specific adjustments for the population or context. Many studies did not include a sensitivity analysis, or lacked confidence intervals, making it difficult to quantify uncertainty. There were a range of data constraints associated with attrition, missing or partial data. Bias concerns emerged due to the impossibility of double-masked trials and because intervention teams conducted their own evaluations.

title:
We are not Poor. We are being Kept Poor. 
Debt, De-industrialisation, Governance and the Structural Chain Stalling Cameroon's Development

detail.title:
We are not Poor. We are being Kept Poor. 
Debt, De-industrialisation, Governance and the Structural Chain Stalling Cameroon's Development
detail.abstract: Cameroon is not a poor country. It holds significant reserves of oil, natural gas, bauxite, cobalt and iron ore, possesses some of the most fertile agricultural land in Africa, and has a young, growing and largely bilingual population. Yet four decades after the peak of its industrial strength, its GDP per capita in 2024 remains below the level recorded in 1986. This paper argues that Cameroon's development challenges are not a collection of independent problems but a single interconnected chain in which debt mismanagement, governance failure, economic de-industrialisation and human capital loss each reinforce the next. Drawing on publicly available data, presidential decrees, national statistics, IMF and World Bank reports, and recent investigative journalism, the paper traces this chain across four interconnected pillars: debt and dependency, economic diversification, governance and accountability, and education and youth. The central finding is that Cameroon's development cannot be unlocked by addressing any one of these pillars in isolation. It requires simultaneous action across all four, beginning with the governance and enforcement conditions that make every other reform either possible or impossible. The paper identifies the SME environment as the single highest-leverage reform available to Cameroon today: it is both the private-sector engine that can replace the state-led industrialisation model that is no longer fiscally viable, and the domestic job market that gives the country's educated youth a reason to stay. The paper concludes with a chain analysis showing that honest debt management, governance accountability, economic diversification and education reform are not four separate policy agendas but four links in the same chain and that the chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

title: A Measurement Framework for Pine Resin (Pinus merkusii Jungh. et de Vriese) as a Non-Timber Forest Product: Characteristics, Data Collection Methods, and Carbon Potential
affiliations: and

detail.title: A Measurement Framework for Pine Resin (Pinus merkusii Jungh. et de Vriese) as a Non-Timber Forest Product: Characteristics, Data Collection Methods, and Carbon Potential

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, clinical trials, or animal experiments.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Pine resin (Pinus merkusii Jungh. et de Vriese) is one of the most strategic non-timber forest product (NTFP) commodities in Indonesia, the country ranking third worldwide as a pine resin producer after China and Brazil (Sukadaryati, 2014). Beyond its high economic value as a raw material for gum rosin and turpentine, resin-producing stands also play an important ecological role in carbon storage. This study develops a systematic measurement framework for pine resin as an NTFP across four aspects: the biological, chemical, and economic characteristics of the resin; field data-collection methods for stand and resin samples; approaches for measuring carbon content in biomass and resin; and integrated carbon potential calculations accompanied by sensitivity analysis of key assumptions. The framework is illustrated using secondary data from a case study of a 139.2-hectare productive pine stand in RPH Karangsambung, KPH Kedu Selatan, Central Java (Khoirina, 2024), combined with resin carbon-fraction values from elemental analysis of a subtropical pine species (Rodrigues-Honda et al., 2023). Results show a stand carbon stock of 255.29 tons C/ha (equivalent to approximately 937.50 tons CO2/ha), with annual resin production of 22,975.38 kg/ha containing approximately 9.46 to 13.14 tons C/ha/year of carbon depending on the resin carbon-fraction assumption used. The net carbon balance of the tapped stand is negative, but the stand's initial carbon stock can sustain this annual deficit for 20 to 29 years, exceeding a normal tapping rotation. At voluntary carbon market prices of USD 5-50 per ton CO2, the economic value of the stand's carbon stock is estimated at between IDR 10.1 billion and IDR 101.0 billion for the entire study area. The main contribution of this paper is a transparent, replicable measurement framework rather than a definitive claim about carbon potential, so that species-and site-specific values still need to be verified through direct field measurement and laboratory analysis before being used for investment or policy decisions.

title: Quantile Restrictions, Revealed Rankings, and the Limits of Multinomial Choice

detail.title: Quantile Restrictions, Revealed Rankings, and the Limits of Multinomial Choice
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes when choice probabilities reveal rankings of deterministic utility indices in semiparametric discrete choice models. It begins with binary choice, where quantile thresholds guarantee ranking recovery, and shows that such thresholds can arise either from behavioral departures from utility maximization (e.g., limited attention) under exchangeable unobservables, or from non-exchangeable unobservables under standard utility maximization. These behavioral and distributional routes are then extended to multinomial choice with J alternatives. Under limited attention, balance restrictions on attention probabilities yield global linear ranking partitions characterized by J(J-1)/2 two-coordinate representations. These partitions are robust to the distribution of unobservables and, given sufficient joint variation in the differences of utility indices, are also necessary. For J ≥ 4, conditions for more general multi-coordinate representations are provided. Absent the required attention restrictions, opposite rankings can produce overlapping probability images. Under non-exchangeable unobservables, a comparable distribution-uniform partition generally need not exist. 
Holding the distribution fixed, however, ranking recovery remains possible via an injective (generally nonlinear) map from normalized utility differences to choice probabilities under both behavioral and distributional extensions. Together, the results distinguish distribution-robust global ranking partitions from structural ranking recovery.

title: Nonlinear Stock Price Detection in Stata
affiliations: and University of New Orleans - College of Business Administration

detail.title: Nonlinear Stock Price Detection in Stata
detail.abstract: This paper examines the profitability of technical analysis stock price pa6erns defined by five consecu:ve extrema, including head and shoulders, inverse head and shoulders, broadening, triangle, rectangle, double, and combina:on pa6erns. We develop an updated detec:on framework using Mata func:ons and batch files in Stata. We employ local polynomial regression of order one with a Gaussian kernel and cross-validated bandwidth on CRSP data, comple:ng the process in under three hours. Our findings indicate that the pa6erns are economically significant-top pa6erns produce nega:ve one-day returns, while bo6om pa6erns yield posi:ve one-day returns. Addi:onally, condi:oning on increased trading volume enhances bo6om pa6ern returns, and smaller sizes intensify the nega:ve returns of top pa6erns. We also demonstrate early pa6ern detec:on using Gradient Boosted trees, offering :mely forecasts and improved profitability compared to previous models. 3 Key Takeaways: 1. Technical stock price pa6erns of head and shoulders, inverse head and shoulders, broadening top, broadening bo6om, triangle top, triangle bo6om, rectangle top, and rectangle bo6om show posi:ve returns 1 day aQer a completed pa6ern for bo6om and nega:ve returns 1 day aQer a completed pa6ern for top 2. Pa6erns are found in a fixed 38-day window using smoothing technology. The process is updated to detect pa6erns on the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) in 3 hours using Stata. 3. Sta:s:cal significance tes:ng shows that the returns are sta:s:cally different when a completed pa6ern is found compared to the average returns that occurred during the lookback period while the pa6ern was formed.

title: State Policy, Individual Odds: A Multilevel Analysis of Educational Financial Aid Receipt Among Young Adults with Experience in Foster Care
affiliations: University of Louisville and University of Illinois Chicago

detail.title: State Policy, Individual Odds: A Multilevel Analysis of Educational Financial Aid Receipt Among Young Adults with Experience in Foster Care

keywords: young adults with experience in foster care

detail.abstract: Young adults with experience in foster care (YFCE) often face major financial barriers to postsecondary education. Many states have created tuition waivers, scholarships, grants, direct-payment programs, or mixed/hybrid supports for this population, but it is unclear whether formal program presence is associated with individual aid receipt. Using four cohorts of the National Youth in Transition Database (NYTD) Outcomes survey (N = 29,291 at age 21; cohorts 2011, 2014, 2017, 2020) linked to NYTD Services records, we estimated multilevel logistic regression models of reported receipt of any educational financial aid as a function of demographics, independent living service receipt, and a time-varying indicator for whether a state had a foster-care-specific postsecondary support program with a documented formal authorization or establishment date by the Wave 3 observation year. The policy indicator captures formal program presence, not implementation quality or receipt of state-specific aid. At age 21, 19.3% of respondents reported receiving educational financial aid. In the multilevel model, female YFCE (OR = 1.74), Asian YFCE (OR = 3.34), and those who had received education financial assistance services (OR = 2.62) had higher odds of receipt. Aid receipt declined across cohorts, with the 2017 cohort showing the steepest drop. State-level variation accounted for 6.9% of the variance (ICC = .069), but formal state program presence was not associated with reported receipt of any educational financial aid (OR = 0.96, p = .558). Sensitivity checks that recoded uncertain policy entries and varied formal authorization timing produced the same conclusion.

title: Early Detection of Recessions in U.S. Housing and Stock Market
affiliations: , University of New Orleans - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics and Finance and Marquette University

detail.title: Early Detection of Recessions in U.S. Housing and Stock Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines the poten:al bubbles in the housing and stock markets in the United States between 2000 to 2023 by applying :me series methods We test the Backwards Supremum Augmented Dickey-Fuller (BSADF) technique to detect real-:me housing bubbles in both the real and nominal housing market indices, as well as in U.S. stock prices. Our findings indicate evidence of bubbles in the U.S. housing market and raw stock markets prior to the iden:fica:on of a bubble using the price-todividend ra:o. We apply a moving average to the Generalized Supremum Augmented Dickey-Fuller (GSADF) technique to assess its effec:veness in :ming an early exit from bubbles. Our results reveal bubbles in the 2005-2007 housing market, 2008 across all markets, and the 2020-2022 price-to-dividend ra:o, with ongoing bubbles in other markets. The GSADF technique is effec:ve in :ming an early exit for the 2005 U.S. home price bubble, the 2008 U.S. price-to-dividend ra:o bubble, and the 2020 U.S. raw stock prices bubble. The economic implica:ons of these findings remain unclear, but further explora:on of these techniques could be valuable for iden:fying future bubbles. Notably, we detect a bubble in the 2020-2022 price-to-dividend ra:o in the U.S. that is no longer ac:ve.

title: Demurrage in the Age of Alternative Marine Fuels

detail.title: Demurrage in the Age of Alternative Marine Fuels
detail.abstract: By the end of 2021, maritime decarbonization had moved far enough to change commercial planning but not far enough to produce a complete contractual vocabulary for the time lost in using new fuels. LNG already had an international safety framework and port-bunkering practice. Methanol had received dedicated interim IMO safety guidance. Ammonia and hydrogen were prominent in decarbonization studies, while their fuel-specific safety rules were still being developed. At the same time, IMO had adopted its short-term greenhouse-gas measures and the European Commission had proposed FuelEU Maritime and an extension of emissions trading to shipping. The result was a foreseeable category of operational delay that conventional pollution-liability analysis did not answer. A vessel could lose time because fuel was unavailable at the nominated port, because bunkering could not be performed within the expected operational window, because a terminal or authority required additional safety controls, or because the ship, supplier, and port were not technically compatible. No spill or casualty was necessary. This article examines that pre-damage problem through the law of laytime and demurrage. It argues that traditional doctrine can price delay only after the charterparty has identified where the relevant time risk belongs. The emerging fuel transition therefore requires a contractual category of fuel-transition delay tied to control over vessel capability, fuel procurement, port nomination, bunkering arrangements, regulatory documentation, and operational readiness. The article uses only authorities available by the end of 2021 and presents the issue as a problem already visible at the beginning of the transition rather than one reconstructed from later regulation.

title: Endogenous Money, Debt Maturity, and the Yield Curve: A Conditional Stock–Flow-Consistent Post-Keynesian Architecture
affiliations: Hanyang University

detail.title: Endogenous Money, Debt Maturity, and the Yield Curve: A Conditional Stock–Flow-Consistent Post-Keynesian Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses public aggregate data and does not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Coherent revaluation across maturities requires a valuation discipline, while stock–flow-consistent institutions identify money creation, duration holders, and the incidence of revaluation. This paper develops a conditional accounting–behavior–pricing architecture in which an administered overnight rate, endogenous bank credit, maturity-resolved Treasury portfolios, and affine bond prices coexist locally. A conditional local continuation result uses a composed total Jacobian to close the feedback from prices to holdings, revaluation, and subsequent stocks; its derivative separates direct quotation from induced stock-state channels. A corollary shows that accounting alone does not identify the sign or magnitude of duration responses. Calibrated state-contingency illustrations compare debt-maturity and asset-purchase interventions across inherited maturity and bank-capacity states. U.S. diagnostics test ATSM zero-return-exposure and zero-short-rate-loading restrictions, estimate predictive duration projections, and examine externally timed LSAP news. The private-duration full-pipeline 95-percent interval is [−11.41, 0.43] bp and the monthly LSAP full-pipeline interval is [−31.32, 6.28] bp, so both span zero. The exact-date daily yield regression is a same-market timing and aggregation diagnostic because the shock factor uses Treasury-market inputs. These results discipline the interpretation of cross-maturity pricing and incidence without identifying a causal or structural duration elasticity; the empirical exercises do not adjudicate the modeled bank-balance-sheet channel.

title: Dependency-Aware Aggregation of Heterogeneous Model Nowcasts for U.S. CPI Inflation: A Real-Data Walk-Forward Evaluation

detail.title: Dependency-Aware Aggregation of Heterogeneous Model Nowcasts for U.S. CPI Inflation: A Real-Data Walk-Forward Evaluation
detail.abstract: We test whether the dependency-aware Pi_L (lead-lag) aggregator of Stanisljevic (2026) improves U.S. CPI inflation nowcasting over a naive equal-weighted aggregate of heterogeneous model nowcasts, in a strict rolling walk-forward out-of-sample backtest on public FRED data. We build five heterogeneous one-step base nowcasters - a random walk, a 12-month climatology, an AR(6), a ridge regression on a lagged nine-series macro panel (core CPI, PPI, industrial production, payrolls, unemployment, housing starts, retail sales, consumer sentiment, fed funds), and a three-factor principal-component regression on the same panel - and aggregate them three ways: equal-weighted, inverse-MSE, and the Pi_L dependency penalty, whose lead-lag matrix L is estimated on data from the trailing window of base-learner forecasts (not hard-coded) and applied strictly out-of-sample. The backtest covers T=309 monthly forecasts, January 2000 to September 2025, for two estimands: headline CPI month-over-month (the hard target) and year-over-year. The honest finding is mixed-to-negative for the dependency penalty specifically, but positive for ensembling. On the MoM target the equal-weighted and Pi_L aggregates are the two best methods overall (RMSE 0.2640 and 0.2636 pp respectively) and both significantly beat the random walk (RMSE 0.3087 pp) under the nest-appropriate Clark-West test (CW = +4.71 and +4.70, one-sided p ~ 10^-6; standard Diebold-Mariano agrees, DM = -4.46 and -4.49, p < 10^-5) and have lower RMSE than every individual base learner - though the margin over the best learner, the AR(6), is not itself significant (DM = -1.34, two-sided p = 0.182; real-time arm -1.73, p = 0.084), and a 90% model confidence set (Hansen-Lunde-Nason T_max statistic, stationary bootstrap B = 10^4, same absolute-error loss) retains four methods in both arms - the three aggregates and the AR(6), eliminating the random walk, the climatology, the ridge and the factor learner - so what the data certify is that ensembling dominates the weaker learners and the RW benchmark, not that it dominates the best univariate learner, and the Pi_L penalty is statistically indistinguishable from naive equal-weighting (DM = -1.06, p = 0.29): on data-estimated dependency among model nowcasts the Pi_L weights are nearly uniform (0.186-0.213), so the penalty adds essentially nothing beyond the gains from simple averaging. On the YoY target the classic result holds: a plain AR(6) is the single best forecaster (RMSE 0.4097 pp) and the random walk (0.4516) beats the multi-learner aggregates (equal 0.6290, Pi_L 0.6294), which are dragged down by the climatology and factor learners that lag a trending series; Pi_L again ties equal-weighting. We therefore report: (i) ensembling of heterogeneous nowcasters significantly beats the random-walk benchmark on the MoM estimand; (ii) the Pi_L dependency penalty does not significantly improve on naive equal-weighting in this model-nowcast setting, because estimated cross-learner redundancy is small; and (iii) on the persistent YoY estimand no aggregation beats a well-specified AR - consistent with the long-documented difficulty of beating AR/random-walk benchmarks in inflation forecasting. We then close the paper's one substantive limitation by re-running the entire backtest on ALFRED point-in-time vintages (2,930 vintage files, 10 series x 293 monthly vintages, fetched with zero errors), holding the specification fixed and scoring against the first published print rather than the revised value. Real-time data degrades every MoM method (RMSE +4.98% to +10.31%), confirming the revision-noise conjecture on levels; but the headline is untouched and in fact sharper - against a paired revised-vintage control on the identical 286 months, the equal-weighted aggregate's advantage over the random walk is 14.45% of RMSE in real time versus 13.39% revised, and Clark-West rises from +4.35 to +5.60 (p = 1.1x10^-8), because the random walk (whose real-time forecast is last month's first print) suffers most. This contradicts our own pre-registered prediction that the statistic would fall to ~+3.0, and we report it as a failed prediction. Decomposing the degradation, only +1.00% of the aggregate's +8.96% RMSE increase comes from real-time predictors; +7.87% comes from the harder first-print target, so the predictor contamination that motivates the objection is real but small. Pi_L remains inert in real time (DM = +0.41, p = 0.684) with an unstable sign across arms, and the YoY conclusion is unchanged. Six of 292 real-time months are unforecastable at all, lost to federal statistical outages (the 2004 PPI interruption and the 2013 and 2019 shutdowns) that revised data conceals. Every number is computed by runnable scripts on the staged FRED panel and the shipped ALFRED archive; we make no claim that Pi_L improves inflation nowcasting beyond equal-weighting on this evidence.

title: When Does Conformal Recalibration Beat Re-specification? Distribution-Free Intervals for Next-Day Earthquake Counts in California, 2017-2023

detail.title: When Does Conformal Recalibration Beat Re-specification? Distribution-Free Intervals for Next-Day Earthquake Counts in California, 2017-2023
detail.abstract: Operational earthquake forecasting issues daily count forecasts whose Poisson predictive intervals are known to be too narrow when it matters most. On 24,744 California events (M >= 2.5, 2009-2023, USGS ComCat, fetched with zero errors), a temporal ETAS model fit on 2009-2016 and evaluated on 2,555 out-of-sample days under-covers exactly where the operational stakes concentrate: nominal 90% intervals cover 0.885 on quiet days but only 0.748 on the 511 days within 30 days of an M >= 5 event, on which daily counts are massively over-dispersed (variance-to-mean 292 vs 13 quiet). We evaluate two competing repairs and report which one wins, by how much, and where the boundary sits. Coverage numbers carry block-bootstrap intervals over the 13 independent burst episodes, which is the effective sample size for a burst statement. (i) Distribution-free recalibration: online adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candes, 2021) restores marginal coverage (0.900, CI [0.879, 0.917]) and lifts burst coverage to 0.849 - a level that, on 13 episodes, is not itself distinguishable from nominal (CI [0.778, 0.919]); a regime-conditional (Mondrian) variant with separate adaptive streams per regime reaches 0.900/0.883, and what resolves is the paired burst-coverage difference against global ACI (+3.3 pp, CI [+0.8, +6.3] pp). (ii) Re-specification: replacing the Poisson predictive with a negative binomial whose single dispersion parameter is fit on training data (r-hat = 1.677; train log-likelihood +3247.1) recovers most of the coverage deficiency parametrically (0.892 burst) and significantly improves the Winkler interval score (Diebold-Mariano -2.28, p = 0.0225) - a calibration gain, not a sharpness one: NB-raw is the widest construction in the comparison (mean width 7.9 against 5.1 for raw Poisson), and it wins because the score prices a miss at 2/alpha = 20 times a unit of width. No conformal layer on the Poisson base reaches that score level - the Poisson-based Mondrian layer is, if anything, worse than the plain NB parametric baseline (DM = +1.72, p = 0.0848, sign favoring NB), and it is also significantly worse than plain trailing split-conformal (DM = +1.97, p = 0.0490). Giacomini-White conditional tests confirm the difference is regime-structured (chi-squared = 29.98, p < 0.0001). On the corrected NB base, even global ACI achieves balanced regime coverage (0.901/0.900) and the Mondrian refinement adds nothing detectable (p = 0.3865) - but that last ordering is a boundary condition, not a fact: sweeping the ACI learning rate over gamma in [0.01, 0.30] flips it, with Mondrian covering bursts 0.914 against global ACI's 0.869 at gamma = 0.01 and the ranking reversing by gamma = 0.10. Absent a principled (validation-split) rule for gamma, that particular comparison is not identified, and we report it as such. The conclusion that does survive the sweep cuts against the fashionable reading: where the base predictive family is misspecified, regime-conditional conformal recalibration is a genuine fix (global ACI's burst coverage never exceeds 0.857 at any swept gamma); but a one-parameter re-specification buys more - coverage and a significantly better interval score. Conformal's residual, non-replaceable contribution here is the finite-sample distribution-free guarantee (0.901/0.906 without trusting any dispersion model), not repair. All methods are off-the-shelf; the contribution is the measured boundary. Everything reproduces from a committed catalog and five scripts.

title: Multihospital System Affiliation and Patient Experience: The Cost of Persistent EHR Misalignment
affiliations: , Florida International University (FIU) and University of Miami - Department of Management Science

detail.title: Multihospital System Affiliation and Patient Experience: The Cost of Persistent EHR Misalignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Multihospital system affiliation is widely pursued to improve efficiency and coordination, yet its patient-facing consequences remain unclear. This study examines how multihospital system affiliation affects patient experience and whether these effects depend on cross-organizational electronic health record (EHR) alignment. We assemble a longitudinal panel combining hospital affiliation histories, EHR vendor information, and Google reviews for nearly all U.S. general acute-care hospitals from 2011 to 2024. Using a quasi-experimental design that exploits variation in affiliation timing, we find that multihospital system affiliation---a hospital's initial transition from standalone to system-affiliated status---is associated with a 9.2% decline in average ratings, largely driven by an increase in the lowest ratings and a decline in the highest ratings. We further show that while affiliation is associated with increased adoption of the parent system's primary EHR vendor at newly affiliated hospitals, EHR misalignment persists for a significant number of systems, and the decline in patient experience is concentrated among hospitals that remain misaligned with the system's primary EHR vendor post-affiliation, with the effect becoming stronger the longer the misalignment persists. Topic modeling of the lowest star reviews indicates that post-affiliation dissatisfaction centers on billing and payment issues, consistent with coordination frictions from incomplete digital integration rather than clinical care deficiencies. By linking organizational integration, EHR standardization, and patient-facing outcomes, we demonstrate that the benefits of system affiliation depend on whether affiliated hospitals operate on a common EHR system and suggest that consolidating ownership without harmonizing EHR systems limits the coordination gains expected from affiliation.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Copyright Ownership in AI-Generated Works Under Indian, EU, and US Legal Frameworks

detail.title: A Comparative Analysis of Copyright Ownership in AI-Generated Works Under Indian, EU, and US Legal Frameworks

keywords: Indian This paper is a purely doctrinal study involving no human subjects
or empirical experimentation. No ethics committee approval was required

detail.abstract: The rise of generative AI tools that generate content in the forms of text, images, music and literature has posed a basic jurisprudential challenge for Intellectual Property (IP) law. In the existing copyright law, the doctrine of human authorship is the basic doctrine that is under attack by the creation systems that can create an expressive work with little or no human creative input. This paper offers doctrinal and comparative consideration of the copyright questions which arise in the three jurisdictions in relation to AI works. The discussion is drawn from a representative sample of 38 academic, judicial and policy publications identified through a well-documented search and inclusion process (see methodology) that were published in the timeframe of 2020-2026. The analysis shows that there are commonalities in the need for human creative input, and distinctiveness in terms of thresholds, ownership, control of the training data and reform paths. The definition of 'computer-generated works' is quite broad in the Act, 1957 at Section 2(d) (vi) which is yet to be tested before the courts. The 'value gap' is not addressed by the EU's Copyright in the Digital Single Market (CDSM) Directive and the AI Act, but is addressed by transparency requirements. The US Copyright Office has a human-authorship requirement and there is uncertainty regarding the application of fair use to extensive use of AI for training. The paper highlights the structural shortcomings that are shared by the three regimes and outlines an integrated five-pillar approach that is based on the harmonisation work carried out by WIPO at the international level.

title: The Knowledge Economy and Its Sustainability: An Alternative Thought Experiment on the Future of AI Disruption

detail.title: The Knowledge Economy and Its Sustainability: An Alternative Thought Experiment on the Future of AI Disruption
detail.abstract: A recent report from Citrini Research has raised concerns that the dissemination of AI would render human labour obsolete, eventually leading to its own demise (Citrini and Shah, 2026). This paper offers an alternative thought experiment, speculating that AI disruption would instead facilitate the transformation of our current economic system from a post-industrialised economy to a human-centred knowledge economy as depicted in Unger (2019a). The paper augments Unger's discussion by elaborating on three extra characteristics in a knowledge economy: i) the democratisation of entrepreneurship and the rise of innovation agents, ii) the paradigm shift from the division of labour to the division of innovation agents, iii) the role of blockchain technology in accelerating such transformation. As the knowledge economy continues to evolve, two challenges may arise: i) the nature of innovation risks in aggravating inequality, and ii) the insatiable appetite for energy consumption from AI and Web 3.0 industries in causing environmental disasters, which would reshape the priorities of public policies in addressing the sustainability issues. The paper also extends the discussion regarding the new challenges and opportunities for the latecomer economies in the coming era of the knowledge economy.

title: When Measurement Becomes Policy
affiliations: and University of Texas at El Paso

detail.title: When Measurement Becomes Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict

detail.abstract: Place-based programs must update the statistical maps that determine which neighborhoods qualify. Updating retargets benefits toward current need but can repeatedly withdraw legal status from places that organize activity around it. Reconstructing every Community Reinvestment Act tract classification from 1998 through 2024, we show that gross reassignment is three to twenty-six times net map growth and that area benchmarks and tract boundaries explain most entry at decennial refreshes. One in eight residents experiences repeated reclassification. Banks respond by redirecting originations toward eligible tracts. Averaging three survey vintages reduces reassignment and improves five-year-ahead targeting at fixed coverage

title: Discussion-Based Literature Teaching in Secondary School: A Case Study of Students Analytical Skills and Learning Outcomes

detail.title: Discussion-Based Literature Teaching in Secondary School: A Case Study of Students Analytical Skills and Learning Outcomes
detail.abstract: In most English literature classrooms in Nepal, the method is still teacher-centric lecture, translation and rote memorization. Students often read guidebooks instead of original texts, and look for one correct answer in an effort to pass the Secondary Education Examination. The objective of this case study was to explore the impact of discussion-based literature teaching on analytical skills and learning outcomes of Grade 10 students in a community school in Kaski District, Nepal. Forty students were involved in an eight-week intervention that included Socratic seminars, literature circles, and bilingual discussion strategies. The data was collected through analytical writing tasks, reading comprehension tests, engagement surveys, classroom observations, and interviews with students. Results indicated important gains in analytical writing, reading comprehension, engagement, and classroom talk. Students also reported greater confidence, more use of textual evidence, and less reliance on guidebooks. The results indicate that discussion-based literature instruction can be effective in Nepal when teachers are trained and employ culturally relevant bilingual scaffolding.

title: From Interpretation to Action: Freire's Critical Pedagogy in the College English Literature Classroom

detail.title: From Interpretation to Action: Freire's Critical Pedagogy in the College English Literature Classroom
detail.abstract: This case study focuses on utilizing Paulo Freire's Critical Pedagogy to teach English literature at the college level in Nepal. Freire's philosophy challenges the conventional "banking model" of education were teachers deposit knowledge into passive students. However, Freire supports a "problem-posing" education that views students as active participants in the learning process. The paper argues that English literature classrooms in Nepali colleges are often based on the banking model in which teachers give interpretations and students memorize them for examinations. This approach does not teach students to think critically, to be socially aware, or to love reading. This paper examines the present status of English literature education in Nepal on the basis of the publicly available data from the University Grants Commission of Nepal, Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, UNESCO and the World Bank. The data shows low levels of student engagement, weak 2 critical thinking and much of the literature students read is considered irrelevant to their lives. Students can recall details from texts but they cannot analyse them critically or relate them to social issues. The paper applies Freire's core concepts the banking model, problem-posing education, dialog, praxis, conscientization and the culture circle to English literature pedagogy. It advocates for linking texts to students lived experiences in literature teaching, for fostering critical dialog, and for empowering students to act as agents of social change. The paper recommends pedagogical approaches rooted in Freire's philosophy, including problem-posing discussion, critical reading of texts, linking literature to social issues, and projects that promote action. It ends with some suggestions for curriculum change, teacher training and classroom practice. The findings are significant for English teachers in Nepal and other developing countries who are trying to develop socially conscious readers.

title: Pratt's Contact Zone as Cultivating Critical English Knowledges in Rural Nepal

detail.title: Pratt's Contact Zone as Cultivating Critical English Knowledges in Rural Nepal
detail.abstract: The case study explores the use of Mary Louise Pratt's (1991) "contact zone" as a pedagogical tool for teaching English literature to rural college students in Nepal. The contact zone is a social space where cultures meet, clash, and grapple with each other often in contexts of highly asymmetrical relations of power. In many ways, classrooms of English literature in rural Nepal are contact zones. These are spaces where local tongues and global English meet, where Nepali cultural traditions rub against British and American literary traditions, and where students from rural backgrounds wrestle to make sense of the expectations of a global academic culture. In this paper I argue that rural English classrooms are often viewed as one-way spaces where global knowledge is imparted to local students rather than as genuine contact zones where local and global knowledges interact, transform 2 and generate new understanding. Based on publicly available data from the University Grants Commission of Nepal, the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, UNESCO and the World Bank, this paper discusses the challenges and opportunities of English literature education in rural Nepal. The data reveal stark disparities between rural and urban colleges on resources, teacher qualifications and student outcomes. English literature is alien to rural students, as the texts and teaching methods are irrelevant to their lived experiences. This paper draws on Pratt's theory of the contact zone to suggest pedagogical strategies for connecting the local and the global. These strategies include using local texts alongside global ones, encouraging students to draw on their own cultural knowledge, creating space for dialog across difference and critically examining power relations in language and literature. The paper ends with recommendations for curriculum reform, teacher training and classroom practice. The findings have implications for English language teachers in Nepal and other postcolonial, multicultural contexts.

title: When Fundamentals Masquerade as Bubbles: Payout Policy and Clean-Surplus Valuation
affiliations: and Heriot-Watt University - Department of Accountancy, Economics and Finance

detail.title: When Fundamentals Masquerade as Bubbles: Payout Policy and Clean-Surplus Valuation
detail.abstract: Bubble tests based on payout-price ratios require payout to span fundamental value. Cash dividends omit repurchases net of issuance, creating a composition effect, while retained earnings defer shareholder value into book equity, creating a deferral effect. We show that both can confound bubble identification. Our main theoretical result derives a threshold on Lintner's speed of adjustment below which the log payout-price ratio is explosive even when price equals fundamental value. Separately, under a Modigliani-Miller benchmark with complete retention, discounted book equity has the same martingale property as a rational bubble while remaining fundamental. For the S&P 500, observable payout wedges reject a stable payout-spanning representation over 1990Q1-2024Q4. Re-anchoring a survey-disciplined bubble model in clean surplus moves 30 to 50 percentage points of dividend-price variation out of the bubble category.

title: Central Bank Digital Currencies: Are Privacy and Personal Freedom at Stake?
affiliations: University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria

detail.title: Central Bank Digital Currencies: Are Privacy and Personal Freedom at Stake?
detail.abstract:
Opponents of Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) in Europe and the USA have made the threat to privacy and personal freedom a center piece of their argumentation. But how real is this threat? This paper argues that in the context of democracy, freedom of choice, and the rule of law both legal and technological safeguards can be implemented to establish CBDCs as a trusted, not feared, medium of exchange.

From an economic perspective, obstructionism towards CBDC adoption results in missed opportunities for drastic improvements in international payments and money transfers. Also, the current diffidence of developed countries in the field has two main beneficiaries - China and the crypto zone.

title: Economic Law of Competitive Transition: How Economic Leadership Shifts from Autonomous Innovation to Mass Accessibility
affiliations: University of the Punjab

detail.title: Economic Law of Competitive Transition: How Economic Leadership Shifts from Autonomous Innovation to Mass Accessibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial or personal relationships influencing the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human subjects, patient data, or empirical experiments. It is a philosophical and conceptual analysis based entirely on publicly available information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author as an independent scholarly contribution.

detail.abstract: This paper formulates the Economic Law of Competitive Transition, which explains a recurring pattern in modern economic history: how economic leadership shifts as innovations move from autonomous-demand origins to mass-demand markets. The law states that innovations initially created through autonomous investment in response to foundational human, social, economic, technological, or strategic needs eventually demonstrate sufficient utility to expand social desire beyond their original users. This expansion generates induced investment, increases production capacity, and encourages economies of scale. As accessibility increases and competitive criteria evolve from innovation and quality toward scale, affordability, and production efficiency, economic leadership tends to shift from actors optimized for pioneering innovation toward actors better adapted to mass adoption. The paper formalises this mechanism, defines its core concepts—including Autonomous Needs, Induced Investment, Accessibility Threshold, and Competitive Transition—and distinguishes the law from existing theories of innovation diffusion, economies of scale, comparative advantage, and industrial policy. Five falsifiable hypotheses and a systematic empirical strategy are formulated. Case studies from smartphones, solar energy, consumer electronics, East Asian industrial development, and the electric vehicle and battery industries provide illustrative evidence. The institutional role of both market-oriented and state-directed systems is examined. Boundary conditions are identified, and the law is integrated within the broader theoretical framework established by the Economic Law of Autonomous Needs. The central theoretical contribution is the identification of a mechanism through which the dominant basis of competition changes during market expansion, creating the conditions for systematic leadership reordering across firms, industries, and nations.

title: Revisiting the Volatility Puzzle of the Beta Anomaly: Replication and Real-Time Evidence
affiliations: Old Dominion University

detail.title: Revisiting the Volatility Puzzle of the Beta Anomaly: Replication and Real-Time Evidence
detail.abstract: We document a consequential discrepancy at the center of the volatility puzzle in Barroso, Detzel, and Maio (2025), hereafter BDM. The authors' released code reproduces the reported results almost exactly, but it applies an additional fixed 0.75 transformation to the portfolio beta spread that is absent from BDM's published betting-against-beta (BAB) equation. Implementing BDM's published equation (4) reduces the headline low-minus-high BAB-volatility six-factor (FF6) alpha by more than 40%, from about 0.97% per month (t = 3.03) to 0.56% (t = 1.67), and reduces the analogous Table 8 own-volatility spread from about 0.63% (t = 1.84) to 0.16% (t = 0.47). Both discrete-state results lose conventional statistical significance, although the fully controlled continuous-volatility result remains. An independent reconstruction through 2024 shows that 0.75 is nearly market neutral during 1965-2016 but not thereafter: the ex post market-neutral coefficient falls to about 0.59 after 2016, and real-time forecasts indicate substantial time variation in the required hedge. Because BAB volatility is computed from hedged BAB returns, the hedge also changes the volatility-state classification. This endogenous reclassification accounts for much of the sensitivity of the discrete volatility puzzle to hedge construction.

title: The Wage Commons, Derived: From the Firm's Markdown to the Macro Wage Norm

detail.title: The Wage Commons, Derived: From the Firm's Markdown to the Macro Wage Norm
detail.abstract: The wage commons is a derivable object. The claim that atomistic wage suppression is a demand externality no firm prices has so far entered a family of papers on distribution-contingent monetary and fiscal policy as a framing supported by citation. This paper derives it. Firms with monopsony power set wage markdowns taking aggregate demand as given; the wage-setting first-order condition deletes exactly the demand term a coordinating chooser would keep. In a two-agent economy where wage recipients spend more of their income than profit recipients, the deleted term is signed: below capacity, a coordinated increase in the labor share raises output and total consumption. Whether it also raises aggregate profits turns on one threshold, the workers' spending propensity plus the induced-expenditure response exceeding one; at the Kaleckian boundary, aggregate profits are invariant to the wage and suppression buys firms nothing while costing output. The externality is pecuniary, and its welfare relevance is established, not assumed: the markdown, the spending gap, and a demand-determined regime that monetary policy does not offset supply the license. The correction is a payroll-side price with a stated decomposition. The model then enters the standard New Keynesian framework as one wedge in the Phillips curve, one term in the IS curve, and a wage rule that nests, and makes structural, the wage norm of the companion general-equilibrium model.

title: Iran and the Persian Gulf Monarchies: Truth Securitization -Risks and Remedies

detail.title: Iran and the Persian Gulf Monarchies: Truth Securitization -Risks and Remedies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The US restored the Pahlavi monarchy and became friends with Iran in 1953; however, in 1980, it severed ties with Iran after the monarchy was replaced by a republic. Later, the US formed a military alliance with six new Persian Gulf monarchies to combat Iran, a "threat”. To understand the extent and features of Iran's threat to the Persian Gulf monarchies, the analysis employs a legal perspective and examines the constitutional provisions, institutional authorities, and people-power interactions. It concludes with a discussion of the dangers of truth securitization and requirements for establishing peace and security to ensure collective advancement of all.

title: The Empty Operator: Autonomous Cyber Weapons, the Cognitive-Agency Standard, and the Reform of DoD Directive 3000.09

detail.title: The Empty Operator: Autonomous Cyber Weapons, the Cognitive-Agency Standard, and the Reform of DoD Directive 3000.09
detail.abstract: Governance of autonomous weapon systems has converged globally on one requirement: meaningful human control. Three successive United Nations General Assembly resolutions, the CCW Group of Governmental Experts rolling text, and the ICRC's 2025-2026 position paper all insist that autonomous weapons deployed without meaningful human control either violate existing international humanitarian law or must be prohibited. Yet after a decade of consensus on the requirement, no authoritative body has given "meaningful human control" the operational content it needs to function as a legal standard. As a concept, it designates a conclusion. As a test, it is empty. This Article proposes the Cognitive-Agency Standard-a four-element test that gives "meaningful human control" its operational content for autonomous cyber weapon systems specifically. The four elements are: contemporaneous situational awareness, capacity for independent verification, real-time cancellation authority, and traceable authorization chains. Each element is derived from an existing legal source-AP I Articles 52(2) and 57(2)(a)(i), Tallinn Manual 2.0 Rule 105, AP I Article 57(2)(b), and the Bemba Gombo command responsibility standard under Article 28(1) of the Rome Statute-rather than from policy preference. Together, they specify the conditions without which a human being's nominal presence in a targeting cycle

title: Single Sources of Truth and Governance Capability in Public Administration: Interoperability, Evidence Readiness and Digital Administrative Reform
affiliations: University of West Attica (UNIWA) - Department of Business Administration

detail.title: Single Sources of Truth and Governance Capability in Public Administration: Interoperability, Evidence Readiness and Digital Administrative Reform

declarations.ethicsApproval: NO ETHICAL ISSUES
declarations.funderStatement: NO.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted for publication in Market Economy: Modern Management Theory and Practice (RINEC), forthcoming, 2026

detail.abstract:
Contemporary public administrations increasingly operate within complex and data-intensive governance environments characterized by digital transformation, fragmented administrative ecosystems, and growing demands for transparency, interoperability, and evidence-based policymaking. Despite significant investments in digital government initiatives, many public sector reforms continue to face persistent problems of procedural fragmentation, inconsistent implementation, and limited institutional coordination.

This paper examines how Single Sources of Truth (SSOTs) may function not merely as technical interoperability mechanisms, but as governance capability infrastructures supporting institutional intelligence, procedural coherence, and evidence-ready public administration. The study addresses the following research question: how can SSOT-oriented governance systems strengthen interoperability, governance coordination, and adaptive administrative capacity within contemporary public administration environments?

Adopting a conceptual and governance-oriented approach grounded in public administration, digital governance, and knowledge management literature, the paper argues that interoperability fundamentally depends on coordinated procedural ecosystems and structured administrative knowledge rather than technological integration alone. To illustrate the practical dimensions of this governance framework, the study analyses the case of the Greek National Registry of Administrative Procedures (MITOS) as an indicative example of process-centric and knowledge-driven governance reform.

The paper contributes to governance literature by conceptualising SSOTs as infrastructures of governance capability and institutional intelligence rather than merely operational information systems. The findings suggest that SSOT-oriented systems may strengthen administrative consistency, institutional resilience, policy coordination, and evidence-based policymaking in increasingly complex governance environments. The study further highlights the strategic importance of structured procedural ecosystems for future digital governance and adaptive public administration reforms.

title: An Integrated Saudi Logistics Network: Strategic Diversification, Services Capability and Project Implementation
affiliations: Stanford University, Center for Sustainable Development and Global Competitiveness, Stanford University and World Bank - International Finance Corporation (IFC)

detail.title: An Integrated Saudi Logistics Network: Strategic Diversification, Services Capability and Project Implementation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Disclaimer: The findings, interpretations, views, and conclusions expressed herein are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the Executive Directors of the International Finance Corporation or of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (the World Bank) or the governments they represent.

detail.abstract: The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz on February 28, 2026 transformed Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline from a contingency asset into the vital backbone of the Kingdom’s energy sector and fiscal health. The crisis also revealed a broader strategic imperative: the necessity of establishing an Integrated Saudi Logistics Network to accelerate long-term economic diversification. Grounded in the World Bank’s Universal Economic Fitness (UEF) framework – which evaluates national competitiveness across goods and services simultaneously – this paper demonstrates that while Saudi Arabia possesses a notable “services premium,” its capabilities remain heavily concentrated in resource-dependent and geographically captive sectors. To mitigate these concentration risks and exploit the Kingdom’s unique geographic position to bypass volatile maritime chokepoints, we propose creating an Integrated Saudi Logistics Network built around six distinct, capability-driven corridors centered on the Yanbu hub. Employing a screening methodology that tests projects for capability readiness, path feasibility, and execution integrity, the paper outlines a practical, three-phase implementation blueprint. Our analysis indicates that successfully developing this network will enhance Saudi Arabia’s services-sector competitiveness, elevating its global UEF ranking from 43rd to a target of 25th, driven by a transition from raw commodity throughput to sustainable, high-complexity service exports.

title: Purchasing Power Is Not Social Rank Re-examining the Indian ₹1 Crore Benchmark Across Countries

detail.title: Purchasing Power Is Not Social Rank Re-examining the Indian ₹1 Crore Benchmark Across Countries
detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether a purchasing-power-equivalent wealth benchmark occupies a comparable position in the wealth distribution across countries. It builds on an earlier comparative PPP framework that estimates that INR 10 million (₹1 crore) in India corresponds to approximately US$490,000 in purchasing-power terms on the World Bank's 2024 GDP-PPP basis.
The central question is whether this purchasing-power equivalence also implies comparable relative wealth status. The analysis finds that it does not. PPP is fundamentally a price-level measure: it can translate an amount of wealth into approximately equivalent domestic purchasing power, but it does not preserve percentile rank within national wealth distributions. For India, the World Inequality Lab's 2022–23 estimates place the top-1% wealth-entry threshold at approximately ₹81.6 lakh, making ₹1 crore a meaningful approximation of the Indian top-1% wealth benchmark. However, the PPP-equivalent of ₹1 crore is substantially below the reported top-1% wealth thresholds in the United States, United Kingdom and Chinese mainland.

The paper then examines the practical accumulation problem. Using country-specific inflation assumptions, a 10% nominal investment return and savings rates of 30%, 35% and 40%, it estimates the time required to reach both the Indian ₹1 crore PPP benchmark and each country's own top-1% wealth threshold. The exercise demonstrates that the same purchasing-power target can require substantially different accumulation periods because income levels, inflation and wealth distributions differ across countries.

The paper therefore proposes a three-layer framework for understanding wealth benchmarks: nominal wealth, purchasing-power-equivalent wealth and relative wealth position. The analysis shows why statements such as "₹1 crore is a millionaire benchmark" or "the PPP equivalent of ₹1 crore represents the top 1% everywhere" can be misleading when purchasing power and distributional rank are treated as interchangeable concepts.

The results are intended as a transparent comparative framework rather than a causal econometric estimation or a personal wealth forecast. The paper also discusses limitations arising from differences in wealth-distribution methodologies, reference years, income definitions and country-specific price structures.

detail.abstract: US federal debt now stands at roughly the size of the economy and is projected to rise substantially in the coming decades. Population aging, rising health and retirement spending, and mounting interest costs are central drivers of this trajectory, while uncertainty about future interest rates and productivity growth widens the range of possible outcomes. Persistent fiscal imbalances would weigh on economic performance and limit the nation's capacity to respond to future shocks. Because the largest and fastest-growing spending programs support older Americans, eventual fiscal adjustments are likely to intersect with retirement policy, with important implications for retirement security.

title: Has Broader Stock Market Participation Changed How Interest Rates Affect the Economy?
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Has Broader Stock Market Participation Changed How Interest Rates Affect the Economy?

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Stock market participation in the U.S. has changed dramatically over the past four decades. In the mid-1980s, fewer than 30 percent of households held equity. By the early 2000s, more than half of U.S. households owned equity, either directly or through mutual funds, 401(k)s, and IRAs. As participation widened, the way stock market fluctuations passed through to household spending may have changed, with potential implications for how the broader economy behaves. An argument can be made that the rise in equity market participation has dampened the response of output to interest rate changes as stock market fluctuations are now spread across a larger share of households, moderating movements in consumer spending, asset prices, and investment spending.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/08/has-broader-stock-market-participation-changed-how-interest-rates-affect-the-economy/

detail.abstract: This chapter examines why governments prefund retirement benefits or rely on pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) financing, drawing insights from US state retiree health plans following the GASB 43-45 disclosure reform. By increasing transparency and revealing large unfunded liabilities, the reform triggered divergent responses: most states moved toward prefunding, while others continued to rely on PAYGO. States facing higher health cost pressures increased funding more. A conceptual framework explains these divergent responses by highlighting how governments jointly determine benefit design (operating leverage) and financing (financial leverage) subject to constraints such as liability size, legal flexibility, and fiscal capacity. Case studies of Kentucky, Hawaii, New York, and Wisconsin illustrate the main mechanisms and show how the interaction of operating and financial leverage shapes transitions to funded systems.

detail.abstract: Unfunded public pension liabilities exceed $3.8 trillion, yet little is known about the economic cost these obligations impose on residents. We estimate the marginal value of public pension wealth using exogenous variation in state pension fund investment returns and a border discontinuity design. Each dollar of pension windfall per property is associated with an approximately two-dollar increase in house prices, implying that pension shortfalls impose costs substantially exceeding their actuarial value. Pension windfalls have no effect on wages or consumer prices near borders, consistent with theory. The pass-through declines steadily with distance from the border and varies systematically with local political orientation.
