publicationDetails.journalName: Wharton Pension Research Council / Boettner Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Municipal bonds are central to retirement portfolios, offering tax-advantaged income that attracts households and institutions alike. Yet the very tax incentives that make these bonds appealing also create segmentation: incremental state-level tax privilege concentrates ownership locally, limits risk sharing, and heightens the sensitivity of yields to local issuance and idiosyncratic shocks. Evidence from primary issuance and secondary trading reveals similar fragmentation, although each margin has attenuated as the market has institutionalized. What appears to be a safe and straightforward retirement asset is, in fact, embedded in a market whose segmentation is persistent but evolving, with important consequences for public finance and retirement security.

title: When Grid Tariffs Meet Renewable Support Schemes: Evidence of Policy Conflicts from a Market Equilibrium Perspective
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology, Technische Universität Dresden and Dresden University of Technology - Faculty of Economics and Business Management

detail.title: When Grid Tariffs Meet Renewable Support Schemes: Evidence of Policy Conflicts from a Market Equilibrium Perspective
detail.abstract: Dynamic distribution grid charges are designed to improve the utilisation of electricity distribution networks. Yet, by changing the temporal allocation of electricity demand, they may create a policy conflict with renewable support schemes by weakening the market conditions those instruments seek to establish. Across all flexibility configurations considered, dynamic distribution grid charges increase the decline in photovoltaic market values associated with renewable expansion by approximately 10 percentage points.This paper analyses these interactions by reformulating the bottom-up electricity-market model ELTRAMOD as an electricity-market equilibrium formulated as a mixed complementarity problem, jointly solving wholesale market clearing and the cost-minimising dispatch of flexible loads facing both wholesale electricity prices and dynamic distribution grid charges. The analysis considers alternative electricity-system and flexibility configurations that differ in renewable energy penetration and participation in demand-side flexibility. The results show that dynamic distribution grid charges systematically shift demand away from periods of high photovoltaic generation, widening the wholesale price distribution and reinforcing the self-cannibalisation of photovoltaic generation. Beyond reducing photovoltaic market values, they redistribute market revenues from renewable generators towards conventional generators, storage operators, and participating flexible consumers. These findings demonstrate that distribution-grid tariff design should be assessed not only against local network objectives but also with respect to its implications for wholesale electricity markets, renewable investment incentives, and the effectiveness of renewable support schemes.

title: Alliance Effectiveness And Spillovers In Climate Investments: Evidence From Net-Zero Banking Alliance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

detail.title: Alliance Effectiveness And Spillovers In Climate Investments: Evidence From Net-Zero Banking Alliance
detail.abstract: Climate finance alliances seek to coordinate banks’ responses to the low-carbon transition, but their effects on lending portfolios remain uncertain. Using global loan-level data on energy and utility financing from 2011 to 2024, we examine whether membership in the Net-Zero Banking Alliance altered fossil fuel corporate lending, renewable energy project finance, and loan pricing after the alliance’s formation in 2021. We also test whether alliance effects spread to non-member banks through syndicated lending networks. Member banks reduced fossil fuel corporate lending and expanded renewable energy project finance, while we find no robust effects on loan pricing. Non-member banks with greater exposure to large member banks also reduced fossil fuel lending but did not expand renewable energy lending. These findings reveal the uneven effects of climate finance alliances, suggesting that large member banks can discourage environmentally harmful lending among connected banks without inducing comparable growth in their renewable energy financing.

reference: University of Chicago Law Review Online (forthcoming)
title: Extra-Legal Bank Capital Regulation
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and

detail.title: Extra-Legal Bank Capital Regulation

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago Law Review Online (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: After decades of deregulation culminated in the 2008 financial crisis, policymakers identified bank capital requirements as the most important tool for preventing the next one. Congress responded by establishing new capital floors in the Dodd-Frank Act, prohibiting regulators from weakening capital rules below specified levels. The Trump administration is now violating those statutory limits in a misguided attempt to grow the U.S. economy through financial deregulation. This Essay shows how regulators' efforts to dismantle the post-2008 capital framework defy the Dodd-Frank Act's plain text, hand the largest and most systemically important banks an unwarranted advantage over their smaller competitors, and increase the risk of another financial crisis. These ultra vires actions also illustrate the challenges of holding agencies accountable when they violate statutory mandates that lack clear enforcement mechanisms.

title: A Review on the CMS and Peace Corps Matching Program
affiliations: The SPRING Institute, , , The SPRING Institute and The Perrin Research Institution

detail.title: A Review on the CMS and Peace Corps Matching Program
detail.abstract: In June 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed the establishment of a computer matching program with the Peace Corps to verify eligibility for Affordable Care Act premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions. The program will check Marketplace applicants against Peace Corps volunteer records, thus automatically disqualifying current and recently separated volunteers from receiving subsidies during their period of eligibility. This brief will explore the potential benefits and setbacks of the program, if implemented. It will evaluate the impact of the program on different groups of people and cover its likely implications. All in all, this program represents a meaningful addition to the overall goal of the ACA. It expands on its current eligibility verification infrastructure while keeping these additions modest and central to the CMS's goals. However, this program's ultimate effectiveness is contingent on consistent agency compliance, regular oversight, and strict care.

title: Central Bank Communication in a Small Open (Unorthodox) Economy
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest

detail.title: Central Bank Communication in a Small Open (Unorthodox) Economy
detail.abstract: This paper studies what central bank communication reveals and how it transmits in a small open economy. Using Hungarian central bank Monetary Council press releases and minutes, we construct text-based measures of monetary policy stance and map them into high-frequency shock decompositions, a communication-augmented Taylor rule, and local projections. We find that communication in a small open economy works not only through interest rates but also through exchange rates, sovereign risk premia, and its effectiveness depends on the style of communication. Contractionary press release tone is mainly monetary policy shocks and responses to news, raising the yield curve and tightening financial conditions, while minutes contain additional forward guidance and central-bank information. Contractionary communication is also associated with exchange-rate depreciation and wider sovereign CDS spreads. However, the interpretation of communication is regime-dependent: under conventional policy, it resembles a pure monetary policy shock, whereas with an unorthodox approach, it is increasingly interpreted as central-bank information and how the central bank responds to news.

title: Embedding Stealth Assessment in Metaverse-Based Training for PC Building: Advancing Technical Education Using Evidence-Centered Design
affiliations: FEU Institute of Technology

detail.title: Embedding Stealth Assessment in Metaverse-Based Training for PC Building: Advancing Technical Education Using Evidence-Centered Design
detail.abstract: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) programs require reliable methods to teach and assess performance-based skills in authentic contexts. Immersive platforms such as the metaverse offer promising environments for simulating real-world tasks and providing scalable training opportunities. In these technology-rich settings, stealth assessment is recognized as a psychometrically sound and theoretically grounded approach. However, its application has been largely confined to video games and primarily in contexts emphasizing creativity and collaboration. This study broadens that scope by embedding stealth assessment within a metaverse environment to develop and evaluate technical competencies in PC building. Guided by evidence-centered design, a two-part investigation examined (1) the suitability of stealth assessment in a metaverse context and (2) the effectiveness of metaverse-based training in improving learning outcomes and facilitating skill transfer. Undergraduate students from computing and engineering programs engaged in structured PC-building scenarios within the metaverse, where their performance was tracked through automated event logs, validated against expert evaluations, and analyzed using inferential statistical methods. Results indicate that embedding stealth assessment in the metaverse enabled reliable and unobtrusive evaluation of learners’ technical competencies. Metaverse-based PC-building training yielded higher learning gains than traditional methods, and learners demonstrated the ability to transfer skills from virtual tasks to physical PC-building. Overall, these findings offer evidence-informed insights for educators, researchers, and policymakers on integrating immersive technologies and embedded assessments in technical education and vocational training.

title: Algorithmic Wage Opacity and Platform Labor Monopsony: A Structured Narrative Review

detail.title: Algorithmic Wage Opacity and Platform Labor Monopsony: A Structured Narrative Review
detail.abstract: Digital labor platforms increasingly use algorithmic systems to determine worker assignments, compensation, incentives, and access to work. This structured narrative review examines whether algorithmic wage opacity can function as an information-based mechanism that generates or amplifies labor-market monopsony, and whether conventional welfare and antitrust analyses adequately capture that mechanism. The review synthesizes evidence from labor economics, platform-work research, information economics, behavioral economics, and antitrust scholarship. The broader literature provides strong evidence of employer wage-setting power, including low labor-supply elasticities and substantial wage markdowns, although estimates vary across settings and identification strategies. Platform-specific evidence documents individualized and dynamically changing compensation, information asymmetries, reduced predictability, and distributional effects, but direct causal estimates isolating the marginal effect of opacity on monopsony remain limited. Information-economics models provide a plausible bridge: opacity can increase effective search and information costs, alter worker beliefs about outside options, and thereby reduce effective responsiveness to platform compensation. Behavioral evidence, however, cautions against assuming that information costs are linear or that greater transparency is uniformly welfare-enhancing. U.S. merger policy already recognizes labor markets as buyer markets; the unresolved issue is whether existing economic and legal tools adequately measure information-mediated and individualized sources of labor-market power. The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore not that algorithmic opacity constitutes a proven new form of monopsony, but that it is a plausible and potentially measurable mechanism through which effective labor-supply elasticity may be reduced. The review identifies a precise empirical gap: estimating the marginal opacity effect while separating it from concentration, search frictions, dynamic pricing, worker heterogeneity, and other sources of power.

title: The Foundations and Principles for Preferred Creditor Status in Sovereign Debt
affiliations: Columbia University, Faculty of Economics and Political Science, Columbia University and The British University in Egypt

detail.title: The Foundations and Principles for Preferred Creditor Status in Sovereign Debt
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for Preferred Creditor Status (PCS) in sovereign debt restructuring. It proposes a rules-based definition of PCS based on function and lending behavior. Eligibility should reflect a genuine development mandate, sufficiently concessional terms, counter-cyclical lending during crises, and genuinely multilateral governance. Essential trade finance for food, fuel, medicines, and other critical imports could also receive protection. Conversely, lending that substantially resembles commercial finance should not qualify. Clearer criteria would reduce uncertainty, limit moral hazard, improve comparability of treatment, and strengthen the ability of multilateral and regional institutions to support stability and development during sovereign debt crises.

reference: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 212
title: The ESMA and its Potential Transformation into a “genuine” EU capital markets supervisor under the Savings and Investments Union (SIU) project: Towards a Capital Markets Single Supervisory Mechanism (CM-SSM)
affiliations: Faculty of Law

detail.title: The ESMA and its Potential Transformation into a “genuine” EU capital markets supervisor under the Savings and Investments Union (SIU) project: Towards a Capital Markets Single Supervisory Mechanism (CM-SSM)

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 212
publicationDetails.journalName: European Banking Institute (EBI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The key objective of this study, on the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), is to develop a proposal for the establishment of an “EU capital markets single supervisory mechanism” (CM-SSM) – like the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in the banking sector, in which this EU agency would have both direct supervisory tasks and an “oversight function” for that mechanism. The proposal goes beyond the current “targeted centralisation model”, whereby supervisory tasks have been conferred upon the ESMA on a selective basis. On the other hand, it is also different from a “fully centralised model”, whereby the ESMA would become the sole EU capital markets supervisor, i.e., for all financial market participants across Member States.
To reinforce the rationale for this proposal, and put it in the context of the gradual evolution of the ESMA (since 2011) and the current discussions on the development of the Savings and Investments Union (SIU) with two legs (namely, the Capital Markets Union (CMU) and the Banking Union (BU)), the study is structured in two Chapter containing five Sections:
Chapter 1 (titled “The status quo”) contains three Sections:
Section A (“Foundations”) develops on the establishment of the ESMA, its role as an agency, its objective, tasks and powers of the ESMA under the initial provisions of its founding Regulation (ESMAR), its independence, accountability and transparency, ant is liability, as well as the quasi-judicial and judicial review of its Decisions. The following Section B (“Gradual enhancement of tasks and powers through amendments of the ESMAR”) mainly deals with the most significant amendments to ESMAR in 2019 by Regulation (EU) 2019/2175. The last Section in this Chapter, Section C (“The evolution of the ESMA in terms of its temporary intervention and direct supervisory tasks”), presents, in turn, the ESMA’s temporary intervention powers under Article 9(5) ESMAR and the gradual evolution of its direct supervisory tasks from 2011 up to date.
Chapter 2 (titled “Current developments and proposals on the way forward”) is structured in two Sections:
Section D (“Proposals under the evolving Savings and Investments Union (SIU) strategy”), discusses the Draghi Report, the Commission’s Communication of 19 March 2025 and the follow-up “market integration and supervision package” (MISP), then develops on the Commission proposals under the MISP in relation to the ESMA, and finally contains some remarks on a seemingly “uncompleted agenda” in relation to the CMU-related leg of the SIU – including on removing barriers to capital movements – and on the BU-related leg of the SIU. 
The author’s concrete proposal on the establishment of the “EU capital markets single supervisory mechanism” (CM-SSM) is developed in the final Section E (“A proposal for the transformation of the ESMA into a “genuine” supervisory authority within a structured EU capital markets “supervisory mechanism”). This discusses the different models of centralisation in capital markets supervision,  the inclusion of the ESMA and the Member States national competent authorities (NCAs) into the CM-SSM, the supervisory perimeter issue, amendments relating to governance and funding arrangements, the case for further maximum harmonisation in EU capital markets law and the need to eventually restructure the Board of Appeal (BoA). The author’s expectation is that the analysis in this Section fully substantiates his proposal to transform the ESMA into a “genuine” EU capital markets supervisor under the SIU project within an integrated Single Supervisory Mechanism. In a final note in Section E (under 5.3), the potential application of the twin peaks approach for the architecture EU financial supervision is also briefly discussed.
The documentation of the study is supported by references to relevant case-law of EU Courts and literature (albeit on a selective basis in certain cases).

title: Dynamic Risk Intelligence Scoring for UK Start-ups: A Multi-Source Operations-Research Framework for Continuous Monitoring

detail.title: Dynamic Risk Intelligence Scoring for UK Start-ups: A Multi-Source Operations-Research Framework for Continuous Monitoring
detail.abstract: Newly incorporated companies are the hardest population in commercial credit to monitor and among the most consequential to monitor badly. They have no accounting history, they file abridged accounts late or not at all, and the statutory record on which conventional failure-prediction models depend arrives with a lag that can approach the median survival time of the firms it describes. This paper develops the Dynamic Risk Intelligence Score (DRIS), a layered monitoring architecture for UK start-up enterprises that fuses eight heterogeneous evidence families-statutory filing behaviour, published accounts, Open Banking cash-flow telemetry, trade payment conduct, legal encumbrance, governance and network linkage, digital traction, and macro-sectoral conditions-into a single point-intime score, a discrete condition regime, a calibrated twelve-month probability of failure, and an explicit monitoring action.

reference: 84 Wash. & Lee L. Rev. Online __ (forthcoming)
title: Life After Moelis: A Trulia Moment for Governance Claims?

detail.title: Life After Moelis: A Trulia Moment for Governance Claims?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: My firm represents defendants in litigation raising issues similar to those discussed in this essay. The views expressed here are solely my own and do not necessarily reflect those of my firm or its clients.

detail.abstract: At the height of the merger-tax litigation bubble, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued its In re Trulia Stockholder Litigation decision, which disincentivized meritless M&A disclosure claims. Similarly, for the past several years, Delaware corporations have faced a wave of facial validity challenges to charter, bylaw, and governance-agreement provisions. Most of these claims end the same way: the corporation amends the challenged provision and pays a mootness fee, often while maintaining that the provision was lawful all along. Two recent Delaware Supreme Court decisions may disrupt that sequence. Kellner v. AIM ImmunoTech Inc. confirmed that a facial validity challenge fails unless the provision cannot operate lawfully under any set of circumstances, foreclosing claims built on hypothetical abuses. Moelis & Co. v. W. Palm Beach Firefighters' Pension Fund clarified that facial invalidity is not synonymous with voidness: a provision the corporation could have implemented by other lawful means is merely voidable, and challenges to it may be subject to cure, laches, and other equitable defenses. Because only a meritorious claim can support a mootness fee, those decisions substantially reduce the incentive to challenge long-standing, voidable governance provisions in the abstract. These opinions signal a preference to conserve judicial resources for live disputes challenging such governance arrangements where the plaintiff has real skin in the game, such as during a pending or threatened proxy contest.

title: Who Can Deliver the Next Step? Distributed Capability Bargaining and the Politics of Execution

detail.title: Who Can Deliver the Next Step? Distributed Capability Bargaining and the Politics of Execution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, or interventions; ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Political agreements often assume that actors able to negotiate an outcome can also deliver it. Yet in security-and technology-intensive settings, authority to agree may be separated from control over the functions required for execution. This article develops Distributed Capability Bargaining (DCB), a bounded meso-level theory of political executability. DCB explains when control over execution becomes bargaining power: an actor becomes necessary to a political transition when it autonomously controls a critical function that cannot be functionally substituted within the relevant execution window. This condition can redistribute bargaining weight, expand the set of necessary participants, and constrain what a centralized political agreement can reliably deliver. The argument integrates but remains distinct from research on partial implementation, veto players, third-party leverage, network chokepoints, and control rights by specifying a transition-specific causal sequence linking critical function, autonomous control, timely substitutability, behavioral effect, and execution boundary. Using evidence through 10 August 2026, the article traces the mature mechanism in Ukraine and uses Taiwan and Hormuz as structured comparative probes of earlier temporal stages. The comparison shows that anticipatory restructuring can precede mature bargaining effects, while activated disruption can generate functional fragmentation before necessary participation stabilizes. Formally bilateral agreements may therefore remain functionally multilateral in execution.

title: A Conceptual Framework for the Accumulated Cost of Fragmented Institutional Authority in Multi-Stakeholder Infrastructure Projects

detail.title: A Conceptual Framework for the Accumulated Cost of Fragmented Institutional Authority in Multi-Stakeholder Infrastructure Projects

keywords: Cameroon Date: July 2026 VS-WP-2026-003 _ The Coordination Tax

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Coordination Tax as a conceptual explanation for the cumulative cost, measured in delay, administrative overhead, and forgone economic activity, that accumulates when a shared process is divided across multiple institutions, each managing its own segment without a unified structure for the whole. Unlike the Ownership Illusion, examined in Working Paper No. 2, which concerns the diffusion of authority to resolve unanticipated obstacles, the Coordination Tax concerns the routine, predictable cost of coordinating separate institutions through an ordinary, repeatable process. The paper positions this proposition against transaction cost economics, the administrative burden and red tape literature, trade facilitation economics, and coordination theory. It applies the doctrine to two structural consolidation efforts: Chirundu (a bilateral One-Stop Border Post) and Beitbridge (a private concession), both of which produced substantial initial gains that subsequently eroded, in contrast to Kasumbalesa, where the same consolidation model has been recommended for over a decade without implementation. This evidence motivates the paper's central finding: structural consolidation reduces the Coordination Tax at the point of implementation, but the gain requires ongoing institutional maintenance and is not permanent. The paper closes with falsifiable hypotheses, including one testing this maintenance dimension directly, for future comparative research.

Keywords: execution economics, coordination cost, institutional fragmentation, trade facilitation, border governance, transaction cost economics.

title: A Paper Can Be Corrected; a Life Cannot Be Restored: The Irreversibility Rule for Posthumous Research-Integrity Proceedings
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: A Paper Can Be Corrected; a Life Cannot Be Restored: The Irreversibility Rule for Posthumous Research-Integrity Proceedings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or non-financial competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This commentary involved no human participants, private records or non-public data.

detail.abstract: Research-integrity procedures are ordinarily designed around a living respondent who can receive notice, inspect evidence, explain context, challenge attribution and use whatever review or appeal route the governing framework provides. When that person dies before a case is resolved, the scientific question may remain while the procedural subject disappears. The resulting problem is not answered by saying that integrity must continue, nor by treating death as exoneration. It requires a principled distinction between correcting an object—the paper, thesis, dataset or institutional process—and reaching a culpability finding about a person who can no longer participate. Prompted by the unresolved procedural questions following the death of Professor Jason Arday in August 2026, this commentary uses a purposive documentary review of current UK, European, US, Australian and publication-governance instruments. Within the reviewed set, UKRIO’s 2025 template expressly contemplates a deceased respondent but leaves further action to a named official; other frameworks specify notice, response, confidentiality, evidentiary access and review protections that presuppose a living respondent, while ORI’s 2026 state-of-mind guidance highlights evidentiary sources such as respondent interviews and written responses without supplying a death-specific substitute. This article calls that under-specified transition the deceased-respondent gap. It proposes an Irreversibility Rule: after death, institutions should take only the least person-attributive action necessary to protect a defined scientific or public interest, and the justification required should rise with the permanence, publicity and moral force of the proposed outcome. A posthumous status freeze, separation of record, conduct and governance questions, a participation-deficit audit, and four carefully labelled outcome routes are set out. The framework permits necessary correction while rejecting posthumous guilt by procedural momentum. It also establishes a role-specific limit: websites, blogs, post-publication-comment platforms and reporting organisations may supply evidence or leads, but visibility, moderation or repetition cannot complete an unfinished misconduct adjudication.

title: Social Connectedness and Real Estate Investment Trusts (Reits) Investments
affiliations: , University of North Texas - Department of Finance, Insurance Real Estate and Law and University of North Texas

detail.title: Social Connectedness and Real Estate Investment Trusts (Reits) Investments
detail.abstract:
This study investigates how social connectedness between Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) headquarters and U.S. counties affects both the geographic allocation of investments and REIT performance. Using the Social Connectedness Index (SCI) as
a measure of social connectedness, we find that REITs allocate a disproportionately larger share of their investments to counties that are more strongly connected to their headquarters, particularly when entering new markets for the first time. We further find
that greater social connectedness is associated with lower total risk and idiosyncratic risk, although not with superior returns. This effect is more pronounced for smaller REITs and REITs with lower institutional ownership. The results are not driven by local or proximity-based bias. Overall, our findings suggest that social connectedness facilitates access to local information, influences REIT investment allocation decisions, and is associated with improved risk outcomes.

title: Fixed Masses, Moving Locations: A Quantile Method for Heterogeneous-Agent Models

detail.title: Fixed Masses, Moving Locations: A Quantile Method for Heterogeneous-Agent Models
detail.abstract: The state of a heterogeneous-agent model is a cross-sectional distribution; the standard way to carry it numerically is Eulerian, a fixed asset grid whose masses move. This paper proposes the Lagrangian alternative: fixed masses, moving locations. Fixed-mass quantile cells carry each earnings type's capital distribution, restored after each policy update by an exact closed-form recompression. The recompression is W 2-optimal, preserves the first moment, and is non-expansive. In the Krusell-Smith economy, the solver tracks the aggregate-saving moment behind factor prices 13 to 69 times more accurately than a lottery histogram, despite the histogram's better Wasserstein approximation of the distribution. The nonlinear transition matches a sequence-space Jacobian benchmark to 2.9 × 10-5 at a one-percent MIT shock; at five-to ten-percent shocks it tracks a fine-grid reference 14 to 40 times closer than the histogram and 4 to 36 times closer than the linear benchmark.

title: Why CFOs Must Retire the Red-Yellow-Green Cyber Risk Map: A Quantitative Decision-Support Artifact

detail.title: Why CFOs Must Retire the Red-Yellow-Green Cyber Risk Map: A Quantitative Decision-Support Artifact
detail.abstract: Most cybersecurity risk practitioners use red, yellow, and green heat maps, a qualitative method that does not provide defensible financial numbers for Chief Financial Officers (CFOs) or the board of directors. This paper introduces a quantitative risk decision-support artifact developed using the Design Science Research theory, integrating the Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR) framework with Enhanced Bayesian Networks (EBN) and Monte Carlo simulations. By mapping conditional dependencies, for example, a multi-week supply chain freeze, the decision support artifact will translate technical cybersecurity threat scenarios into monetary terms that will allow financial decision-makers to allocate resources more effectively. Applying this model to a retail supermarket chain case study showed a measurable preservation of $6.55 million in risk-adjusted enterprise value. It also demonstrated a compression of the catastrophic tail risk from 48% to 35%. These findings provide a repeatable, mathematically rigorous governance framework that bridges the gap between cybersecurity operations and executive capital allocation.

title: Agentic Workflow Drift in Life Sciences: Extending the Reasoning-Layer Risk Taxonomy to GxP-Regulated Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Operations

detail.title: Agentic Workflow Drift in Life Sciences: Extending the Reasoning-Layer Risk Taxonomy to GxP-Regulated Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Operations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is submitted in an individual capacity as original practitioner-led research. The author has no financial relationships or organizational affiliations that influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents original practitioner-led conceptual research. No human subjects, personal data, animal subjects, or experimental protocols were involved. No institutional ethics review was required or applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Unfunded. This research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI is beginning to support regulated activities across pharmaceutical manufacturing, biotechnology, pharmacovigilance, clinical development, and regulatory affairs through emerging copilots, autonomous workflow orchestration, and AI-assisted quality operations. In these settings, consequential determinations turn on the operational meaning of regulated terms, whether a deviation is critical, whether an adverse event is serious, whether a batch may be released, whether a subject is eligible. These deployments change where regulated operational decisions are formed. Rather than executing predetermined logic alone, autonomous agents increasingly reconcile multiple validated sources to determine what a regulated term means at runtime, and act on the resolved interpretation without a qualified reviewer resolving it first. Every checkpoint clears, every system performs as designed, and the organization is still wrong. This shift introduces a distinct governance exposure. Agentic Workflow Drift is the mechanism by which agentic systems satisfy mandatory validation checkpoints while executing under an unauthorized operational interpretation, producing outcomes that are procedurally compliant and substantively wrong. The analysis distinguishes the reasoning layer within the GxP control environment, demonstrates that computer system validation, 21 CFR Part 11 controls, data integrity programs, and quality management system review each govern an artifact that exists before or after the moment of interpretation, and shows that none governs the interpretation itself as a distinct object. The same reasoning surface also permits deliberate manipulation. That deliberate form is Agentic Workflow Subversion, treated here as a distinct and serious exposure, because in medical research and manufacturing the deliberate steering of an agent's resolved interpretation can influence batch release, safety reporting, and trial eligibility, and through them patient safety and product quality. The concepts translate naturally into established GxP practice, mapping the Reasoning Baseline, the Semantic Deviation Index, and the Deterministic Gate onto established GxP concepts such as predetermined acceptance criteria, review by exception, and quality-controlled definitions, rather than replacing the validation disciplines already familiar to regulated organizations. In the preparation of this manuscript, a large language model assistant supported structural editing and consistency checking of terminology and references against the author's prior working papers. The author reviewed and edited all content and remains fully responsible for the manuscript.

title: Patient informed re-design of hospital default meals: Implications for food provision, packaging use and food service costs
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, La Trobe University and La Trobe University

detail.title: Patient informed re-design of hospital default meals: Implications for food provision, packaging use and food service costs
detail.abstract: Hospitals routinely provide default meals to patients who do not select their meals in advance. Despite concerns regarding unnecessary food provision and patient dissatisfaction, these meals are typically designed around nutritional guidelines and operational requirements, with limited consideration of patient food preferences. This study aimed to use patient preferences to redesign hospital default meals and quantify the effects on food provision, packaging use, and costs. A cross-sectional survey was conducted to assess inpatient preferences for foods provided through the hospital meal service. Data from 147 patients across acute (82%) and subacute (18%) hospital wards formed the redesign the default meal, and the impacts of these changes were quantified. Survey findings informed eight modifications, including the removal of seven consistently low preference food items, reducing food provision by 547 g and packaging provision by three single-use packets (13.5 g) per daily default meal. These changes generated savings of $2.37 per daily default meal, equivalent to annual reductions of approximately 50 tonnes of food supplied, 1.2 tonnes of packaging supplied, and more than $215,000 in food costs. Incorporating patient preferences into the design of hospital default meals represents a feasible, low-cost approach to better align food provision with patient preferences while reducing unnecessary food provision, packaging use, and associated costs. Future research should evaluate the effects of these changes on actual food waste, dietary intake, and patient satisfaction.

title: Environmental Sustainability, Healthiness and Cost of Supermarket Retailer Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverage Categories: An Observational Analysis of Retail Transaction Data from Yorkshire and the Humber, UK (2022)
affiliations: University of Leeds, University of Leeds, University of Liverpool - Department of Geography & Planning, Leeds Beckett University, University of Aberdeen, Scotland and University of Leeds

detail.title: Environmental Sustainability, Healthiness and Cost of Supermarket Retailer Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverage Categories: An Observational Analysis of Retail Transaction Data from Yorkshire and the Humber, UK (2022)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This study was conducted in collaboration with a major UK food retailer for data sharing. No funding or other financial interests were received from the retailer for this or any other research. MSG is a director of Causal Insights Solutions Ltd, which provides causal inference research and training. MAM is an inventor shareholder at Dietary Assessment Ltd, but to date has not received any income from the company and has no role in running the company. All other authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study received approval from the Business, Environment and Social Sciences (BESS) ethical review board at the University of Leeds (AREA 18-050).
declarations.funderStatement: This work was part of the FIO-Food project, funded through the Transforming the UK Food System for Healthy People and a Healthy Environment SPF Programme, delivered by UKRI, in partnership with the Global Food Security Programme, BBSRC, ESRC, MRC, NERC, Defra, DHSC, OHID, Innovate UK and FSA (FIO-Food award: BB/W018021/1).

detail.abstract:
Background: Changing our food system to address the dual challenge of population and planetary health requires greater understanding of the environmental sustainability of food products, and how these interplay with healthiness and food cost. Large scale transaction data from supermarket retailers can be used to better understand these factors, and how consumer behaviours contribute to environmental footprints.

Methods: We used anonymised loyalty card transaction data for 2022 from a major UK supermarket retailer for customers living in the Yorkshire and the Humber region (UK) (>160 million sales). These data were linked with product-level nutrition data to derive a binary indicator of product healthiness (High Fat Salt and/or Sugar (HFSS) status). The sales data were also linked with global estimates for greenhouse gas emissions (GHGE), land use, water use per kg.We described environmental impacts (GHGE, land and water use, and a composite of these domains) of food categories according to the Living Costs and Food Survey categories (n = 64), operationalised as unit metrics (per kg) and sales footprints (accounting for the weight of each product sold). We explored the interplay between product healthiness, cost per kg and environmental impact using visualisation methods.

Findings: For the composite index, the food categories with the highest sales footprints were Beef, Cheese and Curd, Milk, Ready Meals and Chocolate. Category rankings were substantively different when operationalised as impact per kg versus sales footprints, and for GHGE, land use and water use separately. Products that were less healthy and high environmental impact per kg had a median cost per kg that was 350% higher than healthier and low impact products, but there was wide variability in food cost across all levels of healthiness and impact. Fruits and vegetables tended to have favourable profiles across healthiness, sustainability and cost domains.

Interpretation: Sales footprints and unit metrics (e.g. per kg) provide different lenses, which are both needed to understand the sustainability of our food system at a product level, and should be considered in data-focussed policy to drive population and planetary health. Policy should support initiatives to minimise discretionary food consumption, particularly chocolate, and increase fruit and vegetable consumption to improve both human and planetary health.

title: A comparative analysis of machine learning and deep learning model-based prediction of Air Quality Index using real-time vehicular count
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati and Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati

detail.title: A comparative analysis of machine learning and deep learning model-based prediction of Air Quality Index using real-time vehicular count
detail.abstract: The accurate prediction and forecasting of the Air Quality Index (AQI) are mandatory for urban environmental planning and public health decision-making. The article addresses the comparative analysis of the performance of machine learning and deep learning models for Air AQI prediction in Guwahati, India. The models were evaluated based on three performance criteria, namely coefficient of determination (R²), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE), and with both training and testing datasets. Among all models, the XGB performed the best with an R² of 0.980, RMSE of 0.031, and MAE of 0.021. These values reflect outstanding generalization and small error. Deep learning models exhibited some overfitting and larger generalization errors due to data size constraints. In general, tree-based ensemble techniques, more specifically XGB was the best-performing models for Guwahati city’s AQI prediction. These results have the potential to aid data-driven air quality management and associated reduction measures.

title: Whatever It Takes: How Neoliberalism Hijacked the Public Purse

detail.title: Whatever It Takes: How Neoliberalism Hijacked the Public Purse
detail.abstract: The 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic are widely understood as moments that discredited neoliberal orthodoxy and some have even declared it dead. This paper argues that, to the contrary, the massive public interventions during both episodes revived and consolidated it by the method of stabilization and use of public finance. Drawing on the theoretical tradition that treats money as a public institution, the paper traces how public finance was captured by private interests across three episodes—2008 bailouts, pandemic-era fiscal transfers, and the subsequent turn to industrial policy. The paper traces how and why this “whatever it takes” commitment to capital became possible, and argues that the same logic must be extended to financing democratic priorities if neoliberalism is to be meaningfully displaced.1

title: Hope, Signals, and Silicon: A Game-Theoretic Model of the Pre-Doctoral Academic Labor Market in the Age of AI *
affiliations: Georgia State University

detail.title: Hope, Signals, and Silicon: A Game-Theoretic Model of the Pre-Doctoral Academic Labor Market in the Age of AI *

declarations.funderStatement: This research was sponsored by the Army Research Laboratory and was accomplished under Cooperative Agreement Number W911NF-23-2-0224. The views and conclusions contained in this document are those of the authors and should not be interpreted as representing the official policies, either expressed or implied, of the Army Research Laboratory or the U.S. Government. The U.S. Government is authorized to reproduce and distribute reprints for Government purposes notwithstanding any copyright notation herein.

detail.abstract: Generative AI can make early research work easier to produce and harder to interpret. This paper develops a compact game-theoretic model of this productionevaluation tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market. In the model, PIs organize RA labor, allocate AI between routine and novel tasks, and choose mentoring intensity. RAs choose effort, while admissions committees infer research potential from noisy task-level signals under fixed admissions capacity. A mechanism-preserving simulation examines whether the model's qualitative mechanisms continue to hold when RAs and PIs are heterogeneous, research outcomes partly depend on luck, admissions evaluation is noisy, and elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed. The analysis yields three implications. First, routine-task AI can increase observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Second, heterogeneous PI objectives and task complementarity can lead laboratories to adopt different AI strategies, with some emphasizing scalable routine production and others emphasizing mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, when elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed, broad improvements in visible records can raise admissions cutoffs rather than expand access proportionally. The simulation reinforces these mechanisms by showing that AI can raise routine output while weakening the link between evaluated scores and latent ability, increasing the risk that high-ability or high-realized-merit candidates are missed. The paper suggests that as routine evidence loses diagnostic content, evaluation should place greater weight on less easily automated forms of contribution, including judgment, interpretation, research design, and process-based evidence.

title: Advancing the Swiss Cheese Model for Proactive Food Safety Risk Management: Organizational Defence System for Preventing Mineral Oil Hydrocarbon Contamination in Malaysian Palm Oil Mills
affiliations: University of Technology Malaysia, University of Technology Malaysia and University of Technology Malaysia

detail.title: Advancing the Swiss Cheese Model for Proactive Food Safety Risk Management: Organizational Defence System for Preventing Mineral Oil Hydrocarbon Contamination in Malaysian Palm Oil Mills
detail.abstract: The increasing occurrence of mineral oil hydrocarbon (MOH) contamination in vegetable oils and fats, including palm oil, as reported by the European Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF), has intensified global food safety concerns due to its adverse effects on public health. Although previous studies have examined MOH contamination, the organizational defence systems influencing food safety remain underexplored. Grounded in the Swiss Cheese Model (SCM), this study investigates how failures across different organizational defence systems influence the prevention of MOH incidents in Malaysian palm oil mills (POMs). The study advances SCM by operationalizing organizational defence systems into measurable constructs, enabling empirical evaluation of their preventive roles against MOH contamination. Using a quantitative survey approach, data were collected from 187 Malaysian POMs through simple random sampling. The research model was analysed using descriptive statistics in SPSS version 29.0 and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. The findings reveal three key outcomes. First, food safety climate (FSC) and hygienic equipment design (HED) are significant organizational defence systems that positively influence food safety practices (FSP). Second, the maintenance program (MP) does not significantly affect FSP. Third, the findings support the applicability of SCM in explaining MOH incidents within the POM context. The study advances SCM by demonstrating how organizational defence systems can be empirically evaluated to strengthen proactive food safety risk management against MOH contamination. It also provides practical guidance for POM management and proposes an SCM-based approach to strengthen food safety risk management.

title: Scroll To Sale: Impact of Social Media Reels and Influencer Marketing on Generation Z Buying Behaviour
affiliations: , George College of Management and Science and George College of Management and Science

detail.title: Scroll To Sale: Impact of Social Media Reels and Influencer Marketing on Generation Z Buying Behaviour

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not undergo formal review by an institutional ethics board (IRB), as it was conducted as part of undergraduate coursework within the Department of Business Administration at George College of Management and Science, under the guidance of Prof. Deepak Kumar Roy. Given the non-invasive, non-clinical nature of the research (a structured survey examining social media usage and consumer/vendor buying behaviour), formal ethics board review was not institutionally required. Participation in both the Consumer Survey and the Vendor Survey was entirely voluntary. All respondents were clearly informed of the study's purpose, scope, and use of their responses before participating, and both survey instruments included an informed consent note on their first page, which respondents were required to acknowledge before proceeding. No personally identifying information including names, email addresses, or contact details was collected from Consumer Survey respondents. Vendor Survey respondents provided business-level contact details (business name, contact number) solely for verification of authenticity, in accordance with the study's methodology; individual identity was not otherwise disclosed or published. All collected data were anonymised prior to analysis and were used strictly for academic research purposes. No data were shared with any third party. Respondents retained the right to withdraw from the survey at any point prior to submission, and participation implied consent to the anonymised use of their responses in this research.

detail.abstract: Social media has become one of the strongest forces shaping how people shop today, with Generation Z standing out as the most affected group. The continuous rise of short-form content, algorithmic marketing, and influencer marketing has reshaped consumer buying in the digital era. This study aims to examine the impact of social media reels on impulsive buying behaviour and the influence of digital influencers on Gen Z shopping decisions, while also assessing their awareness of responsible consumption practices. A mixed-method exploratory strategy was adopted for this study. An online structured survey was used to gather data from more than 130 respondents to probe Gen Z's social media involvement and purchasing behaviour, alongside a second survey polling vendors on their perspectives on influencer marketing and social media. The impact of past digital hype cycles, such as those involving cryptocurrencies and NFTs, on rational and impulsive financial decision-making was also examined. The study reveals a strong association between social media exposure and impulsive buying among Gen Z consumers. Influencer promotions and short videos have a significant impact on how this group perceives brands and makes purchases. Vendors are also recognising that the digital era is displacing old-school sales tactics. The study emphasises the growing influence of social media on consumer decision-making and points to the need for promoting responsible consumption practices, supporting UN Sustainable Development Goal 12.

title: Digital Infrastructure as Development Infrastructure: Connectivity, Productivity, and Economic Transformation in Emerging Markets

detail.title: Digital Infrastructure as Development Infrastructure: Connectivity, Productivity, and Economic Transformation in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Mobile access has already converged. The production stack has not. In a population-weighted reading of World Bank indicators, 67 percent of people in developing economies used the internet in 2023, against 1.4 percent in 2000. Mobile subscriptions reached 105 per 100 people. Fixed broadband reached 15. In sub-Saharan Africa the same three clocks read 33 percent, 91, and 0.7. High-income broadband is 37. The residual is not a digital divide in the 2000s sense-a missing SIM card. It is a stack gap: electricity, fixed connectivity, secure servers, and the public rails that turn a connection into a transaction, a shipment, or a job. Among 129 developing countries with complete data, 42 meet all four thresholds we use for a full stack, covering 40 percent of developing-country population. Sub-Saharan Africa has two such countries, Mauritius and Seychelles, covering 0.1 percent of regional population. Median GDP per capita in developing stack countries is 19,754 dollars at PPP. In countries with mass mobile and internet below 50 percent it is 4,110. Labour productivity is 48,133 dollars per worker against 17,379. The unconnected headcount fell from 5.5 billion in 2000 to 2.2 billion in 2023. In sub-Saharan Africa it rose, from 671 million to 802 million: population outran the network. ICT service exports make the selection visible in trade. Developing-country ICT service exports were 86 billion dollars in 2010 and 284 billion in 2023. India supplied 57 percent of that 2023 total. Sub-Saharan Africa supplied 4.4 billion. A phone is consumer infrastructure. Development infrastructure is the complementary stack that lets a firm, a farm, or a state use the phone as a production input.

title: AI Adoption in Emerging Markets — Productivity Effects, Labor‑Market Shifts, and Barriers to Diffusion

detail.title: AI Adoption in Emerging Markets — Productivity Effects, Labor‑Market Shifts, and Barriers to Diffusion
detail.abstract:
AI reaches emerging markets quickly because the cost of accessing frontier models has collapsed, but the ability to turn that access into real economic gains remains uneven. The report argues that this gap between arrival and absorption is now the central development question. A Kenyan firm or an Indian clinic can invoke a model that once required a frontier lab, yet the productivity payoff depends on electricity, compute, connectivity, data, skills, and institutions—complements that many emerging economies hold only partially. As the report puts it, “the diffusion of the technology is now fast and nearly free; the diffusion of its benefits remains slow and conditional.”

Productivity effects are large but capability‑dependent. Trials show novice call‑center workers becoming 34 percent more productive and developers completing tasks 56 percent faster with AI assistance, yet a Kenyan experiment found high‑performing entrepreneurs gaining 15 percent while low performers lost 8 percent. This pattern reflects a broader truth: AI amplifies existing capability rather than replacing it. Gains materialize where organizations can redesign processes, where workers have basic digital skills, and where infrastructure is reliable enough to support intensive use. Without these complements, the technology can widen gaps within countries as well as between them.

Labor‑market exposure is lower overall in emerging economies, but it is concentrated in the sectors that matter most for upward mobility—business‑process outsourcing, IT‑enabled services, and routine cognitive work. These sectors powered income growth in India and the Philippines, and they are precisely where AI’s automation and augmentation pressures land first. The report stresses that lower exposure does not mean insulation: the structure of employment, the informality of labor markets, and slower task reinstatement all shape how adjustment unfolds. In many cases, the risk is not mass displacement but stalled upgrading.

The conclusion is that AI’s development impact hinges on absorptive capacity, not access. Electricity and compute form the physical floor; connectivity and digital public infrastructure make the technology locally useful; skills determine whether people can direct it; and institutions decide whether gains are captured or dissipated. Countries that build this stack—India with digital public infrastructure, Kenya with payments rails—convert AI into productivity and inclusion. Those that do not risk faster divergence. Any forecast of AI’s effect on an emerging economy is therefore a statement about these complements, and any strategy that ignores them is not a strategy but a guess.

title: The Southeast Asia Digital Productivity Shift: AI Adoption, Platformization, and the Rise of Hyper-Efficient Digital Services

detail.title: The Southeast Asia Digital Productivity Shift: AI Adoption, Platformization, and the Rise of Hyper-Efficient Digital Services
detail.abstract: Southeast Asia's digital decade is being filed as a productivity event. The public files split it into a matching layer and a production residual, and they do not occupy the same countries. In a population-weighted reading of World Bank indicators, 76 percent of people in the ASEAN-10 used the internet in 2023, against 3 percent in 2000. Mobile subscriptions reached 129 per 100 people. Fixed broadband reached 9. High-income broadband is 37. Google, Temasek, and Bain put digital-economy gross merchandise value at 305 billion dollars in 2025, from 40 billion in 2016. That is a platform clock. It is not labour productivity. We score ten ASEAN economies on three clocks. Platform: internet at or above 50 percent and mobile at or above 80 per 100. Stack: electricity at or above 90 percent and fixed broadband at or above 8 per 100. Efficiency: ICT service exports of at least 3 billion dollars, or at least 10 percent of service exports on a base of 1 billion. Eight countries clear the platform. Five clear the stack. Four clear efficiency. Two-Singapore and Malaysia-clear all three. They hold 6 percent of ASEAN's 699 million people and 38 billion of 52 billion dollars in recorded ICT service exports. Indonesia, the Philippines, and Cambodia hold 420 million people on a closed platform and an open wire. Thailand and Viet Nam have the wire and the factory; they do not have a recorded ICT-services residual. Myanmar and Lao PDR clear none. The Stanford AI Index 2026 puts generative-AI adoption in Singapore at 61 percent of the population, against 28 percent in the United States. Optimism in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Singapore exceeds 80 percent. Consumer AI is arriving where the super-app already sits. Hyper-efficient digital services are arriving where the stack and the export file already sit. Treating ASEAN as one digital tiger is how a 305 billion dollar GMV headline gets counted as a 6 percent population club.

title: External Employer Branding Activities: Typology Development via Integration of Information Amount and Content
affiliations: Stockton University

detail.title: External Employer Branding Activities: Typology Development via Integration of Information Amount and Content

publicationDetails.detailsText: Quarterly Review of Business Disciplines, Vol 10, Issue 3/4, Pp. 140-156, 2024

detail.abstract: An organization's employer branding activities strive to communicate to both external and internal stakeholders that it is a great place to work. This paper focuses on an organization's "external" employer branding activities (EEBAs)-recruitment messages used to attract job seekers in the external labor market. The competition for hiring skilled and qualified employees has increased over the years, and thus it is crucial for organizations to be able to attract job seekers and influence them in pursuing a position via appropriate EEBAs. While prior research has explored applicant attraction by considering separately the amount of information and attribute content in recruitment messages, this paper draws on marketing and consumer psychology literature to integrate these two related but theoretically distinct research streams and builds theory around four "external" employer branding activity (EEBA) types and their effectiveness. In addition, the feasibility of using different types of employer branding activities is discussed, based on industry, organization, and job-seeker characteristics.

title: Executive Work Experience and Strategic Financing: How Generalist CEOs Shape Debt Structure
affiliations: University of Essex,  EBS, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Xiamen University, Durham University Business School, Finance and Economics and Xiamen University

detail.title: Executive Work Experience and Strategic Financing: How Generalist CEOs Shape Debt Structure
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether the breadth of CEOs' work experience influences the concentration of firms' debt structure. CEOs with a greater variety of work experience are often referred to as generalist CEOs because they are likely to possess greater general managerial skills. We predict and document a negative relation between generalist CEOs and corporate debt concentration using a sample of S&P 1500 firms from 2001 to 2022. To address endogeneity, we employ propensity score matching, entropy balancing, and a difference-indifferences approach based on CEOs' sudden deaths as plausibly exogenous shocks. We further identify information disclosure as a key mechanism that mediates the negative relation between generalist CEOs and corporate debt concentration. Generalist CEOs, owing to greater career confidence, exhibit a stronger willingness to disclose information, which facilitates a more diversified debt structure by reducing information asymmetry with creditors. The negative relation between general managerial skills and debt concentration is more pronounced for firms with greater CEO power, tighter financial constraints, lower credit ratings, higher default risks, weaker management team ability, and when CFOs are also generalists. Overall, the evidence highlights how CEOs' work experience affect information disclosure and, in turn, firms' financing structure.

detail.abstract: Aggregate-share mean absolute error (MAE) is used in comparisons of discrete choice modeling approaches as evidence of external predictive validity. It is not sufficient evidence for that claim. Holdout validation is intended to protect against concluding that an apparent modeling advantage is real when it instead reflects overfit to the estimation data. Aggregate share error can fail that test. Different patterns of choice prediction can produce the same aggregate share forecast. Aggregate-share MAE is therefore disqualifying as sufficient comparative evidence of external predictive validity for choices. When the aggregate comparison is used to establish that broader conclusion, the inference is invalid.

title: The Thích Minh Tuệ Social-Media Phenomenon, 2024-2026: Decentralized Attention, Platform Ecology, and Value without Capture
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Thích Minh Tuệ Social-Media Phenomenon, 2024-2026: Decentralized Attention, Platform Ecology, and Value without Capture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-Funded

detail.abstract:
Thích Minh Tuệ’s rise from a little-known Vietnamese ascetic pilgrim to a national and transnational social-media phenomenon offers an unusual case of mass attention without centralized media production. He built no audience through an official account, promotional apparatus, institutional organization, or deliberate influencer strategy. Instead, a decentralized network of witnesses, livestreamers, travel vloggers, devotees, critics, news organizations, and commentary channels formed around his visible practice. This study tracks search and readership from January 2024 through July 2026 and reconstructs platform attention during the active view-generating period from April 2024 through July 2026 using Google Trends, Wikipedia readership, direct YouTube and TikTok measurements, sampled Facebook Reels, antagonistic-content discovery, and contemporary reporting. Independent measures agree on three phases: an extraordinary May–June 2024 national attention shock approximately 87 times the pre-viral baseline, a second transnational wave in early 2025, and a smaller but durable 2026 residual sustained by a decentralized creator ecosystem.

Search interest indexed the civil name “Lê Anh Tú” at only 2 against 100 for “Minh Tuệ” on a shared scale. The expanded YouTube inventory identifies 181 unique channels; antagonistic-vocabulary searches recovered 49 additional relevant channels largely missed by name-based discovery. A 72-account TikTok analytical sample and sampled Facebook Reels complete the platform picture. Under an explicit Facebook-Reels-parity assumption, two reconstruction methods place cumulative platform-counted consumption at approximately 8.5–11.1 billion views through July 2026. Across the full Facebook sensitivity analysis, the modeled envelope extends to approximately 13.7 billion. The July 2026 central estimate is approximately 90 million counted views per month. Zalo, X, Instagram, and Reddit are excluded from the headline estimate on separately stated methodological grounds. The case illustrates a decentralized attention paradox: the less the subject participated in the attention economy, the more extensively one formed around him. It also demonstrates value without capture, in which the focal subject generates attention while ownership, audience control, and much of the resulting monetization accrue to third parties.

Keywords: Thích Minh Tuệ; Lê Anh Tú; Vietnam; social media; attention economy; creator economy; platform ecology; TikTok; YouTube; Facebook; digital religion; Buddhism; dhutaṅga; decentralized attention; value without capture
